Lots of coordinating and problem-solving. It's surprisingly stressful sometimes, but I do enjoy it. There’s a new project I'm involved in, trying to streamline the whole process. It's quite technical, actually, involving some AI stuff. AI, is it? Goodness me. Sounds… complicated. Back in my day, streamlining involved a good filing cabinet and a strong cup of tea. You young people and your technology! I still can't work out how to use the telly properly, you know. I can help you with that, Mum. Honestly, it's not as scary as it looks. We can go through it together. It just needs a little bit of understanding. And speaking of technology, have you seen that new series everyone's talking about? "The Gilded Cage"? “The Gilded Cage”? No, haven’t seen it. Is it any good? Is it one of those dreadful things with lots of shouting and everyone running around?

Right, I’m tellin’ ya, this heat is somethin’ else! Proper meltin', isn't it? Makes ya want to just lie down in a puddle. And football... honestly, what  was  that penalty decision against England? Robbery, pure and simple! Oh, come on, Maisie. Don't start. It wasn’t  that  bad. They were under pressure, it was a clumsy tackle… plus, have you seen the state of the pitch? It's like playing on a farmer's field. And anyway, complaining about referees is a national sport in itself, isn’t it? Clumsy tackle? She practically took him out with her knee! And farmer's field?! It was rough, yeah, but a proper pitch it weren't, I'll give you that. Still, gutted. I reckon we should've had a free kick just before that. Proper dodgy. Anyway, how's the translation course goin'? Still wrestling with subjunctive moods? Subjunctive moods are my nemesis, definitely. Professor Dubois is relentless! He keeps saying it’s fundamental to understanding the nuance of French thought. It's just... so complicated! I spent an hour yesterday trying to translate a sentence about wanting to be a butterfly and ended up needing to Google half the words. It felt ridiculous. A butterfly? Really? That sounds dead fancy. My French was always terrible. Remember in sixth form, when I mixed up "crème" and "crème brûlée" in front of Madame Dubois? The look on her face… I still cringe about it. What are you studying, then, apart from the torture of verbs? Don’t remind me about Madame Dubois! I used to have nightmares about her grammar tests. I'm focusing a bit on scientific French, actually. It’s surprisingly interesting. Learning how to accurately translate research papers, and the nuances of describing methodology… Apparently, a slight shift in wording can completely change the interpretation of an experiment. Scientific French? Wow. That’s… actually really clever. Far cleverer than anything I could do. I'm still tryin' to get me head 'round this dissertation on Victorian literature. It's just endless descriptions of moorlands and gloomy estates, you know? Keeps rainin’ on the page, practically. I can imagine. Victorian literature is famously… atmospheric. Anything exciting happening with your band, The Northern Lights? I remember you saying you had a gig lined up. Yeah, we  had  a gig lined up. At The Rusty Mug, last weekend. But the drummer, Liam, he’s got himself into a right pickle.

Honestly, Brenda, I nearly jumped out of my skin this morning. Massive spider. Right on the bathroom mirror. Had eight eyes practically staring back at me. It was… unsettling. Eight eyes, you say? Bit dramatic, love, weren’t they? Probably just a garden spider. They do like a bit of damp, don’t they? I get ‘em in the shed all the time. Not bothered by ‘em, mind. Best leave ‘em alone – they eat the flies. Well, I  tried  to leave it alone. But it was so large! I ended up shooing it out the window with a magazine. Felt a bit barbaric, actually. I’m not normally squeamish, but those things... Bararic! Cor, you’re funny. I’ve had spiders the size of my hand come out of the washing machine. Didn’t give it a second thought. Just scooped ‘em up and chucked ‘em out. No magazine needed. You city folk, eh? Sensitive about a little spider. I suppose you have a point. I did grow up in Boston, remember? A lot more… hushed. Not the same rough-and-tumble countryside you get around Peterborough. Though, speaking of hushed, we’ve had a mouse problem this past month. Small one, but persistent. Keeps scuttling around at night. Mice, eh? That's a right nuisance. I had a terrible time with 'em a few years back. Got right into the loft, they did. Little blighters. Had to get a professional in to sort ‘em out. Traps didn’t do a thing, honestly. They’re smarter than you think. You tried putting out some cheese? Of course! And peanut butter. And chocolate. It’s like it prefers Cheerios. Drives me mad. I’ve blocked up every hole I can find. Thinking about getting one of those ultrasonic repellents. Ultrasonic, you say? Waste of money, that is. They get used to it. Honestly, a good, old-fashioned cat’s your best bet. My Doris, she’s brilliant at keeping the mice at bay. Though she does bring ‘em in sometimes… half-dead... right onto the doorstep. Oh, that’s even worse! At least if it's outside… I have a rather lovely pair of robins in my garden. They’ve nested in the climbing rose. Absolutely delightful to watch them feeding their chicks. Robins? Lovely. We've got loads of blackbirds in my garden. Cheeky little things, they are. Always nicking the worms I put out for the robins.

Please, please do sit down, Nesta. It’s lovely to finally meet you properly. I feel like we’ve been connected through anecdotes and phone calls for ages, but never actually  in person . It's so nice you made the journey up from Bristol. It was a bit of a trek, love, but worth it. It's always wonderful to put a face to a name, isn't it? And to finally meet your family, really. Your mother… well, I’ve heard so much about her. A remarkable woman, apparently. She was. Still is, in a way. It's… difficult, losing someone so suddenly. The diagnosis came out of nowhere, you know? A rare form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Ever heard of it? Creutzfeldt-Jakob...sounds dreadful. No, I can’t say I have. What is it, then? Is it… contagious? No, thankfully not. It's a prion disease, a neurological disorder. It attacks the brain. It deteriorates you so quickly. She was perfectly fine in August, playing with her grandchildren, and then… by November, she was gone. It was horribly swift and… brutal. The memory is still quite raw, I must admit. Oh, dear, that's heartbreaking. It sounds utterly cruel. Losing someone so quickly… it never gets easier, does it? I lost my husband, Dai, a few years back. Lung cancer. A long battle, that one. Gave us time to say goodbye, but still… leaves a hole, a big one. I can only imagine. I’m dreadfully sorry, Nesta. It's lovely you're here now, though. Distraction is welcome, I think. So, you were a school teacher, you said? What subject did you teach? Oh, just general subjects. Mostly English and history, a bit of geography sprinkled in. I taught at a primary school in Bristol for… oh, it must have been nearly thirty years. Loved it, I did. Seeing those little faces light up when they understood something… that was the best part. I miss it, truth be told. Retirement’s lovely, don't get me wrong, but sometimes I feel a bit… adrift. I completely understand that feeling. I'm a teacher as well, though secondary. History, particularly. I’m at a school on the outskirts of Stevenage. It's… hectic, to say the least. Always something going on. But rewarding, mostly. Although, these days, I mostly feel like a referee and a pastoral advisor disguised as a history teacher.

Honestly, this is just glorious, isn’t it? The air smells…clean. Like proper countryside, not just the edges of Norwich. It’s a world away from marking essays. You know, you relax almost instantly when you leave the university. It's remarkable. Did you see that kestrel just now? Hovering over the field. I did! Spectacular. Though I also noticed that ridiculous high-voltage power line slicing right through the view. Ruins the aesthetic a bit, doesn’t it? Seems a bit…insensitive, really, blasting that through such a lovely landscape. They’ve been there for ages, love. Before most of the wildlife got used to them. Though, I suppose you’re right, it's not exactly a picturesque addition. Reminds me of that hot air balloon we saw over Cambridge a few years back. They looked so tiny against that line. Oh, that was brilliant, wasn't it? Such a visual. I’ve always wanted to go up in one. Just once. Imagine the view from up there, beating even these fields. Want to do it for our anniversary? That would be incredible. Costs a fortune though, doesn’t it? Last time I checked, it was pushing £300 a head. And Buster deserves a treat afterwards. He's been such a good boy on this walk. He absolutely does. Maybe we can cut back somewhere else? I could postpone that new pair of boots I was eyeing up. They were rather extravagant, I admit. Don't sacrifice your boots for a hot air balloon, darling. We'll find the money. We’ve got a bit tucked away, haven’t we? Remember that bonus I got last Christmas? Vaguely. You were saving it for…something mysterious, as usual. A little rainy-day fund. Turns out, a hot air balloon qualifies as a 'rainy day' experience! Seriously though, I've been putting some aside. We could even look at booking a camping weekend somewhere picturesque afterward. Proper get away from everything. Camping! Oh, I do love camping. But remember that disastrous trip to the Lake District? The rain for three days straight, the leaky tent… And you kept insisting we could dry our socks on the campfire. They ended up smelling like smoke and damp wool. They did! But still, the stars were incredible. We need to invest in a decent tent this time. And maybe some waterproof trousers. And a slightly less optimistic attitude towards the weather.

Honestly, that was a scorcher! I thought Solihull was supposed to be mild this time of year. July usually brings a bit more… restraint, weather-wise. Restraint? You’re a Brit, love, you're speaking like you're expecting blizzards in August! It’s proper summer, this. Reminds me a bit of summers back in Leeds, actually. Though we always had a bit more rain, truth be told. Yorkshire weather, you know? I’ve only ever visited Leeds briefly. It seemed… vibrant. A bit different from Hertfordshire, which is lovely, but… quieter. I teach languages at a school in Birmingham, actually. How about yourself? Still battling those fitness fanatics? Aye, still at it. Area manager for "Peak Performance Gyms" now. Six gyms under my belt, across Brum and Warwickshire. Keeps me on my toes, that’s for sure. Managing people is a right challenge, though. Far more complicated than getting them to do bicep curls. I can imagine! Dealing with teenagers as a teacher is challenging enough – getting thirty of them to simultaneously conjugate a verb is a feat of management in itself. Though, arguably, fewer dropped weights. I’ve just finished a postgraduate in Applied Linguistics, actually. Thought it might give me some new insights into teaching, particularly with the diverse needs of my students. Postgraduate, eh? Smart lass. I left school at eighteen, Sixth Form. Never really considered uni. Practical things, you know? Gotta earn a living. Though, I often wonder if I missed out. What made you go back to studyin', then? Honestly, a bit of a mid-life crisis, perhaps? No, not really! Just a feeling that I wanted to deepen my understanding of language acquisition. It's fascinating – how the brain processes new sounds and structures. I've been experimenting with some new coaching techniques in the classroom, drawing on principles from sports coaching. Giving students really specific, actionable feedback, rather than just general praise. Seems to be working a treat. Coaching techniques in a classroom… Now that’s a clever idea. We use a lot of that in the gyms. Breaking down exercises, micro-adjustments, positive reinforcement... it's all about incremental improvements. You ever read "Mindset" by Carol Dweck? I have! Absolutely brilliant. The whole growth mindset concept really resonated with me. It's so crucial for language learning – the idea that intelligence isn’t fixed, that ability can be developed through dedication and hard work.

Right then, that’s the kettle on. Arthur, love, could you pop the biscuits out? They're in the tin, top shelf. And Liam, put your feet up, boy, you're lookin' like you’re about to slump into the carpet. Alright, alright. Just tired, Miss Davies. Had a proper busy day with the A-levels. Double geometry, you know? Geometry, eh? Never did understand that stuff. Tried to learn it for Mr. Buckley at school, but it were like a foreign language. All them pointy bits and angles… gave me a right headache. Aye, Elsie's right. Remember tryin' to draw a parallelogram, Elsie? Looked more like a squashed cat! Mr. Buckley, he just shook his 'ead. Oh, I remember. You were determined, though, weren't you, Arthur? Nearly ripped the paper. Liam, don't you go gettin' ideas about ripping paper! It’s important to persevere, but not to destroy the furniture! Yeah, Mum. It’s just... some of it feels completely pointless, you know? Like, when am I ever gonna need to calculate the area of a rhombus? Pointless, is it? Well, it teaches you to think, lad. To look at things in a different way. That’s important, that is. Even if you’re just plottin’ where to plant yer tomatoes. Elsie's got a point there, boy. It's about the thinkin'. Just like rememberin' to look both ways afore you cross the road. Geometry or no geometry, it's all about thinkin'. Exactly! It’s about problem-solving, Liam. Something you'll need no matter what you do. Now, Arthur, are you settin’ the table for tea? I made a Victoria sponge today. Thought you’d both appreciate that. Victoria sponge? Result! That’s proper good. Ooh, a Victoria sponge! Now you're talkin'! Better than all them pointy bits and angles, that’s for sure. Aye, Elsie's fussin' over that sponge again. Always does. Best sponge in Malton, I reckon. Don’t be daft, Arthur! It's a simple recipe, really. Though Elsie here does make a proper job of it. Now, Liam, are you helping your grandad with the table, or just planning your attack on the cake? Alright, alright. Comin', Grandad. Just… maybe after one quick peek? . He’s got yer eyes, lass. Always lookin’ for a shortcut to a good slice of cake. Remember that time you tried to make a sponge, Elsie, and it sank right to the bottom of the tin?

Aye, this thing’s got us round the houses again, hasn't it? Honestly, these satnavs… they think they’re smarter than me, they do. I swear, last week it tried to send me down a farmer’s field! Darlington, you know, we're not exactly flush with Michelin-starred restaurants, but I’d still expect a decent route to a gig. It’s being a bit over-enthusiastic with the scenic route, I’ll grant you that. But look, we’re almost there. And besides, that detour past Thorngill Quarry was rather picturesque, wasn’t it? Good stone, that. Reminds me of the dry stone walling workshop I went to last spring… Picturesque? It was full of lorries and sheep! And I nearly bottomed out on that little bridge. My poor Fiesta... she's seen better days. Speaking of seeing better days, how’s your shoulder feeling? Still twinging? Remember you nearly pulled it trying to wrestle that sheep at your cousin's farm? It’s manageable, thanks. A bit achey after this driving, but manageable. The physio says to be careful with lifting. It's frustrating, though, can't get back to the climbing wall just yet. Though, at least it gives me more time to work on the new collection. Got a new poem finished just this morning – inspired, oddly enough, by a robin I saw in the garden. A robin, eh? You’ll be writing odes to slugs next! You and your poetry. Still, keep at it. Someone’s gotta record all these little moments, even if it’s through a lens of melancholic introspection. So, about this gig - are they still needing you to soundcheck? I'm worried about being late for Maureen's wedding rehearsal. They are, yes, but I’ve told them we might be slightly delayed. Maureen won’t mind, will she? She's probably got a spreadsheet dedicated to the exact placement of every floral arrangement. Remember last year at Sarah's wedding - the debacle with the table settings? Don’t remind me! Poor Sarah! She spent a fortune on those napkins. And then Uncle Barry decided to ‘rearrange’ them for ‘better aesthetics’… Honestly, some people have no sense. Are you sure you have enough wool for that blanket you're knitting for the ceilidh? It’s coming up quick, you know. Yes, I think so. I picked up a good supply from that little shop in Appleby last week.

Honestly, Chloe was  shocking  yesterday. Showed up to the site visit in those heels! Heels! On a building site! I nearly choked on my own breath. Chloe, eh? Always a dramatic entrance. Though, I suppose it's a bit of a Chloe trademark. Did she at least manage to avoid any concrete-related mishaps? Barely. She tripped over a cable and nearly took out poor Mr. Henderson. He’s still muttering about safety regulations. I swear, sometimes I question her commitment to being an architect. She’s young. And definitely has a flair for the… theatrical. Remember when she tried to redesign the town hall using only cushions and fairy lights? Oh god, don't remind me! It was… something else. Right, let's order. I'm ravenous. I need a full English. Sausage, bacon, eggs, the works. I’ll have the granola and yogurt, I think. Something a little less… artery-clogging. You’re going to regret that later when you're drafting plans. Speaking of which, how are you finding that university project brief? The communal living one? It’s tricky. They want something sustainable, affordable, and beautiful. All at once! It feels like an impossible brief. The client wants these dense, modular units, but also insists they have a "feeling of openness and connection." It's a contradiction in terms. I know the feeling. It's the classic architectural tightrope walk. Have you thought about incorporating vertical gardens to give that sense of openness while still maximising space? And what about a shared central courtyard? I’ve been playing with the courtyard idea. It’s definitely promising. But the budget is tiny. We're basically building with air and good intentions at this point. What about you? Still stressed about the Henderson account? You seemed a bit off at the site yesterday. Yeah. It's Mark. He's really struggling. He’s started missing deadlines, and his designs are… lacking. It's not like him. He's always been so meticulous. Have you spoken to him about it? Sometimes just having a chat can make a difference. I did. He just said he feels completely overwhelmed. The pressure to impress Henderson's firm is getting to him. He keeps saying he's not good enough. It's a load of rubbish, of course, but he can't seem to shake the feeling. It’s awful, isn’t it?

Right, love, put your feet up. Long day at the office, was it? You look a bit knackered. Earl Grey, or builders? Builders, definitely. Brain's fried, Mum. Honestly, the parking in town today… it was a nightmare. Double yellow lines everywhere, people cutting each other off… it was utter chaos. Oh, the joys of Grantham traffic. You know, it’s really not getting any better, is it? Used to be able to zip through in ten minutes, now it’s…well, it's a lottery. Did you see that bloke trying to pull out in front of a lorry near the Co-op? Honestly, I nearly had a heart attack just watching it from the car. Seriously! There was one woman, she just  stopped  in the middle of the road to let someone out. Completely blocked everything! People were honking, it was a right palaver. I'm starting to think I need to cycle to work. Cycle? Darling, it’s freezing! Besides, then you'd be battling the buses. No, it’s a losing battle. People just… they don’t understand road etiquette anymore, do they? They think it's a free-for-all. Remember when Dad used to lecture us about yielding and indicating? Nobody does that now. Oh, Dad. He'd have a field day. He'd be out there, waving his arms and yelling at people to use their mirrors. Speaking of Dad, has he booked his eye test yet? You know he needs to. I’ve been on at him, haven't I? He’s being stubborn, as usual. Says he can see perfectly fine. Honestly, it's like talking to a brick wall sometimes. He’ll get round to it, eventually. How was Sarah's birthday dinner? Did you have a good time? It was lovely, actually. She’s getting so grown up, isn’t she? Nearly twenty! We went to that Italian place on Westgate Street - the one we've been meaning to try. Food was amazing. Liam was there too, of course. Liam! How is he? Still playing the guitar constantly? Pretty much. He’s thinking about auditioning for a band. Actually, Sarah says they’re playing at The Venue next Saturday. She was wondering if you and Dad would like to go? Oh, that sounds lovely! Next Saturday, you say? Let me check the diary. . Yes, yes, that actually works! We’d love to go, darling.

Right, so I’ve had another look at this job description for the Digital Content Editor at Midlands Radio. It's… a lot, isn't it? They really want someone who can do everything. Social media, podcast editing, writing snappy headlines, commissioning freelance writers… Honestly, it sounds exhausting. Exhausting, aye, but brilliant potential, love. Think about it - Midlands Radio! It’s got a good reputation, and being a Digital Content Editor would put you right at the heart of it. You’ve been moaning about wanting more creative control at your current job for ages. This is your chance to grab it. I know, I know. It’s just… I’m not sure I’m selling myself effectively. My experience is more focused on language teaching – obviously a completely different field. How do I even frame that in a way that's relevant? "Proficient in grammar and sentence structure – useful for crafting compelling online content"? Feels a bit… pathetic. Don't be daft! It's not pathetic at all. Think about communication, love. That’s what you’re doing as a teacher, isn't it? Breaking down complex ideas, tailoring your delivery to different audiences, engaging people and keeping them interested. That’s practically the same skillset, just applied to language learning instead of radio content. Highlight those transferable skills. “Experience creating engaging educational materials and communications for diverse audiences.” See? Sounds much better. Okay, you've got a point. It’s about reframing, isn't it? I'm so used to academic language, I’m falling into the trap of being overly formal. So, what about this bit about commissioning freelance writers? I’ve never done that before. Should I just say I’m ‘willing to learn’? Sounds a bit weak. Don’t say "willing to learn" – that’s interview suicide. Instead, talk about your experience managing students and giving them feedback. You've essentially guided people to improve their writing, haven't you? You've given constructive criticism, set expectations, and helped them meet deadlines. That’s all commissioning, just with a different title. You can even mention you've collaborated with colleagues on curriculum development – that demonstrates project management skills. That's clever. I hadn’t thought of it like that. Oh, and this section about analytics! I have absolutely no experience with social media analytics. Should I lie? Absolutely not! Lying will backfire spectacularly. Be honest. Say something like, “While my direct experience with social media analytics is limited, I’m a quick learner and eager to develop these skills.

Right, so, let's actually nail down some specifics about this pottery studio thing. "Coastal Clay Creations" – still like the name? It's got a nice ring to it, I think. Coastal Clay Creations is perfect, yes. Catchy, and it really reflects what I’m imagining. Though, I'm still having mini-panic spirals about the whole thing, you know? Leaving teaching...it's a huge leap. Twenty years! Twenty-two, actually. And massive respect for sticking it out that long. But you've been talking about wanting to do this for… well, years. Remember that pottery class we took in Cornwall? You were completely hooked. And you’ve been practicing relentlessly ever since. This isn't a sudden whim, love. I know, I know. Logically, I  know  that. It just feels like I’m jumping off a cliff without a parachute. What if nobody wants to buy my bowls? What if I’m terrible at marketing? What if I run out of money in six months? Those are all perfectly reasonable worries. But we'll work through them. Let’s start with the marketing. I've been doing a bit of research online – Etsy, Instagram, local markets... we need a solid online presence, definitely. I’m happy to help with the techy bits; setting up the shop, photography… that's my comfort zone. That would be wonderful, honestly. I have zero confidence in my online skills. I can make a gorgeous glaze, but a website? Forget about it. And markets… the thought of standing there all day, trying to sell things... We don’t have to start with a big market initially. Smaller craft fairs, maybe even pop-ups in cafes. Something low-pressure to test the waters. And we'll get you comfortable with it. How about we look at some craft fairs in the area near here and see what the vibe is like? Okay, that’s manageable. The pottery itself… I'm thinking I’d like to offer workshops too. Something a little different. Like, ‘Coastal Inspired Pottery’ - focusing on sea-themed decorations, that kind of thing. Appeal to the tourists, you see. Brilliant! That’s a great idea – adds an income stream and builds a community around the studio. It's got potential for some real growth. Have you thought about renting a space, or starting at home initially? Home is appealing to start with, financially.

Honestly, Nana, I'm feeling utterly useless. Another day, another pile of toys to pick up, another episode of Peppa Pig. Finn's just… full of energy. It's exhausting. And you know what? I’m starting to feel like  he’s  engaging with you two more than he is with me. Beard! Papa, beard tickle! Ah, Finn. You've got an eye for the finer things, my boy. A good beard is a sign of wisdom, you know. Though mine could use a trim, I suppose. Margaret, dear, are you alright? You look a bit pallid. Did you have enough of the shepherd's pie? Food delivery was a nightmare this week, wasn’t it? Absolutely swamped. Pallid? Nonsense, Arthur! It’s simply the strain of seeing another school announce it’s oversubscribed. Honestly, it's disgraceful. My granddaughter in Glasgow has been offered a place at  three  different schools, and none of them are within walking distance. They’re talking about putting her on a bus for an hour each way! An hour! At seven years old. Exactly! It’s ridiculous. Honestly, I'm terrified Finn won't even get a place at the local primary. They’re bursting at the seams. And it's all well and good the Council talking about building new housing, but the schools can’t keep up. It's like they're breeding families and then forgetting about educating them. It's a national crisis, Margaret, truly. We built so much during the post-war boom, catering to a growing population. Now? It’s all catch-up. And the problem's compounded by the influx, isn’t it? I read an article just yesterday about the sheer number of Polish families moving to Cambridge. Good people, mind you, and vital for the economy, but puts even  more  pressure on the schools. Don't start with the 'influx' again, Arthur. It’s a simplistic view. People are seeking opportunity, safety… things we take for granted. And they're filling jobs that locals often don't want. It's not as black and white as you make it out to be. Sorry, what were we saying about schools? Finn just drew on the table with a marker. Again. I swear, sometimes I feel like I'm just a glorified marker remover. A very important marker remover, dear. You’re doing a wonderful job. Speaking of jobs, have you thought about doing some online tutoring, Margaret?

Honestly, Brenda, I still can’t quite get my head around that referendum result. Even now, years on, I wonder what would have happened if… well, you know. Aye, love, don’t we all. You can’t go back, can you? It's just… the way it all unfolded. Remember all the passionate debates at sixth form? Half the class were convinced one way, the other half the opposite. Absolute chaos! Mr. Davies nearly lost his hair trying to keep order. Oh, yes! Mr. Davies! He did have a temper. I remember Sarah Millington, she was  so  pro-Europe. She practically wore a flag. And poor Mark Bailey, utterly convinced we'd be better off on our own. He spent weeks researching trade deals. Mark Bailey! Goodness, where  is  Mark Bailey now? Last I heard he was working down in Bristol, wasn't he? Still obsessed with saving the pound, I bet! Reminds me, I saw young David at the football match Saturday. Little mite's grown up so fast. Playing midfield, apparently. That’s lovely! Little David’s already better than I ever was. I’ve been meaning to get back to the piano, you know. It’s been gathering dust. I used to be quite good, remember? Before the marketing and proofing took over completely. You were brilliant! Remember that recital you gave at Sutton Coldfield Grammar? Mrs. Peterson was practically swooning. You should get back to it! Keeps the brain active, doesn't it? Speaking of active, have you heard about that new walking group starting up in Fradley? The one organised by the village hall? No, I haven't. Might be something to look into. I'm feeling a bit stiff these days, need to move more. Though, with little Leo arriving, finding the time will be… tricky. How’s Emily coping? Still exhausted? Terribly, bless her. Absolutely shattered, but over the moon, of course. She says bringing a baby into the world is like being hit by a bus, then having to run a marathon. And Paul’s been a star, taking on a lot of the night feeds. That's wonderful. Paul always was a good egg. We should pop over and see them next week, bring a little something for Leo. I’ve been meaning to knit him a blanket. That would be lovely. It’s just… parking is a nightmare around their place.

Och, this is grand, isn’t it? Proper peace and quiet for a change. Away from the digital din for a wee bit. Though I’m battling a Twitter storm myself, to be fair. A Twitter storm, eh? Let me guess, some disgruntled blogger taking umbrage with the latest comms campaign for the university? Happens every other Tuesday, doesn’t it? Near enough. It's about the alumni fundraiser. Seems someone’s decided it's exploitative, because it features a picture of a former student who's faced hardship. The usual online pile-on. I’m trying to navigate it diplomatically, but it's a right bother. Social media, aye, a tool for connection, but also a magnet for misery. Aye, it’s a fickle beast. I'm finding myself using it more and more, though. Not in a 'likes' chasing way, mind you. Mostly for sharing departmental news, stuff about upcoming lectures, that kind of thing. We're trying to build a more robust online presence for the education department. Smart move. We considered it at the comms office, but the engagement levels are invariably so shallow. People scroll past, rarely actually  reading  anything. It feels like shouting into a void half the time. Do you find students engaging with it? Some do. It depends on the platform, I suppose. Instagram seems to work best for the visual stuff – showcasing student projects, a peek into lab life. Twitter’s more for announcements and quick updates, mostly. TikTok… I’m still terrified of TikTok. My students keep urging me to join, but the thought of doing a dance challenge fills me with dread. Och, you’d be a disaster! Don’t even go there. I tried Reels once, for a “day in the life” thing. It ended up looking like a particularly awkward, poorly lit home movie. Deleted it quicker than you can say ‘Edinburgh Fringe.’ Good call. I stick to what I know. Though, I did have a rather peculiar encounter on LinkedIn the other day… Someone contacted me, claiming to be a recruiter for a university in Dubai. Offering me a Director of Studies role with a ludicrous salary. Dubai?! Now that’s impressive. You thinking of applying? Honestly? No. It felt… off. The language was a bit too enthusiastic, and the profile of the recruiter was suspiciously bare. I suspect it was a scam. Reported it, of course.

Honestly, I need a full body massage. This weekend was… intense. Like, non-stop intense. Three stakeholder meetings, two presentations, and a crisis with the printer that almost made me cry. Oh, you poor thing! Sounds brutal. Glad you’re back though. Smells like I managed to salvage dinner despite your absence. Chicken korma, your favourite. You absolute legend! You know the way to my heart. Seriously, I was staring down the barrel of instant noodles tonight. How did you even have time? You were on shift all weekend, right? Yeah, pretty much. Double shifts Saturday and Sunday. But honestly, I was so bored with the usual hospital drama, cooking something decent was a welcome distraction. Mrs. Henderson tried to feed me a biscuit again, I swear. She thinks I'm starving. Oh, bless her. Still saving biscuit offerings for you, is she? That woman! So, anything actually  interesting  happen at work? Besides the biscuit situation? Actually, yeah. We had a new patient admitted, Daniel. Seems like a really lovely young guy, struggling with anxiety and depression, triggered by… well, a messy breakup, classic. He’s being really open though, which is a good sign. That’s good. It takes courage to be that vulnerable. Are you assigned to his case? For now, yeah. It’s early days, but I'm hoping to build a good rapport with him. It’s that initial trust that makes all the difference. What about Liam? Still being…Liam? Don’t even start. He ‘forgot’ to confirm the catering for the launch party  again . Like, how do you forget something that crucial? I spent a solid hour on the phone this morning trying to sort it out. I swear, sometimes I think he does it just to wind me up. He's testing your project coordinating abilities, darling. A trial by fire. Honestly, you need to give him an ultimatum. "Catering sorted, or you’re making tea for everyone for a month.” I considered it. But then I imagined him making lukewarm tea and being all sulky. Not worth the aggravation. Besides, I need him for the phase two rollout next month. It's just… frustrating. It’s not like I’m asking him to climb Mount Everest. I get it. You’re carrying the whole project on your shoulders. You deserve a medal. And a very large glass of wine. Which, incidentally, is ready.

That was a lovely roast, Sarah. Really lovely. Proper Sunday dinner this is. Better than anything I managed to rustle up back in the day, that's for sure. Though, to be fair, 'rustling up' wasn't really my forte, was it? More of a 'delegating' kind of man, me. Glad you enjoyed it, Dad. Mum really outdid herself. It’s nice to have everyone together like this, isn’t it? Especially with Uncle George coming next week. Are you looking forward to seeing him? Absolutely, darling. He'll be chattering a mile a minute as usual. Though goodness me, remembering his voice… sometimes it's so different from how he is now. A bit… strained, you know? Like he's putting on an act. Does anyone else notice that? Notice what, exactly, Margaret? George putting on an act? He’s always been a bit of a showman, hasn't he? Remember that dreadful karaoke night in Bournemouth back in… oh, what was it, '98? He tried to do ‘Bohemian Rhapsody’… bless his heart. I’ve only heard the stories, Dad! Trying to imagine Uncle George doing ‘Bohemian Rhapsody’ is… a lot. Mum, what about George’s voice? Do you ever think it sounds odd? It's not just the karaoke, love. It’s deeper than that. It's his default tone. Used to be much richer, more… resonant. Now it's like it’s being forced. Almost as if he’s trying to project, to sound louder than he feels. Perhaps it’s the medication? Medication? What medication are we talking about? He never mentioned anything to me. He’s been on those painkillers for his back, Dad. Remember when he slipped on the ice last Christmas? He said the pain was excruciating. Mum, do you know if those could affect his voice? They could be a contributing factor, I suppose. But I think it’s more than that. I worry about him, you know? He's always been so independent, and I suspect he's struggling more than he lets on. We need to be extra attentive when he's here next week. Attentive, yes. Offer him a cuppa, tell him he looks well... the usual. Don’t want to fuss him too much, mind you. He hates a fuss. Dad, he’s our brother! We  should  fuss him a bit. And we need to make sure he has everything he needs.

Right then, Arthur. Another evening, another wrestling match with the subjunctive. Honestly, it's like they  want  to confuse you. They could’ve just, you know, had one tense. Is that really too much to ask? Now, now, Brenda. Don’t get yourself in a right state. Spanish is a glorious language, it’s just…complex. Remember what the bloke said at that evening class? Something about the romance of the irregular verbs? Romance, he called it! I call it a linguistic minefield! I spent an hour trying to decipher a sentence about a cat chasing a mouse. An hour! I’m a teacher, for goodness sake! I teach English to people who  want  to learn! This is supposed to be enjoyable, not a test of endurance. Liverpool lasses have been through harder things, and they didn't have to conjugate adverbs along the way! You’re just being dramatic, Brenda. You’ve always been a bit…theatrical. Look, when I was learning French in school – and that was a disaster, let’s be honest – my teacher used to say, ‘don’t translate word-for-word, think about the  meaning .’ Maybe you’re getting bogged down in the grammar. Easy for you to say, Arthur. You’re a natural linguist, remember? Picked up bits of French just from watching telly. I’m having to consciously  work  at it. I think my learning style is all wrong for this. I need more immersion, maybe. Like those language holidays they advertise. Portugal wouldn’t do, would it? They speak Portuguese, don't they? Spain, then. You could go to Barcelona. You’d get a bit of Catalan mixed in with the Castilian, wouldn’t you? That’s fascinating, really. All those languages coexisting. My nephew’s wife is from Catalonia. She says it's a constant negotiation between the two – speaking Castillian when her family visit from Madrid, Catalan at home. It’s a case of pragmatism, isn’t it? It is, isn't it? Clever, though. Imagine having two languages running around in your head all the time. Though, I can see how it might get confusing. I can barely keep track of my shopping list, let alone two entirely different linguistic systems! I was reading about Esperanto, you know. That planned language. Seemed simpler, somehow. Esperanto? Never took to that. Too artificial for me. It lacked…flavour. Proper languages evolve, don’t they?

Right, this is… a lot. Dad, seriously, how much paperwork  do  you accumulate? It's like a small archive in here. Well, someone’s gotta keep track of things, doesn’t there, Ben? You youngsters, you just put everything on the cloud. It's not always reliable, you know. Remember that outage last year? Nearly cost me a fortune with the broadband. Valid point, but this  is  bordering on hoarding. We need to scan these, at least the important stuff. I can set up the scanner in the living room; it's quicker than rummaging through the loft. Is there anything in here absolutely vital we need to keep in paper form? Like, birth certificates or wills? Birth certificates are okay, I think, originals. Wills definitely. Bank statements… Hmm. Most of these are old anyway, pre-online banking. You know, I miss the days of just going into the branch and having a proper chat with the manager. This online stuff, it’s impersonal. Yeah, I get that. So, banking statements – scan the pre-2010 ones? And wills… yes, those are staying put. Anything about investments? Remember you were talking about that share portfolio? Ah, yes. There are a few letters about that. Let's flag those. By the way, did you see Kelly Brook's in the paper the other day? Still looks smashing. Dad! Seriously? We're sorting through your financial history and you're thinking about Kelly Brook? Well, a man can think about something nice, can’t he? Keeps me young. Anyway, related to the financial stuff, I’ve got a letter about a revised direct debit. Need you to have a look at that; it seems a bit high. Right, let's put Kelly Brook on hold. Direct debit. Okay. You know, this would be a perfect project for a corpus linguistics study. "The evolution of financial correspondence: A comparative analysis of paper-based and digital documentation." Corpus… what now? You and your posh words, Ben. Sounds like a right faff. It's basically looking at a large collection of texts – like these letters – to analyse patterns in language. I could compare the language used to explain banking terms in letters from the 80s to the language used in online banking interfaces. It’s revealing how much simpler they used to be! No jargon. Sounds a bit pointless, if you ask me. I just want to pay my bills!

Honestly, this petrol price is  criminal . Criminal, I tell ya! Used to be able to fill up for a fiver, now it's like…twenty quid! And for what? So some bloke in a suit can buy another yacht? Dramatic as ever, Liv. It's annoying, yeah, but twenty quid isn't  that  bad, is it? And you know, there's a correlation. Demand, supply, geopolitical instability… Geopolitical instability! Don't start me on that. Just saying, it’s daylight robbery. And all these fancy petrol station forecourts, too. Sells posh sandwiches and artisan coffee now. Used to be just a sticky bacon roll if you were lucky. No loyalty points worth a toss either. Well, the forecourts  have  improved. Less chance of your windscreen wipers getting snapped off by a rogue shopping trolley now, at least. And those coffee machines are pretty decent. You did like that flat white we got at the one near Cambridge last week. Alright, alright. The flat white  was  good. But that doesn’t excuse the overall cost! It’s costing us a fortune to get up and down, isn’t it? And you’re driving like a maniac, I swear. A maniac? I’m maintaining a perfectly legal speed. Just…efficient. This road can be a bit boring, you know. Got to keep things lively. Anyway, you were saying about petrol prices? I was! And that reminds me...did you see that biker gang parked up at the services back near Peterborough? All leathers and chrome. Proper intimidating lot. Vaguely. I saw a few bikes. Didn’t really pay them much attention. Were they, like, Hells Angels or something? Nah, didn't look like that. More…rough and ready. Big bikes, though. Massive. One of them had a sidecar with a little dog in it! A tiny Pomeranian! I nearly choked laughing. A Pomeranian in a sidecar? That’s brilliant! Opposites attract, I suppose. Imagine the conversation they must have. "Right, Winston, let's go terrorize the motorway!" Exactly! It was surreal. Makes you think, doesn't it? They're roaring about on these powerful machines, all serious and intense, then they’re popping to the services for a biscuit with their little fluffy pal. It’s a world I don't really understand, to be honest. I mean, I appreciate engineering – the mechanics of the bikes, the performance…but the lifestyle? The whole image?

Right, so, the coaching sessions. How did they go this week, love? Did Mr. Davies push you hard? Yeah, alright. He made us do a lot of volleys. Like,  a lot . My arm feels like it's going to fall off. Volleys are important though, aren’t they? Keeps you on your toes. Don’t complain, you’re not exactly Federer yet. Easy for you to say, Dad. You haven’t been hitting them for two hours straight. And he kept shouting "Aggressive! Aggressive!" Like I can just  will  myself to be aggressive. He's just trying to get you thinking strategically, darling. Think about where you want the ball to go, anticipate your opponent's move. That's part of the aggressive play. Less just bashing the ball, more controlled power. Exactly. Remember when I was playing in that local league tournament back in '98? I was beating a chap who was clearly much better than me, right? But he was getting complacent. Just gently lobbing the ball over the net. So, I started to anticipate, and I just... ripped a forehand down the line. Game, set, match. All about seizing those opportunities. Seriously, Dad? '98? That’s prehistoric. Hey! That was a good tournament. I even got a trophy! It was a rather garish shade of gold, if I remember correctly… somewhere in the loft. The point is, tennis isn’t just about strength. It's about smarts, too. He’s right, you know. It’s like marketing, really. You can have the most brilliant product in the world, but if you don't know  how  to market it, nobody's going to buy it. Anticipate the customer's needs, target your messaging… you see the parallel? Mum, are you going to start explaining tennis through marketing now? Well, it's all connected, isn't it? Strategy, analysis… It's transferable skills! She’ll find a way to relate everything to her marketing, won’t she? Anyway, did you watch the Djokovic-Alcaraz match on Sunday? Incredible stuff. The sheer athleticism... Yeah, it was good. Alcaraz seemed to be struggling with the heat towards the end. Djokovic is just… relentless. It’s almost boring how good he is. Don’t be ridiculous! Relentless  and  brilliant. He’s a master tactician. That serve return… simply phenomenal. He reads your intentions before you even hit the ball. I thought Alcaraz showed great composure though, considering how young he is.

Right, this is boss, Mum. Proper boss. You've outdone yourself this year. Though… these napkins are weird. They look like… well, like Dad’s underpants. Don't you start, Liam! Your dad bought them. Said they were “festive.” Honestly, men and their senses of humour… They  are  a bit much, aren’t they? Anyone else thinking the same? They are odd, yeah. But kinda funny. Though I’m not sure I want to wipe my mouth with something resembling… well, you know. How's uni, Liam? Still drowning in essays? Nah, Christmas break, remember? That's what it's for. No essays until the New Year. Although, I was just telling my mates the other day about how bizarre Christmas is here. They’re all proper jealous. Jealous of  what , lad? The novelty underwear napkins? No! Of the whole thing! The turkey, the presents, the telly… they’re used to celebrating with tamales and stuff. It’s a right culture clash, see? They can’t get their heads around the wishbone tradition. Honestly, I had to explain it like I was teaching a toddler. Wishbones are lovely, aren't they? Always brought me luck. Remember when your Dad and I used to pull them as kids? Sometimes we'd both get the bigger piece, and then we’d fight like cat and dog! Oh, I remember that well, Mum! He always cheated. Always. You two haven’t changed a bit. Speaking of tradition, anyone looking forward to the Queen’s Speech? Not really. It’s always the same. A bit… dull. Though, I do like the Downton Abbey vibes. All that poshness. I’m with Liam on that one. It’s a bit of a formality, isn't it? I'd rather listen to Christmas music. Have you heard that new Mariah Carey remix? Gets right in your head. Mariah Carey? Honestly, Sarah! It’s Christmas Eve, not a club night. Though, I must admit, a little bit of festive music is alright. Remember that awful caroll singing on Parklife? Parklife? What's Parklife? It’s a Blur album, Liam! You’re missing out! My uni friends all have nicknames for each other. I'm "Sazzy-B" apparently. It's ridiculous. Sazzy-B? Right then. Sounds like trouble. Liam, you mentioned going to America? Are you still thinking about Florida next year? Yeah, Dad and me are planning it. Proper excited.

Right, so, update time! Work’s been absolutely mental. We're launching this new sustainability project, and it's just... a lot. Endless meetings, spreadsheets, stakeholder management. You know the drill. But honestly, it's really rewarding. We're trying to reduce the company's carbon footprint, engaging with local businesses, it's all quite exciting. Oh, that sounds intensely busy, love. Sustainability, eh? Good on you. Back in my day, 'sustainability' meant not wasting your leftovers! Everything went into a casserole. Now it’s all buzzwords and committees, isn't it? How's the boyfriend, Mark? Still keeping you on your toes? Casseroles were the backbone of a good family meal, weren’t they, Brenda? Proper resourceful. And Mark, eh, Amelia? Still sending you flowers, is he? You were telling me just the other week he was taking up pottery. He is, actually! It's a disaster, honestly. He’s making these… abstract things. He calls them “interpretations of feelings.” They look like misshapen lumps of clay. But he’s really enjoying it. And yes, flowers still arrive, thankfully. He’s genuinely lovely. Work’s the bit that's stressful, not the relationship. Though, finding time for both is tricky. Pottery, you say? Well, bless his cotton socks! He's trying, at least. It's lovely to have a man who's attempting to be creative, even if the results are… questionable. Remember when Derek tried painting landscapes? Ended up looking like something a toddler did! Oh, Derek’s paintings! Don't even get me started! He swore he was a “natural artist.” The cows looked like mutated sausages. Amelia, your Mark sounds alright though, bits and bobs. At least he’s having a go. Business is… well, same as always. Field prices are fluctuating like mad. It’s a constant worry, keeping the books balanced. Less exciting than your sustainability project, I can tell you. It's not all glamorous, believe me. It requires a  lot  of paperwork. And convincing people that reducing plastic use is good for their bottom line. Sometimes I just want to scream. But then I see the impact on the local community and it makes it worthwhile. Have you two been up to anything nice lately? We went to the coast last week, just a little trip to Cromer. So bracing! The air smelled lovely and salty, and we had fish and chips, of course.

Right, so, chicken and chorizo fajitas tonight. Feeling ambitious. Do you think we have enough tortillas? I bought a multipack last week, but they do vanish remarkably quickly. I'm fairly certain we do. Though, you know, if we don't, we could always do wraps. Or, daringly, just eat everything in a bowl. Less faff. How was the appraisal today? You seemed a bit quiet when you got in. Oh, it was… fine. Perfectly fine. A little predictable really. They just reiterated that my speed is excellent, which, yes, it is, but it would be nice if they acknowledged the accuracy as well, you know? I’m not just a typing machine. It’s just… well, it felt performative, if you know what I mean. Like they had a script to follow. Right. Standard corporate nonsense then. Did they at least offer a raise? Don't tell me just the usual platitudes. A token gesture, honestly. Five percent. I practically choked on my own saliva. I said, “Thank you, that’s… generous.” But internally, I was screaming. Honestly, sometimes I think about just chucking it all in and opening a little pizza place. A pizza place? Now  that  would be something. We could call it “The Transcribed Slice.” Catchy, isn’t it? We'd need a proper blender though, a powerful one. Mine’s pathetic. Trying to make a smoothie yesterday, it just whined at me rather than actually blending. You and your blenders. We should really go to that new Marks and Spencer food hall they opened. They apparently have some incredible blenders. And the pre-made pizzas... allegedly, they’re quite good. Better than the usual supermarket fare, supposedly. M&S food hall, yes! Need to check it out. I was reading an article about the increasing importance of equine welfare. Apparently, some of the equestrian centres are…well, let’s just say, not ideal. Horrendous, actually. It makes you think. It does. It always does. Makes you want to adopt every single horse in need. Though I suspect the cat would have something to say about that if we brought another animal into the house. Remember last time you tried? Oh, don't remind me. Whiskers reigned supreme. He held the entire household hostage for a week. Speaking of reigning supreme, did you manage to finish the crossword today? The one in the Telegraph? It was brutal. Nearly.

Right then, listen to this! I’ve just been online, and Primark’ve got a new range of sparkly heels. Like,  proper  sparkly. Think New Year's Eve, but for a Tuesday. I'm thinking of getting a pair, but I’m not sure if they’ll be practical for a night out. You know, dancing and all that. Sparkly heels? At Primark? Are you having a laugh? Seriously though, you gotta get ‘em! Life’s too short for sensible shoes, lass. I’m off to town later, wanna come? We could have a look ourselves. My mum’s been on at me to get some new jeans, so a shopping trip’s inevitable anyway. Oh, heels! Don't even get me started. I bought a pair last week, thought I was being all grown up and sophisticated. Turns out, I can barely walk in 'em. Ended up hobbling back to the taxi like a proper loser. Jeans are much more my speed these days, to be honest. Anyone else got anything exciting planned for the weekend? A night out! Now you’re talkin’. I’m definitely in for a shopping trip too. Primark’s always a gamble though, isn't it? You find absolute gems, and then you find things that look like your nan knitted them. I’m wearing this awful jumper at the moment, sent by my auntie Brenda. It’s… beige. And full of bobbles. Beige and bobbles? Oh, bless. Brenda’s jumpers are legendary. My grandma makes similar ones. They’re… cozy. Sort of. I’m actually quite happy with what I’m wearing today – a proper comfy hoodie and leggings. Don’t want anything too fancy before a night out, need something I can dance in without feeling restricted, right? Regarding those heels, Gemma - if they're sparkly, get ‘em! You can always stash ‘em in your bag and swap them out when your feet start screaming. Good point, Chloe ! Stashing 'em is a brilliant idea. I’m terrified of blisters, honestly. Last time I wore heels, I ended up lookin’ like I'd walked across the Sahara. Beth , you’re right, life’s too short, I'll just have to risk it. What are you wearin' tonight then, if we do go out? Oh, I'm thinkin' somethin' with sequins, maybe? Got a wee black dress that  sparkles  like mad, actually. Need to iron it though.

Honestly, Mark, sometimes I think you're deliberately trying to wind me up. Bringing up Roman centurions at breakfast? Really? What’s wrong with Roman centurions, darling? They were disciplined, organised, and knew how to build a decent road. Something this country could do with learning now. Besides, it’s a perfectly legitimate thought given we’re discussing Ms. Eleanor Vance and her… eccentricities. Don’t you think she has that sort of, I don't know,  focused  energy? Like she’s commanding a legion. Focused is one word for it. Intense is another. And a bit… overwhelming. I mean, telling the director he should be channeling Julius Caesar during the quarterly review? He nearly choked on his granola. You know he hates being told what to do! He needs a little shake-up. And Eleanor’s just being… Eleanor. She’s on a spiritual journey, remember? She’s exploring different energies. You can't fault her for that. It's rather lovely, actually, this whole thing she's got going on – finding her soulmate in a Victorian poet. Lovely? It’s utterly bizarre! A vegan, crystal-loving sound therapist convinced she’s linked to Tennyson? And she keeps saying ‘past lives’ like it's the most normal thing in the world. Honestly, Mark, sometimes I wonder if  I’m  the one who's missing something. Am I just… too grounded? Too pragmatic? You are wonderfully grounded, love. That’s what I adore about you. Someone needs to keep their feet on the earth while Eleanor’s floating among the stars – and Tennyson. But don't dismiss her journey completely. You know, I was reading about Jungian archetypes the other day... Please don’t start with the Jungian archetypes. I had enough of that in university. No, no, just… it's interesting how people seek meaning, isn't it? We all do it in different ways. Remember that imaginary party we planned, the one with all the historical figures? Oh, yes. Cleopatra, Marie Curie, Freddie Mercury... a slightly chaotic mixture, wasn't it? The catering alone would have been a nightmare. Exactly! And Eleanor would have been right at home, explaining to Queen Elizabeth I the benefits of sound healing. Imagine the conversation! It would be… epic. I was thinking, we could revisit that idea, actually. But make it a charitable fundraiser? A historical costume party fundraiser? For what cause? The local animal shelter.

Honestly, Sarah, this whole Etsy venture is proving… more complicated than I initially anticipated. People want bespoke everything, but they also want it for next to nothing. It’s exhausting trying to balance artisan quality with bargain-basement prices. Right? Like, you're putting hours into these knitted blankets, aren't you? Beautiful ones, too. My Nan makes amazing tea cosies, but she's got years of experience. It takes time to build that reputation and skillset. You gotta charge accordingly, love. You’re both right. It’s the 'instant gratification' culture, innit? People expect everything delivered yesterday, perfectly made, and cheaper than it should be. Remember when I was trying to convince Liam to pay a decent rate for his gardening services? He was moaning about the cost! He’s out there sweating buckets! Exactly! It's just the general attitude. And the marketing... ugh. I’m battling algorithms and influencers who seem to generate wealth from thin air. It’s demoralizing. Reminds me of those personality tests they used to make you do at work – utterly useless for assessing actual ability. Oh, them! I did loads of those applying for civil service roles. Remember the one that asked you to ‘rank the importance of teamwork, initiative, and problem-solving’ and then completely contradicted itself later on? Maddening. Did you ever get a pet, Fiona? I’m thinking of finally getting a cat. Little rescue, of course. No pets yet, darling. Too much upheaval with the business. It's all-consuming. Although, I did see a video online of a tiny kitten riding a Roomba… utterly delightful. Speaking of delightful, how’s Liam's mum doing? Still convinced he’s going to marry a princess? She is! Still pinning photos of Meghan Markle on Pinterest. It’s priceless. But honestly, she’s been a bit poorly lately – just a persistent cough. I've been ensuring she’s taking her vitamins and reminding her about her inhaler. First aid is crucial, you know. Especially with the pollen count this year being absolutely ridiculous. It's like living in a yellow storm. Tell me about it! My eyes have been streaming. It's so humid too, isn't it? I wish we had air conditioning. This heat is just oppressive. Makes you want to lie in a graveyard. Peaceful, cool... morbid, I know. You and your graveyards, Sarah! You always did have a fascination with old tombstones.

Right, this is a disaster. An absolute blooming disaster. What's up, Liv? You sound like you've just stubbed your toe on a badger. Worse, Rach. Much worse. Remember I said I was meeting up with Chloe and Liam tomorrow? Vaguely. Something about them needing help moving a sofa? Typical student move, innit? Aye, well, it's turned out Liam's parents are coming to visit. And they're… posh. Like, ‘skiing in Switzerland every winter’ posh. And now I've got to pretend I'm not from Barrow-in-Furness and don't eat chips with mayonnaise. It's mortifying! Oh, Liv. You'll be fine. Just, you know, don’t mention the industrial estate. Or the seagulls. Easy for you to say, Danny. You’re practically London royalty, with your Filipino heritage and everything. You can probably charm their socks off talking about, I don’t know, the correct way to eat dim sum. Hey now! Don’t underestimate my ability to be charming. And I'm not practically royalty, I just know where the decent pho is. Seriously though, just be yourself. They’ll see through any act. He's right, Liv. Just be normal. And if they start asking probing questions, deflect. "Oh, my family are quite busy, you know, with their…hobbies." Hobbies? My dad’s hobby is watching telly and complaining about the weather. That'll go down a treat. Right, let’s move on before Liv descends into full panic. Any news from Maya? She said she’d be sorting out that tax thing. Getting confused about student loans is a nightmare. She texted me earlier. Apparently, HMRC are being absolute cowboys. Said they needed some random form filled out by her nan, proving she’s… something. I didn't quite catch. Something about agricultural land? Agricultural land? Maya lives in a flat above a kebab shop! This is bonkers. Classic. The system's designed to confuse young people, I swear. Speaking of confusing, did you see that Arsenal game last night? Absolutely dreadful. Tell me about it! Honestly, they played like they’d never seen a football before. My nan, she’s a massive fan, she nearly threw her biscuit at the telly. My brother sent me a video of his mate attempting to do a keepy-uppy. It was… something to behold. He managed three before falling face-first into a flowerbed.

This is dead lush, isn’t it? Proper good grub. Better than anything we get back in Bolton, that’s for sure. Though, I do miss a decent chippy… Aye, it is lovely, love. Absolutely lovely. Though, I must say, I did miss a good cup of tea when we arrived. Croatian coffee's a bit strong for me. Still, this setting… being here with you all... it makes up for it. How’s your uni going, El? Settling in alright? I know moving to Leeds was a big step. Leeds is alright. Loads of buses, though. Properly confusing bus system. I got lost going to the library the other day. Ended up in some dodgy looking estate. Dodgy looking estate, eh? Typical teenage experience, I imagine. London’s just as bad, you know. The tube map looks like a plate of tangled spaghetti. Still, at least they’re reliable. Unlike some… . Oh, don’t you start, David. You’re forgetting the time you missed your train back from a conference because you were convinced you could “just pop into” Harrods. That was a one-off! And Harrods is a vital strategic asset for anyone interested in understanding consumer trends. You two will be arguing about Brexit next, I swear! Seriously though, uni's good. It's busy. Loads of reading. I'm really getting into the sociology side of things. I’m even thinking about getting a tattoo, inspired by Durkheim or something. Something proper academic, you know? A tattoo? Seriously? What, like, a diagram of social stratification? Don’t be daft, Liam. Something a bit more… subtle. Maybe a symbol or something. I was thinking about getting it on my ankle. An ankle tattoo? Oh, El. Your dad will have a fit! He still complains about that little silver stud you had in your ear when you were twelve. He does, doesn't he? But he secretly likes it. He just pretends to be embarrassed. Anyway, what about you, Mum? How’s the hospital been? Busy as ever, I imagine? Always. You wouldn’t believe the things I see. Had a woman in last week, convinced her dog was giving birth. Turns out it was a very large, round… well, never mind. It was a weird day. Still, it's rewarding, you know? Bringing new life into the world. Makes all the paperwork worthwhile. Facebook's gone mental with people sharing birthing videos lately though.

Cor, that was a proper trek back, wasn’t it, Brenda? Thought we’d never get off that A14. Roads were busier than a Saturday market in Dereham. You’re telling me, Arthur! I swear, every lorry driver in the country was using it. But it was worth it, wasn't it? Cornwall was just…beautiful. The light, you know? Proper different to Norfolk. Glad you both made it back safely. Bit of a downpour as I was heading over, but cleared up nicely once I got closer. So, Cornwall! Heard the pictures were fantastic. Let’s have a look, shall we? Right then, have a look at this! Porthleven Point Lighthouse. Gorgeous thing, innit? Reminds me a bit of that little one down at Cromer, only a bit taller. I always liked lighthouses. Something solid, you know? Holding firm against the weather. Proper dependable. And look at this one, Arthur! All those rocks and the sea. We were crabbing there, you know. Little Emily – John’s granddaughter – caught three! Three, I tell you! She was absolutely thrilled. Ah, is this the YHA volunteering crew? Looks like you were putting in a good shift, Brenda. What were you doing? Clearing paths, were you? We were. Mostly clearing overgrown paths and a bit of painting. Lovely group of people, though. All sorts, really. A couple of young lads from London, an older German woman... It's nice to feel like you’re doing something useful, isn't it? Especially after all these years. Useful? Aye, I suppose so. I never was much one for volunteering, mind. Always preferred a bit of peace and quiet with the telly. Though Elsie – bless her cotton socks – she used to volunteer at the church fete every year. Made the best Victoria sponge, she did. My wife, Sarah, volunteers at the school fete. It’s a constant battle to get her to come home. Anyway, look at this one. This is truly stunning. Did you manage to cycle much while you were down there? Oh yes! We hired bikes for a day. Absolutely brilliant cycling. The coastal paths are mostly well-maintained, you know. Arthur wasn't quite as keen on the hills though. Hills! Don’t talk to me about hills! My knees weren’t built for climbing hills, Brenda. I couldn't 'ave cycled to the end of the road let alone across Yorkshire in a day!

Cor, this is reet nice, ANON. Proper good grub. Yorkshire puddings are a bit… well, they’re Yorkshire puddings - massive! I’ve barely chipped at mine. Yeah, they're a bit much, innit? ANON’s Mum doesn’t mess around when it comes to Sunday dinner. Glad I came though, beats beans on toast again. Don't be dramatic, Liam. Beans on toast isn’t  that  bad. Anyway, it’s lovely to be here, ANON. Thank you for having us. And yes, the puddings are a bit… enthusiastic. You could use them as shields, honestly. Tell me about it! So, Liam, you were saying you were thinking about moving on from the construction site? What's the plan then? Yeah, I was. It's alright, the work’s fine, decent lads. But it just...it feels dead-end, you know? I've been thinking about trying something different. I saw an ad for an apprentice mechanic at that garage down the road – Miller's. Seems alright. Less… physical, more problem-solving. That sounds interesting! A complete change, but a good one, if it’s what you want. Mechanics are always needed. Did you look at the pay rates? Being an apprentice can be tough on the wallet initially. Yeah, I had a quick look. It's not amazing, obviously, but it’s a start. Got to start somewhere, haven't I? I'm just worried about… well, I'm not exactly a genius with engines. My dad used to tinker with cars, but I never really paid attention. Everyone starts somewhere, Liam! My nan always said, ‘if you’re willing to learn, you can do anything.’ Besides, Miller's has a good reputation. They train their apprentices properly. It's a far better shout than just staying where you are, feeling stuck and miserable. Exactly. And you’re a quick learner. Remember when you taught yourself to fix that bicycle wheel last summer? You were moaning about it for a week, but you figured it out. This is similar, just a bit more complex. True, true. It's just… daunting, I guess. It feels like a big jump. I get that. Change always does. Speaking of changes… Amy, you've been a bit quiet. Everything alright with you and Ben? You seem a bit withdrawn this last few weeks. It’s… complicated. We’ve been arguing a lot. Silly things, mostly.

Oh my god, it’s  so  good to be back. Barcelona was incredible, seriously. You wouldn’t believe it. Welcome back! You look exhausted, though. Barcelona, huh? I saw your Insta stories, looked stunning! How was it  really ? Did you eat all the paella? All the paella. And tapas. And churros. Possibly too many churros. Honestly, the food alone was worth the trip. But it was more than that, you know? Just… the vibe. The architecture, the people, wandering around getting lost… It was magic. I think I needed that, to be honest. I can imagine. You've been working so hard lately. The Miller project has got to be a nightmare. Did Liam come? Yeah, Liam came. He was... Liam. You know? He spent most of the time checking his phone and complaining about the flight. Thankfully, the city distracted him a bit. We did manage to see the Sagrada Familia, which was unbelievable. He actually looked impressed for a solid five minutes, which is a minor miracle. Five minutes? That  is  impressive. So, relationships still... complicated? Let’s just say we're navigating. It's fine. For now. Anyway, enough about Liam. Tell me  everything  that happened here while I was gone! Did you manage to finally finish that Bridgerton marathon? I did! And I'm officially obsessed. Penelope and Colin are just…  sigh . It’s cheesy, I know, but I needed something light and fluffy. How was the weather? I was worried about you getting rained on. It was gorgeous! Mostly sunshine and blue skies. We only had one brief shower, but it cleared up quickly. We spent a lot of time on Barceloneta beach – people-watching and just chilling. I even attempted to learn to paddleboard. Oh, you and water sports! You'd sink like a stone. Did you get any decent souvenirs? Just a few little trinkets. A fridge magnet with Gaudi on it, some slightly overpriced olive oil... and a ridiculous amount of chocolate. I think I brought enough to feed the entire neighbourhood. Honestly, I feel like I’ve gained five pounds just thinking about it. What about you? Anything exciting happen whilst I was gallivanting around Europe? Not massively exciting, no. Mostly just work, work, work. I had a particularly tricky patient this weekend – really struggling with anxiety after a bereavement. Took a lot out of me, to be honest. But rewarding, you know?

Honestly, this is just… bliss. I didn’t realise I needed this so much. Teaching can be utterly draining, you know? It’s lovely seeing the children learn, of course, but the paperwork… the meetings… it's relentless. Tell me about it. Though my relentlessness usually involves spreadsheets and chasing investors, rather than lesson plans. Different flavour of stress, I suppose, but equally pervasive. It’s good to actually  get  somewhere peaceful. You're a teacher, you said? What age group? Year Six. Eleven-year-olds. A whirlwind of hormones, burgeoning independence, and a surprising amount of misplaced confidence. It’s a challenging age, but also rewarding. Before that, I was a special needs assistant for a few years. That taught me a  lot  about patience. And resilience! It's amazing how resourceful children can be, when they need to be. What about you? Entrepreneur, you said? What kind of venture is that? It's… complicated. Started with an app, initially for small businesses to manage their social media. Grew unexpectedly quickly – which was brilliant, and terrifying in equal measure. Now we're branching out into AI-powered marketing tools. Basically, I’m trying to automate the things that small businesses find tedious, so they can focus on what they're good at. It's a rollercoaster. One minute you’re celebrating a major deal, the next you’re firefighting a server crash at 3 AM. Sounds positively exhausting! I can relate to the 3 AM firefighting, though mine usually involves a child's parent emailing me halfway through the night about a forgotten permission slip. Slightly less high-stakes, admittedly. Before teaching, before the special needs assistant role… I actually worked in a bakery. For about five years. A bakery? Really? That’s quite a switch from teaching and supporting children. It was! My mum ran a small family bakery in Dorchester. When I finished university, I just drifted back home and ended up helping her out. Long hours, stood on my feet all day… it was physically brutal, but the smell of fresh bread baking… there's something incredibly comforting about that. And the satisfaction of creating something that people enjoyed – a proper Victoria sponge, nicely iced… that was good. What's the most unexpected job  you’ve  had? Before the tech world, I mean. Unexpected is putting it mildly. I spent a summer in Ibiza, bussing tables at a beach club.

Honestly, Liam, I'm proper stressed about this house situation. It's gettin' to me, it really is. Still on about it, eh, lass? What's cropped up now? You were alright about it yesterday. Alright? Alright?! There's mould growing in the bathroom, Liam! Proper black, slimy mould. I took photos. I'll show you when we get back. And Ben left his dishes piled up in the sink again. Like a mountain of questionable leftovers. Ben's Ben. He's always been a bit… chaotic. Remember when he tried to 'bake' a cake in a flower pot? Don't remind me. But this is different. It’s not just about a messy flat anymore. It's about the damp, and the fact that Chloe’s been leaving her hair all over the shower, and now I'm pretty sure Mark is using my shampoo. My  expensive  argan oil shampoo! Right, expensive stuff. So, what's the plan? You can’t be havin’ a full-blown meltdown every other day over a bit of mould. I'm not having a meltdown! I'm being perfectly reasonable. I just... I feel like I'm the only one who’s actually trying to keep the place livable. I even cleaned the oven last week, and did I get a thank you? No. Ben just put a pizza in it and left the grease splatters. You’re a good lass, Elsie. Always tidyin’ up after everyone. But you can’t carry the weight of the whole house on your shoulders. Have you spoken to them about it, properly? Like, sat them down and had a little chat? I tried, I did. But it's like talkin' to a brick wall. Ben just shrugs and says he'll "get around to it eventually," and Chloe just rolls her eyes and says I’m being "too uptight." Mark just… avoids eye contact. Honestly, the lot of 'em! Avoidin' eye contact, eh? Sounds about right. Maybe you need a more... direct approach. A proper showdown. A showdown? Liam, I’m not confrontational! I'll end up crying, and they’ll all look sorry for me, and then nothing will change. No, not a full-blown screaming match. Just a calm but firm chat. Write down a list of the things that bother you, give 'em a copy, and say, "This is what needs to happen, and this is when.

Cor blimey, that were a mission, weren't it, Doris? Felt like I were luggin' bricks, I did. My back's givin' me a right ol' ache. Oh, Arthur, you always say that! You make it sound like you’ve climbed Everest. Let me take some of those. Heavens, what have you got there? Looks like the whole of Sainsbury’s came with you. Well, we needed a few bits and bobs, didn’t we? You said you were runnin' low on sugar. And I thought I’d get a little somethin' for tea, see? A nice bit of cod, fresh this mornin'. And a few apples, too. Doctor says I need more fruit. Cod, lovely! You remembered I was craving fish. You're a good man, Arthur. But honestly, apples? We’ve got a whole bowl full! You’re spoiling me. Well, they were on offer, weren’t they? Can’t argue with a bargain, can ya? Remember that time, years ago, when the greengrocer had them pears for a penny each? We practically cleared 'em out! Oh, I do! Your eyes lit up like a Christmas tree. Honestly, you'd have bought the whole shop if I hadn't pulled you away. Did you manage to get that mint sauce you wanted? Aye, got the mint sauce. Mrs. Higgins was sayin' they didn't 'ave much left, so I snatched a jar while I could. She’s a lovely woman, Mrs. Higgins. Always has a kind word, she does. Shame about her grandson though, spendin’ all ‘is time playin’ those computer games. Such a waste, isn’t it? All that potential. Kids these days...no appreciation for a bit of fresh air. Did you see young Emily at the checkout? She’s gotten so tall. Practically a young woman now. I did! Didn't recognise her at first, she's blossomed, she 'as. Gave me a little wave, mind. Good girl. Reminded me of your Sarah when she was that age. Always had a smile on her face. Yes, she did. Seems like yesterday she was a little girl, building Lego castles in the living room. Time just flies, doesn't it, Arthur? It does, Doris, it really does. Makes you think about things, don’t it? About all the years gone by. Remember that summer, back in '78? The heatwave? We spent every evenin' sat in the garden, drinkin' lemonade.

Right then, that’s the kettle on. Arthur, love, could you pop the biscuits out? They’re in the tin, top shelf. And Liam, put your feet up, boy, you're lookin' all scrunched up like a bit of crumpled paper. I’m just tired, Gran. A-Levels are killing me. Just finished a mock essay on Victorian social reform. Honestly, who cares about the Poor Law Amendment Act? Victorian social reform, eh? That’s nothin’ compared to when Hull was dealing with the cholera outbreak! Now  that  was somethin’ to write about. Folks droppin' like flies, you know. No proper sanitation back then. Smelled awful, it did. Cholera! Aye, I remember my mum tellin’ stories. Thankfully, we’ve come a long way since then. Still, a good scrub with carbolic soap never did any harm, did it, Elsie? Never! My grandma swore by it. Used to clean the whole house with it. Smelled like a hospital, but it was clean as a whistle. Elsie, are you alright love? You look a bit flushed. You are a bit pink, love. Had a bit of a walk in the fresh air, did you? Don't overdo it, mind. Arthur, get Elsie a glass of water. Liam, put the kettle on again, that one's gone cold now. So, Arthur, have you managed to sort out the plumber about the leaky tap in the downstairs loo? It’s drivin’ me mad. Drip, drip, drip, all night. He said he’d pop round Tuesday afternoon. Said he was busy today, got a burst pipe in a row of cottages up on the outskirts. Apparently, some elderly lady was stuck without water. Burst pipe, is it? Happens every winter. Should've lined those pipes better in the first place. Back in my day, things were built to last! Solid as a rock they were. Not like this flimsy stuff they use now. You always say that, Arthur. Everything was better in your day. You'd think the world was fallin' apart now. It is, Elsie! Look at the telly! All doom and gloom! And the youngsters glued to those infernal screens. Don’t know the meaning of hard work these days. Oh, Arthur, don’t start. Liam’s working his socks off with those A-Levels. You know he's aiming for Cambridge, don’t you, Elsie? Cambridge! Fancy that. My brother nearly went to university, he did.

Right, so, another fifteen minutes until Dr. Anya's appointment. Feel like I’ve been sat here ages. Anyone else feeling restless? This waiting room’s proper drab, innit? Tell me about it. I'm bored senseless. Been scrolling through TikTok for the last half hour. Found a bloke trying to make a smoothie with a drill. Honestly. A drill? Seriously? People on the internet are wild.
