Oh my god, it’s  so  good to be back. Seriously, this sofa is like a hug. London was… intense. Intense is one word for it. You look knackered, Liv. Glad you made it down. Mum’s already made a mountain of roast dinner, your favourite. Just needs the gravy. Roast dinner? You’re an angel, Soph. Honestly, I’m practically inhaling the smell already. London food just isn’t the same. It’s all trendy quinoa bowls and £12 avocado toast. Gives me indigestion just thinking about it. Tell me about it. It’s all style, no substance. So, tell me everything. How was the copywriting gig? Did you land that big account you were buzzing about? Almost, yeah. Really close. They went with another agency in the end. Apparently, they needed someone with specific experience in… sustainable packaging. Sustainable packaging! Who even  thinks  about that?! It's not exactly my usual beating heart, you know? Still, the interviews were good, the office was lovely, and the people seemed decent. But the commute... Soph, the commute nearly killed me. An hour and fifteen minutes each way, crammed onto the tube like a sardine. Blimey. No wonder you’re exhausted. Mum kept asking about you, you know. She's been leaving little plates of biscuits out in case you came home unexpectedly. You know how she is. I do. She’s the best. Tell me, how’s work been? Still dealing with Mr. Henderson and his stubborn refusal to swallow properly? Don’t even remind me. Mr. Henderson’s a character. He’s convinced his soup is plotting against him. We're making progress, slowly, but it's a delicate dance. But honestly, it’s rewarding. Seeing people regain their abilities, even small things… it makes the difficult days worthwhile. This week, I've been working with a lovely woman who had a stroke. She just started saying a few words today. It was amazing. That’s brilliant, Soph! You're doing such important work. It sounds so much more fulfilling than my endless copy about moisturiser and mobile phone contracts. Hey, someone has to write those! Anyway, Mum's trying to convince me to start thinking about getting a place with a garden. Apparently, I need ‘a bit of space to breathe’ and ‘a proper vegetable patch.’ Oh, she’s onto you, isn’t she? You do spend a lot of time talking about wanting to grow your own tomatoes.

You know, reminiscing about childhood… it strikes me how different things were. I remember cycling from Almondsbury to Weston-super-Mare when I was about ten. Just me and my bike, all those miles! No sat nav, no concern about traffic... just the open road. Weston-super-Mare! Goodness, that's a fair trek for a little one. I used to cycle everywhere in Ramsgate, of course. Not quite as far, being a coastal town. Though, the wind off the Channel could be a beast! Though I must confess, I never quite had the endurance for that kind of long ride like you. Not the adventurous sort, I suppose. Endurance? That's putting it mildly! When I was a lad in Manchester, a cycle from the city to the Peak District was a serious undertaking. We’d pack picnics and spend the whole day. These days, the thought of it leaves me quite breathless! Speaking of journeys, David, how were those early years as a dentist? Must have been a completely different world. Oh, it was different, alright. Very different. Fresh out of university, full of ideals. And the NHS… well, the NHS perks back then were… generous, let’s say. Sailing regattas, free tickets to concerts… there was this one lecture series on oral surgery ironically held on a boat! "Lectures all at sea with your oral surgeon," as the organiser grandly put it. Utterly ridiculous, but we loved it! We could get holidays for a song too. Prague, for example. I’ve got a neighbour going there next month, return flights and bed and breakfast for under two hundred quid! You wouldn't believe it. Prague! I've always wanted to go. What’s it like? Beautiful. Stunning architecture, Charles Bridge, the Old Town Square… a real fairytale city. Loads of history, good beer, and relatively cheap. You could easily spend a week just wandering around. It does sound tempting. Though getting theatre tickets these days… a nightmare. Remember trying to get into  Hamlet  at the Globe last year? Fully booked weeks in advance. You practically need to bribe someone. Tell me about it! Still, there’s that jive event we’re putting on, isn’t there? At the old barn on the edge of town. It's shaping up nicely, I understand. It is! They've done a marvelous job converting it. It used to be a milking parlour, apparently.

Right then, let’s tackle this moving image case study thing properly. I’ve been mulling over how to make it really sing, you know? It can't just be a dry overview of filmmakers' techniques. It needs to  grab  the students. What are your thoughts after that initial read-through of the brief, love? It was a pretty hefty brief, wasn’t it? My immediate feeling is that we need to anchor it in something relatable. All the talk of ‘auteur theory’ and ‘mise-en-scène’… it’ll fly right over the heads of most fifteen-year-olds. We need a case study, a specific film, that they’ll actually  know  or, at least, be willing to engage with. Something accessible. Absolutely. You’re spot on. I was thinking maybe something like  Paddington ? It's got appeal across ages, it's visually stunning, and we can unpack a surprising amount about cinematic storytelling through it. The colour palette alone… the way they use light and shadow… it's masterful, really. Reminds me a bit of Wes Anderson, actually.  Paddington  is brilliant! Much better than my initial idea of  The Greatest Showman , which, let's be honest, is more about sparkly spectacle than anything truly insightful. Paddington offers subtle, layered storytelling. We could look at how they build Paddington’s character through the visual cues, the costuming, the setting… it’s all incredibly deliberate. But how do we make it engaging for students who are mostly glued to TikTok? That's the challenge, isn't it? We can’t ignore the social media elephant in the room. Maybe we could build in a task where they have to re-create a short scene from  Paddington  using only their phones? A mini-TikTok version, focusing on a specific cinematic element, like framing or camera movement. That combines their existing skills with what they're learning. I love that! It's practical, encourages creativity, and leverages what they're already comfortable with. We could even have a judging panel – maybe inviting some local film students to provide feedback. That adds a layer of authenticity. It's like, you’re not just learning theory; you're  doing  it. Precisely! And we could create a whole series of these, with different films and different focus areas. We could call it… hmm… "Film Deconstructed"? Bit cliché, I know. It's not terrible. Or, "Behind the Screen"?

That was glorious, wasn’t it? The air just… smells of salt and freedom. I honestly needed that. My students were particularly… lively today. Lively is one word for it. I heard the faint echoes of a debate about the socio-political implications of TikTok influencing ancient Athenian pottery from across the hall. You win the prize for most dedicated lecturer today. Oh, don't exaggerate! But yes, they’re certainly passionate. Do you think they actually  listen  to anything I say, or are they just waiting for the chance to contradict me? A bit of both, I suspect. It’s the modern student, innit? They want to feel like they're contributing, even if their contribution is occasionally… tangential. Did you see Sarah and Mark's photos on Instagram? They're in Cornwall. Oh, lovely! Cornwall. I bet they’re having a proper time. Remember that disastrous holiday they had in the Lake District a few years ago? The tent collapsing in the middle of the night and all that. How could I forget? Mark blaming the entire incident on a rogue badger. A badger! As if badgers routinely dismantle nylon tents. They looked utterly miserable in those grainy photos. Poor Sarah. She deserves a nice, relaxing beach holiday. I hope this one is proving better. I'm sure it is. They needed it. Mark’s been working ridiculous hours at the firm. I think he was genuinely starting to fade. It's rather sad, isn’t it? Everyone rushing about, chasing careers and whatnot. Sometimes you just need to stop and breathe the sea air, like we just did. Absolutely. Speaking of which, did you manage to find any sea glass? You were scouring the beach like a hawk. I did! Three pieces. A lovely emerald green one, a pale turquoise, and – get this – a tiny fragment of cobalt blue. I’m going to make a little mobile for the kitchen window. Bring a bit of the seaside in. That's lovely, love. You’re always making something. You should start selling them! People would buy them. Handmade things have such an appeal. It's authentic. Don’t be silly. It’s just a hobby. Besides, I'd be terrible at marketing. I'd probably just end up talking about the geological processes that create sea glass to potential buyers. You probably would. Alright, alright, no selling. But you should definitely display them.

Right, this is comfier than I thought. Honestly, ANON’s got good taste in furniture, she does. Though, I still reckon my sofa back home is better for a proper kip. What are we watchin' then? Just about to put on ‘Next in Fashion’. I saw a little preview and the designs looked wild. Honestly, some of the stuff people come up with now is just… mental. ‘Next in Fashion’? Ooh, good choice! I'm starving. These are ginger snaps, anyone? And yes, the designs are often bonkers. Remember last season with that guy who made a dress out of recycled traffic cones? Traffic cones?! Cor, that’s proper creative, innit? Though a bit scratchy, I'd imagine. Ginger snaps sound brilliant, thanks! So, fashion, eh? It’s a strange thing, isn't it? Down in Doncaster, it’s mostly about wearing what's on offer at Sports Direct, re’ you know. Not much high fashion goin' on. Haha! That’s fair. London’s a whole other level. You've got the established designers, the experimental stuff bubbling up in Shoreditch… it's overwhelming sometimes, to be honest. I’m trying to be more conscious of ethical fashion, though. It’s hard. Exactly! It’s so tricky. There's so much fast fashion surrounding us. I try to buy second-hand whenever possible. I found a vintage silk scarf at a market last week – absolutely gorgeous. It’s amazing what treasures you can find. And the kids at school are surprisingly savvy about it too - they're always asking where my clothes are from. Second-hand's brilliant, I agree. I’ve got a fair few bits from charity shops. You get some proper gems. Though my mum ends up having a good rummage and declaring everything too “old-ladyish”. She’s terrible! But ethical fashion… that's a good shout. I just get a bit lost, re' all the different brands and materials. It’s like full-time job tryin' to keep up. It  is  a full-time job! There are apps now that’ll rate brands on their sustainability. I’ve downloaded a couple, but honestly, they're a bit of a minefield. It’s all percentages and complicated jargon. The jargon is the worst. But it helps to start small, I think. Like, choosing a brand that uses organic cotton or donates a portion of profits to a good cause.

Honestly, Mum, Mr. Davies is  killing  me with Shakespeare. Like, why are we still studying  Romeo and Juliet ? Everyone knows how it ends! It's depressing. Oh, come on, Elara. It's a classic for a reason. And Mr. Davies is a good teacher, isn't he? He makes it interesting. Besides, it's good practice for your English Lit A-Level. Easy for you to say, you’re not facing exams! And interesting? He spent twenty minutes today explaining the symbolism of Juliet’s ring. A ring, Mum! It's jewellery! I'd rather be photographing the waves down at the beach. Did you see the sunset last night? It was incredible. I got some really good shots. I did see it. Absolutely stunning. Send me some of your pictures, love. You’re getting really good, you know. That portrait of old Mrs. Higgins with her cat? That was brilliant. You’ve got a real eye. Thanks. I’m thinking of entering some into the Hastings Photo Competition. But what if they're not good enough? What if everyone laughs? That’s my biggest fear, I think - people laughing at me. Oh, sweetheart. Don’t be ridiculous. People will appreciate your talent. Honestly, the worst that can happen is they don’t choose your photo. It’s not the end of the world, is it? And I highly doubt anyone will laugh. You put your heart into your work. That counts for a lot. I guess. It's just...everything feels so important right now. Exams, the competition, college applications looming... It's a lot. It is. But you're handling it wonderfully. Remember that time you were terrified to present your history project in Year 7? You practically hid behind the whiteboard! Look at you now. Don’t remind me! I wanted to disappear. But at least I’m not  that  awkward anymore. Speaking of awkward, did you have a nightmare shift at the reception desk today? Mrs. Peterson complaining about the biscuits again? Don’t even mention Mrs. Peterson and her digestive biscuits! Honestly, she's a trial. But no, it wasn't that bad. We had a film crew in today, surprisingly. They were filming a comedy pilot. Really? What kind of comedy? Anything good? I love stand-up, you know. Have you seen Jack Whitehall? He’s hilarious. I haven’t, actually. I’m more of a Romesh Ranganathan girl myself.

Cor blimey, that's a bit of a sit-down that is. Feel like me bones ‘ave gone all matchstick-y, they 'ave. Just came round, did ya? Lovely to see ya both, though. Kettle's on, isn't it, dear? Yes, dear, it is. Earl Grey for you, Barry? And a proper cuppa for you, John? You look tired. Are you sleeping alright? Morning, both. Barry, you look like you’ve wrestled a badger. And yes, tea would be grand, John. John, are you still struggling with that application form? It looked a beast when I saw you poring over it last week. Struggles is the word for it. Beast is putting it lightly. They want to know me entire life history, don’t they? Everything from the day I was born, right down to what me favourite kind of jam is! What's relevant, I'd like to know. Never worked, you see. Never  had  to. Bit different to your lot, havin’ jobs and things. Well, it's just procedures, love. They have to tick all the boxes. Don’t let it fluster you. We can go through it together again. Did you manage to fill in that bit about hobbies? Hobbies? What hobbies does a man o’ me age have? Watching the telly, mostly. And… well, watching the birds. Got a right busy nest in the old apple tree this year. Little brown things, chirpin’ away somethin’ awful. Reminds me o' the neighbours’ kids, always shoutin'. Speaking of kids, John, you remember little Timmy from your street? The one who used to glue his shoes to the floor? Timmy! Blimey, that was a trial, wasn’t he? Made my blood boil, that boy did. Used to steal me rhubarb, he did! Oh, don’t start reminiscing about difficult children, darling. John needs to focus on the form. You were saying, John? About not sleeping? It’s that cockerel next door, y’see. Starts up at four in the mornin'. Absolutely dreadful racket. Used to be alright, not so loud. Now it’s like a banshee screechin'. Keeps me awake. Been thinkin’ of gettin' one meself, give him a taste of his own medicine, I ‘ave. Barry! Don't you dare! You’ll have the whole neighbourhood up in arms. You know Mrs. Henderson next door would have a coronary. Besides, I was reading about 3D printing the other day.

Honestly, Margaret, I still feel a bit…surreal about it all. Bringing Eleanor here permanently. After all these years. Well, surreal in a good way, I hope, dear? It’s wonderful news! You've been talking about it for ages. It’s about time she settled somewhere properly. That flat in Rome, lovely as it was, never felt like a home to her, did it? No, you’re right. It was lovely for a time, a bit of an adventure. But she's been saying for months how lonely she gets during the winter. And the language… she never truly mastered Italian, did she? She’d muddle through, of course, but…it was never truly hers. It’s just…a huge undertaking, isn’t it? I’m a bit daunted. Daunted, yes. But also incredibly exciting! Think of it, having her here, proper Sunday roasts, walks along the seafront… We can finally have those family Christmases we always talked about when we were younger. Remember all those plans we sketched out? Oh yes! With the ridiculous paper chains and the awful sherry trifle. Those were the days. But it’s more than just Christmases, isn't it? It’s about having her near, being able to offer support… God knows, she's been through a lot these past few years. The divorce, the job losses… Precisely. And she needs stability, a solid anchor. And you, my dear, are that anchor. Don't underestimate how much that means to her. She'll bloom here, I just know it. We'll help her find a good place, maybe something not too far from us, so we can pop over for a cuppa whenever she needs it. I’ve been looking online. Property prices are absolutely scandalous, you know. Finding anything remotely affordable… it's a nightmare. And she's a bit fussy, you know Eleanor. Needs light, needs space, needs a balcony for her herbs…the list goes on. That does sound like Eleanor alright. Don’t worry about the property hunt too much just yet. Let's focus on getting her here first. We can look together, we'll find something. We have contacts, remember? Mrs. Peterson down the road mentioned her nephew works for a letting agency… I'll have a word. That would be wonderful, thank you. It's just... financially, I'm a bit stretched, as you know. Retirement hasn't been flush, to put it mildly.

Dreadful weather, isn't it? Still, it’s quintessential Brighton, I suppose. So, you were saying about the referendum… I've been trying to get my head around the implications for universities, specifically. Do you think the potential disruption to funding will be significant? Significant is an understatement, James. Absolutely significant. The uncertainty alone is damaging. Universities rely on EU funding and collaborative research. A hard border, or even the  perception  of one, throws a real spanner in the works. I taught history, you know, and the sheer upheavals caused by borders throughout time… it’s fascinating, but utterly frustrating when you're trying to secure a research grant. It feels like we’re going backwards. Exactly! And the political rhetoric… it's hardly conducive to a stable academic environment. Speaking of disruption, have you heard anything more about Eleanor’s replacement in the English department? The interviews are happening this week, aren’t they? Yes, they are. A rather… interesting pool of candidates, apparently. Apparently, one of them spent a good portion of their interview discussing their prize-winning ferret. A ferret? Seriously? Well, that’s… memorable, at least. I'm worried they’ll end up with someone utterly unsuitable. Eleanor had such a grounding influence. Remember when young Timmy Baker nearly set fire to the library with a Bunsen burner trying to prove a point about Shelley? Eleanor’s gentle but firm hand saved the day. Timmy! Good heavens, that was a disaster waiting to happen. He ended up writing a rather brilliant essay on the dangers of Romantic poets, though. Still, you're right about Eleanor. A loss to the department, she was. I'm hoping they find someone with a similar level of dedication. My daughter, Chloe, she's been applying for jobs herself. Took an interview yesterday. Oh, really? What sort of position? And how did it go? Marketing, believe it or not. She did a degree in Media Studies. Said the interview went… well, it was a  panel  interview, you see. Six of them. And one of them spent the entire time checking his phone! She said he barely looked up. That's appalling! Honestly, the lack of basic respect these days… It’s just lazy. I had a student once who clearly hadn't read the essay question. He’d written a passionate treatise on the mating habits of the Bolivian tree frog. Completely irrelevant.

Right, so where were we with this… mousetrap game? Honestly, Leo, it’s ludicrous. A mousetrap game! But Finn seems utterly engrossed, and you’re encouraging him. Well, he's been obsessed with Rube Goldberg machines lately. This is a simplified version, really. Teaches him about cause and effect. And honestly, it’s more fun than watching another episode of that cartoon he loves. Besides, it gives me a break from paperwork. It's going to be EPIC! I’ve got the dominoes all lined up and the marble track is almost finished. I just need to figure out how to make the final lever trigger properly. Dad, can you help me with this spring? It's a bit stiff. Sure, mate. Needs a bit of lubrication. Here you go. Just be careful not to hurt yourself. Sorry, interrupting. Just needed a quick snack. What’s all the commotion? Sounds like a workshop in here. We're building a contraption designed to… well, theoretically trap a mouse. But let's be honest, it’s more likely to collapse on itself. It’s all Finn’s idea. Classic. He’s always been inventive. Remember that cardboard robot he made out of cereal boxes when he was seven? It almost set the kitchen on fire. Oh, goodness. Burning kitchens and mousetraps. This is rather chaotic, isn’t it? I thought I heard a small explosion. Just the usual family fun, Margaret. Finn’s teaching us about engineering. Engineering involving potential structural failure, clearly. When I was over in Boston, for that library conference, they had an amazing children’s museum. They had a whole section dedicated to levers and pulleys… far more sophisticated than this, of course. That reminds me, you were talking about your cousin Sarah's children, weren't you? The ones living in America? How are they getting on? Last I heard, they were in Florida. They’re good! Ethan’s really into baseball now. Proper fanatic. Little Mia is obsessed with cheerleading, which is… quite something to watch. Honestly, Sarah sends videos. It's all pom-poms and athleticism. Quite different to the gentle games we played as children. It’s extraordinary, isn’t it? The American enthusiasm for everything. They do seem to embrace… extremes. I remember reading a report about how children’s birthday parties are just these lavish, themed extravaganzas. It's all about showmanship, isn’t it?

Honestly, darling, you won't  believe  what I've found. Absolutely incredible! I'm practically buzzing. Let me guess, another haul from that silk market we passed? You know your willpower is showing cracks when you're approaching those places. Did you at least manage to haggle properly this time? Haggle? Please! I was a force to be reckoned with. I got almost thirty percent off the whole lot. And it’s not  just  the market, although there were a few treasures there. I also went into that little boutique near the Bund, the one with the incredibly stylish woman running it. The one that looks like she walked straight out of a Vogue spread? I remember. She gives off serious ‘I judge your style choices silently’ vibes. What did you buy? Don't keep me in suspense! Well, first, a stunning silk cheongsam. Deep jade green, embroidered with tiny silver cranes. It's just… exquisite. The fit is perfect, even with my slightly stubborn waist. I thought you’d really appreciate the craftsmanship. They hand-sewed those cranes, apparently. Jade green, you say? That'll look fantastic on you. Very sophisticated. Did you try it on in the shop, or are you planning a dramatic reveal later? I did try it on! And it made me feel like Audrey Hepburn meets… well, a very chic Chinese opera singer. It's completely different from anything I own. I needed something a bit… striking for the conference next month, you know? Something that says "intelligent British lecturer" but also, "I travel and appreciate beautiful things." You always manage to combine those two descriptions perfectly. What else? Don't tell me you stopped there. No, of course not! I found this amazing cashmere scarf. It's a sort of charcoal grey, with these subtle geometric patterns woven in. Perfect for layering when it gets chilly. I thought it would go nicely with that navy blue coat I got last year. Good thinking. Cashmere is a necessity here; the air conditioning can be brutal. Is it soft? Because if it’s scratchy, you have my permission to return it. It's like being enveloped in a cloud, darling. Honestly, you have to feel it to believe it. And then... there's this. . Right. That's... something. What  is  that? It looks like a parrot exploded on a garment. Don’t be ridiculous! It’s whimsical!

Well, that was a match, wasn’t it? A right scrape it was! Thought we were done for there for a bit, didn't ye? Ulster put up a good fight, I'll give ‘em that. But the lads held on. It was mental, Dad! Absolutely mental! That try in the last ten minutes? Unreal! I was shouting the house down. Are you gonna watch the Ireland match next week? Please say yes! Honestly, I was near having a heart attack! My nerves are shot. Though, I did enjoy it, I suppose. More exciting than the telly, that’s for sure. Did you manage to see Oisin’s face during that try? He was a picture! Aye, a good win indeed. Though, modern rugby… it's a lot faster than when I was a lass, that’s for sure. All this sprinting and tackling. Used to be a bit more… measured, you know? Like a strategic dance, back then. Reminds me a bit of the school games we used to play, though we didn’t have all the fancy gear. Strategic dance, Mary! That's a grand way of putting it. But it does need the heart, doesn’t it? The grit. Ulster had plenty of that. Oisin, love, you were quiet during the crucial moments. Were you enjoying it? Yeah, Dad! I was. I was just… concentrating! I was thinking about what the players would do next. It's like chess, but with tackling! That’s my boy! Always thinking. Right, well, I’ve signed the birthday card for Auntie Moira. It’s lovely, isn’t it? I got her a little something too, a scented candle. She loves a good lavender scent. Good woman. We should get moving on that, Sarah. I'll pop down after I've had a wee rest. This match took a lot out of me. I’ve got a card for her as well. Simple, but heartfelt. It’s important, you know, to let people know you're thinking of them. Especially now. I’m a bit sleepy now, Dad. Can we have a look at the stars later? If it's clear out, I mean. Mr. Davies said we might see meteor showers. Of course, son. We’ll have a wee peek. After Oisin’s tucked in, mind you. He’ll be needing his beauty sleep. Sarah, are you going to get him ready for bed?

Honestly, Liv, I’m completely overwhelmed. This whole moving thing is just… colossal. I thought coordinating language data sets was stressful, but finding a flat in Cambridge? It's a whole different level. Tell me about it. Lincoln's surprisingly competitive for rentals, but Cambridge… you’ve chosen well for potential job opportunities though, haven't you? So, what’s the biggest hurdle right now? Aside from the general panic, obviously. The estate agents. They're either ridiculously pushy or completely unresponsive. And the sheer number of viewings! I feel like I spend all my free time dodging people’s elbows to get a look at a damp patch. And all the places are either ridiculously tiny or cost an arm and a leg. Did you ever feel like that when you found your place in Lincoln? A little. It took a while, yeah. I ended up going with a slightly older place, but it had a lovely garden, which was a big plus. Honestly, just try to stay calm. You'll find something. What about your sister, Emily? Has she offered you any of her old furniture? She’s been lovely, actually. Offered me her sofa, which is brilliant. And you know how Emily is, always hoarding clothes. She was saying she has loads of stuff she's ‘just holding onto’ that I could have. It's a goldmine, really - barely worn designer bits she bought on sale and never used. It's almost embarrassing to take so much! Emily being Emily! Don't feel bad. Sharing is caring, especially when it’s designer! Saves you a fortune and helps declutter her place. It’s win-win. Speaking of families, my brother, Tom, is finally thinking about having kids. He and his wife, Chloe, are going all out with the baby prep – nursery themed around dinosaurs, the works. Dinosaurs? Seriously? How delightfully nerdy. That’s amazing though! Are they nervous? I remember feeling completely terrified when I realised I'd be responsible for a tiny human. Massively. Chloe's reading all the books, doing all the courses. Tom pretends he's not phased, but you can see the worry in his eyes! They’re debating what language to introduce early. Chloe wants to start with French, she always regretted not sticking with it at school. Tom's leaning towards Spanish, says it’s more widely spoken. That’s a good debate to have.

Right then, so, you two actually  enjoy  watching those proper posh accents on telly? Like, the ones where they sound like they’re swallowing a dictionary? Well, relax, Liam, it's not about  enjoying  posh accents. It’s about understanding how language evolves, you know? The Received Pronunciation thing - there’s a structure to it, a history. Fascinating, really. Besides, some of the acting is pretty good. I’m re-watching 'The Crown' actually. Sounds a bit dull to me. Give me something with a bit of grit. Like, proper East London geezer accents. Those are brilliant. Can’t beat a good bit of slang. Right, because  your  Luton accent is just the pinnacle of linguistic achievement, is it, George? You sound like a pigeon with a mouthful of gravel half the time. Hey, it's authentic! Where's your sense of heritage, Liam? You're supposed to be from Bedfordshire, defending our regional pride! Besides, I’ve picked up bits and pieces growing up around my Cypriot family. Proper mix of influences. That’s true, George, there's a lot to unpack with your background - Cypriot influences in Luton… interesting dialectal shifts. It’s why linguistics is so compelling! Have you ever thought about documenting it? It would be a really clever project. Documenting Luton pigeon? The world wouldn’t thank you for it. Anyway, speaking of skills, did you see that UFC fight the other night? Proper brutal. Makes you think about self-defence, doesn't it? Always good to know how to look after yourself, innit? Yeah, absolutely. I've been considering taking a Krav Maga class. A gardener needs to be able to handle himself. You get some weirdos trying to haggle you down on prices. Actually, I was reading about the neurological benefits of martial arts. Apparently, it's fantastic for cognitive function. And it’s not just about fighting; it's a discipline, a mindfulness practice. Mindfulness? You’re taking this a bit far, aren’t you? I just like the idea of punching someone in the face if they're being a right pain. Though, thinking about it, I've been feeling a bit sluggish lately. Maybe I need to cut down on the fags and biscuits. Don't talk about biscuits! Mine are playing up something fierce today. Too much cheese and onion, I reckon. Classic George! You never fail to entertain us.

Honestly, I don't know why I bother trying to make a remotely healthy dinner on a weeknight. It's always a race against the clock, and then I just end up eating half of it standing over the sink. Don't be dramatic. It smells lovely. And you’re trying to save money, remember? Takeaways add up fast. We talked about this. I  know  we talked about it. It's just... the commute alone saps so much energy. And then I’m thinking about that dreadful near miss I had this morning. Near miss? Tell me everything. What happened? Was it the usual nightmare on the A1? Worse. It was on a back road, trying to avoid the A1, ironically. Some idiot in a shiny, brand-new BMW decided he  absolutely  needed to overtake a tractor. On a blind bend. I saw him just in time, had to slam on the brakes. My heart’s still hammering. Oh, wow. That’s terrifying. You alright? Did you get out and check everything was okay? Yeah, I did. He was being all apologetic, the typical ‘my mistake, terribly sorry’ routine. He didn’t seem to realise how close he came to seriously hurting someone. Honestly, I'm beginning to hate driving. I get it. It's stressful. But public transport around here is… a joke. It wouldn't work for your hours. Have you looked at electric cars again? Electric cars? Seriously? You know how much those cost! And the charging situation is still a mess. Plus, with the commute, the range anxiety would be crippling. I’d spend half my life searching for a charging station. True, the upfront cost is a hurdle. But think about the running costs though. No petrol, drastically reduced maintenance… over time, it could actually work out cheaper. I did some digging the other day and there are some decent government grants still available, even for used EVs. I did glance at some figures, but I dismissed it. It felt like a massive leap. And what about finding a parking spot with a charger? That’s another nightmare. Okay, fair points. But think of the environmental benefit! And they're actually quite fun to drive, surprisingly nippy. Remember when my uncle got that little electric Fiat? He loved it. Actually, he used it for his commute into London. He did. It was cute. But his commute isn't nearly as long as mine.

Right then, love. Grandparents are settling in nicely, aren't they? Nan and Grandad seem right pleased to be 'ere. I made that rhubarb crumble they like so much. Reckon they'll be wanting a bit more later. Aye, they've been having a good natter with you, Auntie Brenda. Grandad was just telling me about when he used to go fishing down the River Hull. Said he caught a whopper once, a proper monster carp. Monster? That’s a load of claptrap, lad! It were a bream, a decent bream, mind you, but a bream! I were fibbing a bit to impress yer Auntie Brenda, you see. She's always been keen on a good story. Don't be exaggerating, Martha. You were embellishing, that’s what you were doing. A bream, indeed! Should've brought the photos, I reckon. Proof of my angling prowess. Oh, you two! Always arguing. Honestly, it’s like being back at school watching my lads bicker. So, are you both comfortable enough? Needed any blankets? It's a bit nippy this evening, innit? I’m alright, Auntie B. Grandad’s complaining a bit about his knees, though. Said they’re playing up something fierce. This damp gets right into 'em, you know. Should've built a proper house, not this draughty thing. Now, now, Grandad. Don’t you start! This “draughty thing” is a perfectly good home and we're grateful you're here. And you know your knees started complaining years before I bought it! Right, I’ll go and see if I can find some heat rub for you. Did you want a cuppa, Grandad? Aye, a cuppa would be lovely, love. Strong, mind. Like you used to make it for me when I were a lad. Speaking of lad, Auntie B, you were saying you needed to order some new light bulbs? The hall light's been flickering something awful. That's right. I’ll have to do that online tomorrow. I was thinking, maybe a warmer tone for the living room? It's a bit harsh with the overhead lights on. What do you reckon, love? Warmer sounds nice. Maybe some of those smart ones, too? You know, the ones you can control with your phone. Smart bulbs! What’s wrong with a good old-fashioned switch, eh? All this technology... causing nothing but bother, it is. Back in my day… Don't you start your “back in my day” spiel, Martha.

Right, pirates sorted for now. Leo, you were a  very  convincing Captain Bluebeard. And Elsie, your parrot was brilliant! Squawking and everything. I said, "Polly wants a biscuit!" Wasn't I good, Mummy? I found treasure! You did! Excellent treasure hunting, Leo. Now, we need to fuel these pirates. Fish fingers tonight? Or do we need to sail to a different island for something else? Fish fingers! With beans! Please! Can I have ketchup?  Lots  of ketchup? Of course, you can have ketchup. So, pirates aside, we have a very busy week ahead! Shakespeare Week at school starts on Monday. I’m so excited. We’re doing  A Midsummer Night’s Dream  - lots of fairies and mischief. Fairies! Can I be a fairy, Mummy? A sparkly one! Absolutely, sweetheart. You’d be a brilliant fairy. And remember what we talked about? We’re actually going to Stratford-upon-Avon at the weekend! To see a proper Shakespeare play! Stratford?! Is that where Shakespeare lived? It is! It's a really beautiful place, Leo. Full of history. We can look at his house and everything. It'll be like stepping back in time. Will there be real swords? Like Leo’s? Maybe some! Depending on the production. But even better, we've got that circus workshop booked for Saturday afternoon. Remember? A  real  circus! Not just a tent, but a proper circus school. Really? Can I learn to juggle? Or walk on a tightrope? We’ll see what they offer, won't we? They’ve got everything from juggling to acrobatics to… even magic! I’ve seen a little preview online, and it looks amazing. It's going to be much more than just learning tricks; they'll talk about the history of the circus too. Magic! I want to learn magic! Can you teach me, Mummy? I can try! I'm not exactly David Copperfield, you know. But we can definitely learn some basic card tricks. Or, did you know we could even make our own little stop motion animation film? Stop… what now? It’s like making a little movie, but photographing something very slightly different each time, then playing the pictures back really fast. Like those old films of Lego characters moving. We could make a pirate movie! With Leo as Captain Bluebeard, of course. With my parrot squawking! And I can be the mermaid who gives them treasure!

Honestly, David, you wouldn’t  believe  the trouble I got into. It still makes me chuckle, even after all these years. It was back when I was teaching in Jeddah… trying to sail from there to Cyprus. Sounds romantic, doesn't it? Romantic until you’re being questioned by the Saudi police, I imagine, Penelope. Jeddah to Cyprus? That’s quite the ambition for a novice sailor, even a determined one like yourself. What happened? Determined is one word for it! Reckless is another. I’d bought this beautiful, slightly-past-its-prime sailboat. And I thought, “Right, I’ll just pop across the Red Sea.” Didn't realise the paperwork alone would be an entire saga. Apparently, leisure sailing is… frowned upon in Saudi Arabia. Very frowned upon. Frowned upon? Penelope, you were practically committing an act of rebellion! I can just picture you, defiant and covered in seawater. Reminds me of the student protests I used to witness at the university. So, what was the arrest like? Elaborate! Well, they stopped me about an hour out of Jeddah. Quite sternly, I might add. Lots of pointing and shouting in Arabic, which, naturally, I didn’t understand. Eventually, a young officer, who spoke a little English, explained I was violating numerous maritime laws. And apparently, insulting the nation’s sensibilities. Something about a foreign woman sailing alone. I was hauled in, questioned for hours, the whole shebang. I was rather indignant, I must say. "I’m just going for a little sail!" I kept protesting. Good heavens, Penelope! How utterly preposterous. Insulting the nation’s sensibilities? The world's gone mad. I can’t say I’m surprised about the paperwork, though. Saudi Arabia is notoriously… meticulous. Did you ever make it to Cyprus? No, Reginald, I did not. I was deported the very next day. My boat was… impounded. Let’s just say I learned a valuable lesson about international maritime law. Teaching English to wealthy Saudi families was considerably less stressful! You know, it reminds me somewhat of my own experiences. Though less dramatic, of course. Teaching in Riyadh was fascinating. The absence of alcohol was quite… noticeable. Though, we did find some rather ingenious ways to acquire it. Let’s just say some expatriate gatherings took place on rooftops. Rooftop gatherings. That's a classic. I recall a similar phenomenon in Cairo. It was surprisingly difficult to find a decent pint.

Right, so, update time. Leo's been… spirited this week, hasn’t he, Brenda? Honestly, the bathroom situation is just escalating. He's leaving his wet towels  everywhere . Seriously, I walked in this morning and there was one draped over the cat. The cat looked utterly bewildered. Oh, teenagers! They do try, don’t they? Mine used to leave trails of socks like little breadcrumbs leading to the sofa. It’s a phase, love. Though, a cat? That’s a new level of rebellion. At least he’s not trying to dye his hair blue again. Remember that fiasco? What’s all the shouting about? And it wasn't a  trail  of socks, Mum. I put them in a pile. A perfectly reasonable pile. A pile strategically placed to trip unsuspecting adults, apparently. And 'shouting'? I was merely observing a domestic situation, Leo. A situation involving feline distress. The cat was fine. He likes towels. Anyway, can we talk about the summer trip? Mr. Davies is arranging a trip to the Eden Project for the geography club. It’d be amazing, but it’s £150. The Eden Project! That sounds brilliant, love! You should definitely go. Fifteen quid is a lot though. Have you thought about earning some of it yourself? It teaches you responsibility, you know. Remember when I got my first bit of pocket money doing Saturday mornings at the bakery? Yeah, but I don’t want to work at a bakery. I'm thinking about asking Mrs. Henderson down the road if she needs a babysitter. She has those twins, remember? That’s a fantastic idea! Mrs. Henderson's lovely, and the twins are adorable. You’d be brilliant with them, Leo. It would look great on your CV too, you know. Speaking of opportunities, I've been looking at some work experience placement options for you for next year. There’s that digital marketing agency in Tamworth… it’s a bit of a commute, but could be a good insight. That’s clever, Sarah. You're always thinking ahead. Though, remember when I tried to convince Mark to do work experience at a car dealership? He lasted half an hour! Said it was ‘soul-destroying.' Oh, bless him. He was always more interested in football. Speaking of, did you see his refereeing performance on Saturday? He was actually quite good, remarkably fair, considering he was officiating his mate's match.

Right, so, another two hours until we get to Rovinj, roughly? This road is a bit… intense, isn't it, Dad? Like, seriously winding. I’m getting a bit travel sick. Aye, love, it’s Istria. It's all hills and valleys. Best lookin' at somethin' still, then. Don’t be lookin’ at the road constantly. Lessen the sickness. You alright, Liam? You've been quiet. Fine. Just… bored. And hot. Can we put the air con up a bit, Nan? Already done, pet. Just not on full blast, don't want to drain the battery. Your Uncle David’s been telling me all about the truffles they find around here, mind. Apparently, they’re proper gold dust. He reckons we should try and find a restaurant with a proper truffle hunting experience. Gold dust is a slight exaggeration, isn't it, Margaret? They’re undeniably valuable, of course, but the market is… volatile. Besides, you’ll end up paying a fortune for a few shavings on your pasta. Remember that restaurant in Florence? The truffle oil was synthetic! A travesty. Oh god, don’t remind me. That was awful. I’d rather have undercooked chicken than fake truffle oil. Seriously, Nan, David's always going on about the food. It's like he thinks he's suddenly become a Michelin star chef. Remember when he tried to make Yorkshire puddings? Disaster. He’s enthusiastic, that’s all. He means well. Your Uncle David used to be brilliant at football, y’know. Could have gone professional, he could. Shame about the knee injury. Did he  really ? He always seems… boring now. Talks too much about work and stuff. He was quite the footballer, actually. I saw him play once, many years ago. Good pace, decent touch. It's a pity. However, comparing that to culinary pursuits… a tad ambitious, wouldn't you say? Speaking of ambition, did you ever hear about that new research with stem cells? Apparently, they're getting closer to being able to…regrow damaged cartilage. Maybe Uncle David could get his knee fixed! Stem cells, eh? Fancy that. I remember reading somethin' about it down the paper. Seems like science fiction a bit, doesn’t it? Still, if it could help people… It’s an incredibly exciting field, Eleanor. The potential is astonishing. Ethically complex, of course, but potentially transformative. You know, I was discussing this with a colleague the other day, a specialist in regenerative medicine.

Honestly, this quinoa is tougher than a week-old biscuit. I swear, they’re trying to actively discourage us from eating lunch here. Dramatic, Elara. It’s quinoa. You’ve had worse. Besides, free lunch isn't exactly something to complain about, is it? Especially in this economy. Tell me about it. My student loan repayments started this month. Suddenly, free quinoa looks very appealing indeed. I’m rationing the crisps, you know. Rationing crisps? You’re a soldier, Tom. I’m genuinely impressed, if slightly concerned. Mark, you’re usually surrounded by a mountain of those cheesy puffs. What's happened to you? I’m attempting to be fiscally responsible, Elara. My boss is on a 'wellness initiative' kick. Apparently, horrifying amounts of processed cheese aren’t conducive to peak marketing performance. Peak marketing performance… Sounds terrifying. What are you working on at the moment, Mark? Something to sell me more things I don't need? Guilty as charged. Right now, it's a campaign for a new AI writing tool aimed at academics. Very meta. Basically, we’re persuading people to use AI to write persuasive copy. That  is  meta. And slightly dystopian. My research team is actually looking into the impact of generative AI on language evolution. Trying to figure out if these tools will fundamentally alter how we speak and write. It’s… complex. Wow, that sounds heavy. I’m just coordinating project timelines and battling spreadsheets. Far less apocalyptic. Though, honestly, battling spreadsheets  can  feel apocalyptic sometimes. What kind of impact are you seeing, Elara? Early stages, really. But there’s already a noticeable shift in online communication. More standardized phrasing, a flattening of nuance and… frankly, less interesting prose. It’s like everything’s being homogenized. People are starting to sound like they're all using the same template. That could be a good thing, in some respects. Clarity, consistency… My clients are always complaining about jargon and unclear messaging. A little standardization might be beneficial. Beneficial for  you , maybe, Mark. But what about the richness of the English language? The beauty of regional dialects? The sheer joy of a well-crafted sentence that deviates from the norm? We’re losing that, aren’t we? You're painting a very bleak picture, Elara. But I suppose you  do  spend your days analyzing language data. I just hear more and more people using the same buzzwords – ‘synergy’, ‘leverage’, ‘disrupt’…

Honestly, this is lovely, isn’t it? So much greener than Cambridge, even after all the rain we’ve had. And so… peaceful. I can't believe we're actually in Poland, Elara. It feels rather surreal. Aye, it’s cracking, isn't it? Proper change of scenery. Though I'm trying not to think about how little Polish I actually speak. "Dzień dobry" and "proszę" only gets you so far, doesn’t it? Are you sure this route is right? The GPS is being a bit unreliable. Oh, don’t worry about the Polish. Agnieszka says she'll sort everything out. She's fluent, of course. Naturally. She’s ever so clever, that one. And the GPS is usually fine, just a bit...assertive. I remember last time we were driving through the Cotswolds, it insisted we reverse down a one-way street! We'll be fine. Just keep an eye on the signposts. They’re surprisingly clear. Right, assertive is a good word for it. Last time it sent me on a 'shortcut' through a farmer's field. Covered in mud, I was. Anyway, so, Agnieszka’s house… are we sure this is a good idea? I mean, it's only been a few weeks since we organised this last minute. I’m worried she won't have space for us. It's a bit cramped, isn't it, her flat? She assured me it wouldn’t be a problem. Said she’d cleared out a space on the sofa for me, and you can have the spare room, of course. Don’t fret, darling. Agnieszka wouldn't leave friends stranded. Besides, it's only for a few days. A chance to recuperate before the long drive back. I'm starting to feel a bit travel-weary already. The ferry crossing was rather choppy, you know. Aye, I remember. I felt like I was going to be sea-sick. Still, it's worth it to see her, isn't it? It's been ages. She seemed a bit...stressed when we spoke last. Something about the pressures of her new job. Exactly! That’s why I was keen to come. A bit of English friendship and cake-baking should cheer her up. She misses our chats, she said. And a hot cup of tea. Polish coffee just isn't the same, is it? No, it's not. Fair enough.

Honestly, look at that badge! It's just  swallowing  the crest, isn't it? This new sponsorship deal with ApexTech… it's ruining the whole look of the kit. Proper clashy, it is. Like they’re trying to advertise electronics on a football shirt. It’s the trend, isn’t it? The money talks, as they say. ApexTech are throwing a lot of cash around, and Newcastle need it. Can’t deny that. Though, I agree, it’s a bit… much. Remember when it was just the brewery on the shirt? Simpler times. Aye, simpler times! Gala, wasn’t it? We’d all be queuing up for a pint at the end of the match. You don't get that loyalty anymore. It’s all about the bottom line. They're treating the shirts like giant billboards, and it takes away from the history, doesn't it? Think back to Shearer's shirt...you wouldn't put a massive tech logo on  that . You're right. Nostalgia’s a powerful thing. It’s not just the Newcastle kit, either. Look at Man City’s - practically a giant Etihad Airways logo. It's become less about the club and more about the corporate entity. Though, I think some of the designs themselves are getting pretty awful, too. Remember that Chelsea shirt a few years back, with the abstract pattern? Looked like a rejected textile design. Don't even go there! That was horrific! It looked like a confused optical illusion. Mine's always been a bit iffy, to be honest. I prefer the classic stripes, but they keep trying to "modernise" it, and it just ends up looking… corporate. I'd love to see a retro-inspired kit for one season, just to remind everyone what it used to be like. Proper tradition. That would be amazing. A subtle nod to the history. Maybe just the collar and the sleeve trim. Done tastefully. But you're right, the current obsession with neon colours and clashing patterns... it's a head-scratcher. What do you reckon about those Adidas templates they've been using? Feels a bit… factory-made. Exactly! Like they have one design and just slap different logos on it. It lacks character. It’s all so sterile. Speaking of sterile, I'm starving. Fancy a McDonald's after this? They've got that new spicy McNugget dip. McDonald’s? On a Sunday evening?

Honestly, Dad, it's just… exhausting. Absolutely knackering. Every single day. What is it now, then, Liv? You know I can relax for five minutes? The news is on. Relax? You can relax when you've spent three hours arguing with the Jobcentre about whether I’ve ‘actively sought employment’ after sending out seven applications that haven’t even  acknowledged  my existence. Seven! And they want to know why I’m not volunteering. Where exactly am I supposed to volunteer when I'm spending all my time applying for jobs?! They’re just doing their job, love. Bureaucracy, innit? You know how it is. Used to be the same when I was… well, never mind. You'll get something. Something will turn up. Easy for you to say, Dad. You don't have rent to pay, and student loans looming over you like a very large, very judgemental cloud. It’s not just the job hunt, it’s everything. Mum was on about the gas bill again. Said it’s gone up another ten quid. Ten quid! How are we supposed to cope? Well, turn the heating down. Obviously. And eat less. Cook on the George Foreman. Healthy and cheap. Remember that chicken and peppers I used to make on there? Oh, yes, Dad. The George Foreman delicacies. Trust me, I'm living for it. Seriously though, it's just… I saw Mrs. Henderson from down the street yesterday, flapping about saying her electricity bill was astronomical. Blaming the government, naturally. And all I could think was, ‘Are you even turning your lights off when you leave the room, Mrs. Henderson?’ Honestly, some people! Well, can’t help people being… people. Speaking of people, did you see that bloke on eBay? Trying to sell a box of old buttons for £50! Fifty quid! Cheeky git. It’s just… all these people complaining. And then Aunt Carol’s been going on about how much she’s spending on holidays. Holidays! While I’m budgeting for instant noodles! It’s just not fair, you know? Your Aunt Carol's always been a bit… flashy. Says she deserves it after looking after Mum all these years. Deserves it? She drops round for tea once a week with a box of biscuits and a dramatic recounting of her bunion. And suddenly she's earned a Mediterranean cruise? Now, now, Liv. She’s your aunt.

“Honestly, ANON, you've really got a lovely home. And thank you, Sarah, for doing such a fantastic job, as always. It’s a weight off my shoulders just knowing it’s all so… serene.” "It’s alright, love. Not much to it, really. Just a bit of elbow grease. Glad you like it. Your daughter’s got good taste, she does.” “Elbow grease! That’s what we used to say, Sarah. Back in my day, you'd scrub those floors 'til your arms ached. Not like these new mops – easy peasy, eh?" “Easy peasy indeed, Mum. Though I still prefer a good old-fashioned duster, I must admit. Speaking of aches, I seem to have developed a rather unsightly wart on my hand. Absolutely dreadful, you know. Is it something you can catch, do you think?" “Warts? Ah, my Derek used to get them something awful. My Nan always swore by rubbing them with dock leaves. Said it drew the poison out. Didn't work for him, mind you. Ended up going to the doctor.” "Dock leaves! Now you're talking! My mother used to swear by dandelion and burdock too, for everything. Every ailment under the sun! Though everything tasted like mud, of course." “Dandelion and burdock! I haven't had that in years. Reminds me of being a child. Sarah, are you off to the Co-op later? I’m running low on oat milk.” “Aye, probably. Got to grab some bits for tea tonight. Derek’s got his eye on that ready-made lasagne from Iceland, fancy as he is. It's a nightmare driving through town these days though, absolutely gridlocked. The traffic's something else.” “Traffic! Don't get me started! Remember when you could just… drive? No roundabouts, no sat navs telling you to turn left into a brick wall! My poor Harold, bless him, he had a terrible accident. A lorry, you see.” "Oh, Mum, I'm so sorry. Was it… serious?" “Terrible. They found bits of the car for miles. So sad. Happened just down the road, near the old airfield. Makes you think, doesn’t it? Reminds me of that plane crash they had a few years back. Awful business that. They say it was pilot error.” “I remember that. Proper shock. The news was on all day. Never could understand how they could just  fall  out of the sky.” "It’s just… terrifying, isn’t it?

Honestly, this week has been  brutal . Mr. Davies set us another essay on ‘The Significance of the Green Light in The Great Gatsby’. Like, seriously? We just finished Gatsby! Don't they think we've got anything else going on? Tell me about it. Mrs. Hawthorne sprung a pop quiz on us in Biology. All about mitosis! Mitosis! Who even remembers that stuff? I swear, she just likes to see us squirm. Squirm is an understatement! I practically blanked. I wrote about... I don't know, plants. Just something green. Hoped for some vague connection. Did you do okay? Not really. I panicked and drew a diagram. A really bad diagram. It looked like a purple amoeba trying to eat a sunflower. Mr. Sharma saw it and just... raised an eyebrow. It was mortifying. Oh my god! A purple amoeba? That’s brilliant, actually. Way better than my vaguely green plant theory. He has a good sense of humour, doesn’t he? Remember when he pretended to be a volcano for the Year 7s? Legend! Okay, but back to misery. My mum says I need to start thinking about my Art portfolio. Apparently, I need to show "creative vision" and "technical proficiency." What even  is  creative vision? It sounds pretentious. I know, right? Like everything’s gotta be so serious. I quite like just, you know, making things. I’ve been messing around with charcoal portraits lately. They’re terrible, obviously, but it’s fun. Ooh, can I see? You’re really good at drawing, you know. Better than most people, even. I keep trying to do landscapes, but they always end up looking like slightly melted broccoli. Broccoli landscapes… that's a new one! Look, I’ll show you some of my sketches. They're on my tablet. But honestly, I'm stressed about English. This essay… It’s due Monday, and I haven’t even started. Monday's ages away. You'll be fine. Maybe look at some critical analyses online? That always helps me, although half of it just goes straight over my head. I've had a look, but it's all so complicated. "Symbolic representation" this, "the inherent patriarchy" that... It's exhausting! Do you think they're using trainee teachers to set the work, just to give them practice marking? My sister said something like that! Apparently, there's loads of them this year.

This is boring, Mum. Peas again? And we're talking about  religion  again? Seriously? It's important, love. And it's good to talk about these things. Liam’s going to grow up knowing a bit about different beliefs, isn’t he? Besides, your Grandpa was very religious, and I think it’s nice to keep the conversation going. But Grandpa was obsessed. He used to tell me stories about nuns chasing him with rulers when he was a kid. It wasn't exactly inspiring. And then you were going on about  The Matrix  the other day? What's that got to do with anything? Well, think about it. The Matrix is all about questioning what's real, choosing your own truth. It’s a bit like… finding your own faith, isn't it? Adapting something to  you , rather than just blindly following. I don’t know. It just seems… complicated. My friend, Finn, his mum's really into Scientology. He says it’s all about unlocking your inner power. Sounds a bit… weird. Scientology... that is a complex one. I read something about it once, it seemed… controlling, somehow. Liam, darling, do you want a bit more apple? . See? Sometimes simple things are best. A good lunch, a happy baby… that’s its own kind of blessing, isn't it? But what about bigger questions? Like, why are we here? What happens when we die? Finn reckons Scientology has all the answers. Finn’s mum seems a very intense woman. Answers aren’t always what they seem, love. Sometimes, the  searching  for answers is more important than finding a definitive one. Remember Mrs. Peterson from school? She was convinced she’d solved the mysteries of the universe. Turned out she was just reading a lot of science fiction. Yeah, but… she seemed happy. Happiness isn’t about having all the answers, Daniel. It’s about having good people around you, finding joy in the small things, and being kind. Remember what your nan always said? "A full heart is better than a full head." Yeah, I remember. But still… what about those nuns? Grandpa swore they were after him for stealing sweets. Oh, your Grandpa! He always did embellish a story. He probably just didn't like doing his chores. It doesn't mean all nuns are bad. They dedicate their lives to helping others. It’s a different kind of faith, a different path.

Right, so are you sure this is the right way, Liam? 'Cos it feels like we've been driving around in circles for ages. I swear, my stomach’s doing flips. Reckon I need another ginger biscuit. Relax, Chloe. It's fine, it's just… these country lanes aren't exactly intuitive. The sat nav's a bit dodgy sometimes. And yes, you can have a biscuit. Honestly, you and your constant need for ginger biscuits. It’s a miracle you’re still a size ten. Cheeky! And for your information, I like to keep my blood sugar stable, alright? Especially after spending all morning wrestling with the weirdest data sets for the corpus. Apparently, someone's been trying to codify the use of 'thee' and 'thou' in 18th-century novels. Proper head-scratcher, that. Like, who even uses that anymore? Feels like Old English homework. You’d probably know more about it than me. I was knee-deep in stress analysis for a new bridge design all day. Far more practical, wouldn’t you say? Though, I did stumble across a fascinating paper on the historical development of standardised weights and measures. Metric versus imperial… a surprisingly contentious issue, even now. Ooh, tell me more! I’m always up for a good debate. Did you know my granda used to rage about having to convert pints to litres? "They're tryin' ta take away our heritage, lad!" he'd shout. Proper dramatic, he was. Speaking of dramatic, did you see that documentary about Billie Eilish last night? Honestly, she’s handling all that fame so well, for someone so young. There’s a lot of ageism out there, isn’t there? People expecting you to be a certain way at a certain age. Absolutely. Although, I wouldn’t put myself in the same league as Billie Eilish, obviously. But I agree. The pressure on young people, especially in the public eye, is immense. It's mad really. Did you finish that series we were watching on LoveFilm? That Scandinavian detective one? 'Borga'? Aye, finished it last night! Gripping, wasn't it? Proper bleak though. It made me wanna book a beach holiday, just to get away from all that gloom. Thinking Barbados, maybe? Or is that too extravagant? Remember when we talked about going to Greece? Greece is still top of my list. Barbados would be nice, but a bit pricey.

Right, so, are we actually  going  to talk about this driving, Dad? Because honestly, you're gripping the wheel like you’re wrestling a badger. Mum, tell him! Now, Elodie, your dad's just… thorough. He likes to know where he's going. And this road! It's winding like a snake. Doesn’t want to end up in Slovenia by mistake, does he? Slovenia is lovely, actually. We could detour. A bit of Ljubljana wouldn’t hurt. Although, considering the pace, we’ll be there by next Tuesday. Can we  please  put on some music? This silence is killing me. Something a bit… louder, maybe? Sons of Anarchy soundtrack? Or something? Now  that’s  what I'm talking about, Finn! Anything but Dad's classical playlist. Seriously, Dad, you’ve got more Bach than sense sometimes. Bach is a cornerstone of Western civilisation, Elodie. And I find it immensely soothing. Unlike some people’s… preferences. Alright, alright, settle down, you two. John, put something on Finn can enjoy. Elodie, be nice to your dad. It's a long drive, and we’re in beautiful Istria. Look at those olive groves! Absolutely stunning. Remember that little restaurant we found last year, near Rovinj, that served the most incredible olive oil? Oh, yeah! The one with the tiny terrace overlooking the sea? We absolutely  have  to go back. And find some more of those lavender sachets they used to have. I’m practically running on lavender right now. This is much better! Whoa, this is good. Lavender? Really? I was thinking we should focus on wine this trip. Istrian Malvasia is divine. And the vineyards around Motovun… spectacular. We could spend a whole day just wandering through them. We should. Though I’m still picturing that market in Pula. All those fresh vegetables, the local cheeses… Finn would love it. He's always been partial to a good bit of cheese. Proper cheese! Not that processed stuff. And maybe some gelato? A big one. You and your gelato! We'll get you plenty, Finn. Maybe we could look at camping a few nights? Found this blog post about some amazing campsites with little caravans, right on the coast. Imagine waking up to the sound of the waves… Caravans? Good heavens, no. That’s a holiday from a holiday. I'd rather face a boardroom full of disgruntled CEOs. We’re renting a villa, remember?

Right, so you’re  sure  you got the whole thing? Like, all of it? Because I’m having a right mental blank trying to remember the specifics, you know? Absolutely, Liv. I recorded the whole thing. Every… embarrassing… detail. It's safely on my phone, password protected, of course. No need to panic. Though, honestly, I still can’t believe you guys agreed to let me. Agreed is a strong word, El. More like… peer pressured by you. And, fair do’s, it was hilarious. Remember when Maisie accidentally kicked the sofa? Oh my god, yeah! She went flying. Thought she'd broken her ankle. Honestly, that whole session was just chaos, wasn’t it? Pure carnage. But seriously, El, why did you even want to record it? Not like you’ve never filmed us playing games before. This is different. Well, yeah, but… it was a particularly special game night, innit? Besides, I thought it’d be hilarious to look back on, years from now. Remember us being… well,  this  ridiculous. It’s likely we'll all be proper boring grown-ups by then. Tax returns and sensible shoes and all that. Don’t even speak of grown-up stuff. I’m still trying to figure out how to pay for laundry. Tell me about it. My overdraft is weeping. Though, laughing at our past blunders might be a decent distraction from financial ruin. So, what game  was  it, exactly? I’m drawing a complete blank. Something silly, I remember… Jackbox! We played Fibbage XL and Quiplash. You were  brutal  in Quiplash, Liv. Absolutely brutal. Remember that answer you gave about cats stealing socks? It got everyone. Oh yeah! I remember that one now. It was hysterical. Maisie’s face was priceless. She thought I was being serious! Honestly, she's a bit daft sometimes. A bit daft? Maisie's a legend. She’s the one who suggested we all wear matching onesies. That was peak game night. Okay, that was a good idea. I still have the unicorn onesie. A unicorn onesie! You wore a unicorn onesie while attempting to be witty in Quiplash? That’s peak Doncaster right there. See? Exactly what I was talking about! That’s why I recorded it. Evidence of our glorious, chaotic youth. I’m going to make a highlight reel. Maybe even add some cheesy music. Oh god, please don't. You'll traumatize us.

Right then, this coffee's alright. Not brilliant, mind you. Reminds me of that stuff they used to serve at the old Pelaw Social Club. Could strip paint with it. You two grabbin' somethin' to eat later? I'm starvin'. I was thinking about the student union. They've got that new Thai place, didn’t they? Heard it’s pretty good. Though, last time I went, the queue was ridiculous. Ridiculous is an understatement, Liv. It snaked right past the library entrance. I spent half an hour just trying to see if there was any actual movement. Ended up with a soggy cheese sandwich from the shop instead. Not ideal. Thai, eh? Never been a massive fan, to be honest. Too many…bits. I'm a simple lad, me. Give me a good pie and peas any day. Proper Northern comfort food, that is. Remember Betty’s Bakery in Gateshead? Their steak and onion pasties…now they were somethin' special. Oh, you and your pies, Derek! We get it. You’re a traditionalist. But Thai food can be amazing! It’s all about the balance of sweet, sour, spicy, and salty. Have you  ever  tried Pad See Ew? It’s basically noodles with soy sauce and vegetables… pretty mild, even for someone who’s wary of "bits”. Liv's right, Derek. There are plenty of options that aren't fiery. Plus, it's a nice change from the usual suspects around here. Everything’s either burger or chips, isn’t it? Or a vaguely depressing salad. Aye, that's it, isn't it? Burger, chips, or sadness. Not much in between. I had a pasty for lunch, though. A proper Cornish one, not some cheap imitation. Got it from that little deli down by the station. Best I've had in years. That reminded me, I need to pop in tomorrow and stock up. A Cornish pasty? Wow, you’re spoiling us! I keep meaning to try one. Are they really as good as people say? They are, lass. They are. A proper hearty meal in a pastry casing. Full of potato, turnip, beef, onion… simple ingredients, but done well. No fancy sauces or weird spices. Just good, honest food. It's filling too – you won't be hungry for hours. Sounds tempting, actually. Maybe I'll join you tomorrow, Derek. I don’t think I can face another soggy cheese sandwich.

Right then, social media. It's the bane of my existence, really. I spend all day dealing with people's queries, some of which could have been easily resolved with a quick Google search. And you lot, with your fancy library services, you've got to be on Facebook and Twitter and… whatever else is popping up these days. It feels like a full-time job on top of the one I already have. You’re not wrong, Pete. It  is  a beast. But think of it as outreach, really. We’re trying to connect with the students where they are. Trying to show them we’re more than just dusty books and shushing. I saw a student the other day, googling “where’s the library?” He was standing right outside the entrance! A quick post about opening hours and directions on Instagram would have saved us both a lot of time. You fellas are moaning a bit, aren’t you? It’s brilliant! I've got this group on Facebook, “Salford Uni Lit Lovers,” and it's just  thriving . People recommending reads, swapping opinions on authors… I even managed to get a local author to do a Q&A live stream. Far more engaging than those dreary library flyers we used to stick on the noticeboard. A live stream, eh? Sounds a bit… flashy for Radcliffe lads like me. I keep picturing myself trying to explain hashtags. I wouldn’t even know where to start. My niece tries to show me TikTok, and I just end up looking bewildered. Apparently, there’s a dance I’m supposed to do to a sped-up 80s song? Absolute madness. Pete, you’re a legend! TikTok dancing? That’s pure gold. You wouldn't be the first to struggle, though. I tried to explain memes to my mum last week. She just stared blankly and asked if it was a new brand of tea. My grandkids keep trying to teach me about “challenges.” Apparently, you have to recreate a scene from a movie using household objects. I tried to do 'The Godfather' with a mop and a colander. It didn't quite capture the gravitas, I must admit. Though my cat did look suitably menacing as the consigliere. A cat consigliere! That’s fantastic. See, you’re having fun with it. Maybe I'm being too cynical. It's just… the sheer volume of information is overwhelming.

Right then, David, thank you for fitting me in. This office is… rather more impressive than my little workspace at home! It’s lovely to be in Tunbridge Wells, though. A bit more…refined than Stratford, let’s say. So, the tape, as you mentioned. I've been having a think about it. I think a documentary style approach would be best, capturing the real heart of the project - the people. Showing the consultation process, interviewing families, nurses... Aye, that’s what I was hoping for, Eleanor. Something that doesn't feel staged or forced. The glossy brochures are all well and good, but they don’t convey the  need . We need to show why this hospice is essential, not just a nice-to-have. Have you had a chance to properly review the business case the team put together? I have, yes. The numbers are solid, absolutely, but I think a visual element will really amplify the argument. The rationale for the location is… interesting. Why Tunbridge Wells, specifically? There are hospice beds needed across the county, aren’t there? It’s a complex decision. We looked at several locations. Primarily, access and demographics. Tunbridge Wells has a relatively affluent, ageing population. Good transport links, too. But crucially, the existing local health services are… stretched, to put it mildly. We can provide vital support that's currently lacking. The funding models, you see, don’t really encourage proactive end-of-life care. It’s all reactive rather than supportive. That's so frustrating. The postcode lottery of healthcare still exists, doesn’t it? What about relationships with the existing hospices? Have you consulted them? We don't want to be seen as competing, but rather collaborating. Absolutely. I’ve had several meetings with the heads of Hospices of Hope and Demelza. It's been… delicate. They’re understandably concerned about resource sharing, but I've stressed that our focus will be on the more complex cases, the patients with specific needs they might not be able to accommodate. And, importantly, we are committed to providing training for local healthcare professionals. That benefits everyone. Good. That proactive approach is vital. Now, about the patients themselves… Have you considered how we might sensitively document their stories? We need informed consent, of course, and to protect their privacy. The nursing care, particularly at the end of life, is such a delicate and precious thing.

Oh, look at this! Remember this, David? From Sarah's wedding? Honestly, she looked like a princess. And young Tom, so skinny! He's practically a man now. Sarah’s wedding… yes, a lovely day. Though the weather was frightful. Remember that downpour just as they were saying their vows? Everyone was huddled under those ridiculous parasols. Still, they managed to pull it off. Tom  is  a man now, isn’t he? Can’t believe he’s interviewing for that graduate scheme at Barclays. Wow, look how tiny I was! I had such a weird haircut. And Auntie Carol’s dress! Honestly, it glowed in the dark. Did you see that one of Grandad on his motorbike? He looked so cool! He was quite the rebel, your Grandad. Always causing a bit of mischief. Though his riding was probably terrifying back then. Speaking of cool, have you seen those new phone cases, Chloe? The ones that double as little wallets? I was looking at them online earlier. Want to take a look? Might be useful for you, always losing your cards. Ooh, yes! Show me. I’m practically glued to my phone these days, especially for work. Need something practical, though, can't be too bulky for my bag. What about you, Dad? Still clinging onto your flip phone? Flip phone? I have a perfectly good smartphone, thank you very much! It’s just… I don't have the inclination to learn all the new fangled apps. I use it for calls and messages, that’s enough for me. Besides, I’m busy thinking about this Henderson report. It’s a nightmare, honestly. Numbers just aren’t adding up. Sounds stressful, love. You need to put your feet up later. Perhaps we can watch that Ascot documentary we downloaded? All that finery! Makes you want to go, doesn’t it? Though the price of a ticket these days… Royal Ascot! I’d love to go someday. It looks so glamorous. Although, knowing my luck, I'd spill champagne all over myself. Where did you get that recipe for the beef casserole, Mum? It smells divine. Oh, that’s from my nan. She used to make it every Sunday. Bit of Worcestershire sauce, loads of herbs… the secret ingredient is a touch of marmalade, believe it or not! Gives it a lovely sweetness. Right, a bit embarrassing now… this one. Remember your school play, Chloe?

Honestly, Chloe, you're winding me up. "The Babadook"? It's just a load of shadows and mum-guilt dressed up as horror. I've seen scarier things down the aisles of Asda on a Saturday. Right, okay, massively dramatic response, Maisie. You’re seriously missing the point. It’s  subtle . It's psychological. It's about grief and loneliness manifesting in… well, a very unsettling creature. It’s not jump scares, it's creeping dread! You’ve got to appreciate the artistry! Artistry? It's a bloke in a furry suit! I’d be laughing my head off if I saw that thing proper. Remember that film "Red Lights" we watched last year? Now  that  was unsettling. The whole premise – the psychic who was actually a conman – sending shivers down your spine. That’s proper horrifying, innit? Okay, "Red Lights"  was  good, I'll grant you that. But it relied on manipulation and a twist. “The Babadook” builds this atmosphere... it burrowed into my brain! I couldn’t sleep for two nights! It’s about the female experience of motherhood... Oh, ‘experience of motherhood.’ Here we go. Always with the deep analysis, aren’t you? Look, I’m just saying, I need something that actually shouts at me a bit! Something with, like, a monster. Not a metaphor for something clever. Give me a zombie apocalypse any day. Zombies are  so  overdone, Maisie. They’re predictable. Where's the challenge? The nuance? We’ve seen zombies shuffle around for decades. “The Babadook” offers something genuinely new. It plays with your perception. “Plays with your perception." You sound like one of those arty students who try to explain why a beige wall is meaningful. I’m just craving some good, old-fashioned gore. Like “Evil Dead.” Now  that ’s a film. Chainsaws, demons, practical effects… Oh, please, “Evil Dead”? That's just… messy. Gratuitous. It’s trying too hard. It’s like a teenager’s idea of horror. And the acting! Don't even start on the acting. Reckon it is a bit much, I’ll admit. But it’s fun! It's cheeky. You can scream and laugh at the same time. Do you not want a  bit  of fun with your scary films? Everything with you has to be a profound exploration of the human condition! There's nothing wrong with a bit of depth! It enriches the experience.

Right, Grandpa. All settled in for the night? Feeling cosy? Fairly so, love. Though this draught… it’s got a nip to it, even with the fire roaring. Devon air, eh? Takes some getting used to. Wolverhampton was generally a bit milder, you know. Though the winters could be bleak. I’ll see if I can get the heating turned up a little. You’ve been complaining about the chill all day. You know, I was reading an article today about how much energy we’re all wasting on these new gadgets. Ipad batteries draining overnight, smart speakers blabbing away… seemingly pointless, really. Gadgets, eh? I remember when a telephone was a significant innovation. You needed a operator! Now, you’ve got things that order you pizza and book holiday homes! It's all rather bewildering. Speaking of pizza, did you order one for later? My stomach's been rumbling something fierce. Thought you'd never ask. I’ve ordered a large pepperoni from Papa Luigi's. Should be here in about half an hour. And speaking of holiday homes… remember that conversation we had about Airbnb? I was thinking, if we were to ever redo the furniture in the spare room, perhaps we could put it up on Airbnb for a few weeks a year. Extra income, you see. Airbnb! Fancy! In my day, if you wanted to let a room, you put a little sign in the window. "Rooms to let." Simple as that. This digital age... it's complicated. Redoing the furniture though… that’s a good idea. That awful floral sofa is an abomination, frankly. It clashes with everything. You’re not wrong! It was Mum's and she insisted on keeping it. I’ve been browsing online, actually.
