It was a nightmare. Everything was different. I felt like I was back at primary school! Thankfully, Mum talked me out of it. Windows 8?! Don't mention it! Gave me palpitations. I still haven't fully recovered. Stick to what you know, I always say. Speaking of things you know… any progress on this dissertation? Yeah, it's coming along. I'm researching how poorly planned industrial towns affected public health in the 19th century.

Cor blimey, Doris. Another one of them scorchers, eh? Feel like a kipper left out in the sun, I do. Honestly, Arthur, you always exaggerate. It's warm, yes, but a kipper? Really? I’ve put the fan on, dear. Is that alright? Fan’s alright, Doris. Just… takes the moisture right out of ya. Remember '76? Now  that  was a summer. Proper drought. Fields were like dust. Your mum had the best roses though, even then. Remember the scent? I do. A proper cloud of fragrance. She used to say it was all about talking to them, you know. Silly, really. Though I did try it with little Emily when she was a toddler, and she  did  seem to perk up. Children. Magic, them. Always were. I never had the chance, though, did I? Always… around. Don’t dwell on it, Arthur. You’ve got me now. And the telly. Plenty of company there. Aye, the telly. Though half of it's rubbish these days. Not like the olden days. You remember  Dad’s Army ? That was proper comedy. Of course I do! We used to record it on VHS. Your nephew, David, was forever trying to erase it to record football. Dreadful boy. Still is, probably. He’s a grown man now, Doris. Shouldn’t be messing with recordings. Though, come to think of it, he’s always been a bit… clumsy. Got his head stuck in a drainpipe once, remember? Trying to get his kite out. Oh, Arthur, you and your memories. Always something to chuckle about. Did you see that piece on the news about the rising cost of… well, everything? Don't you start with that, Doris. It's enough to give a man the wind-up, it is. Can’t even afford a decent cuppa these days. These price hikes… it's scandalous, it truly is. Used to be able to get a bag of sugar for tuppence. I know, dear. It’s dreadful. I was looking at the price of bananas the other day. Absolutely outrageous. We’ll have to stick to apples, I think. They seem to be holding their own a bit better. Apples are alright. Not quite the same as a good banana, mind. Give me a proper English apple, though. Cox's Orange Pippin. Now  that's  an apple. Remember those? Of course. My grandfather used to have an orchard.

Right, so, I was listenin’ to The Sugarcubes again yesterday. Proper nostalgia trip, that was. Remember when we were obsessed with them? Björk’s voice was just… unreal. Still is, mind. I do! Absolutely. We used to blast ‘Birthday’ at every house party. You’d always be trying to do the dance moves, bless you. Aye, well, someone had to provide the entertainment. It’s just, it's funny how some stuff just sticks with you, isn’t it? Like, I hadn't thought about The Sugarcubes in ages, and then suddenly, boom, a full-on flashback. What have you been listening to lately, then? Still drowning yourself in obscure Baroque composers? Not  drowning  myself, per se. Research demands it, you know. Though, I did rediscover some Vivaldi yesterday that was… magnificent. But, for pleasure? I’ve been on a bit of a Dry Cleaning obsession. Dry Cleaning? Never heard of 'em. Are they any good? You know I’m gutted I missed that gig in Newcastle last year. Mark was supposed to get tickets, but he’s hopeless. They’re brilliant. Post-punk, very deadpan delivery, spoken-word vocals over this really angular guitar and driving bass. Think early Wire, but… drier, you know? I'll send you a playlist. You'd probably love the irony. It's a proper clever band. Aye, I like irony. Right up my street, that. Speaking of clever... how's the thesis coming along? Still battling with Chapter Four? You looked completely frazzled last time I saw you. Chapter Four remains a formidable foe. I think I've finally cracked a key argument, though. It's just… translating that into coherent prose is proving surprisingly difficult. The methodology section is particularly tricky. Methodology, eh? Sounds dreadfull. You need a good head-scratcher and a strong cup of tea. Speaking of cracking things, the tomatoes are finally ripening in the garden! I've got a proper glut coming on. You need to come up and help me make a batch of chutney, honestly. Chutney? That sounds amazing. Actually, I could use a break from the endless theoretical debates. Fresh air and tomatoes… definitely a plan. Did you manage to stop the slugs from getting to the courgettes this year? Barely! It’s a constant battle, isn’t it? I've been using beer traps. Surprisingly effective, though the smell... don't get me started. It’s like having a tiny pub for slugs in your garden.

Honestly, it’s just… bewildering, isn’t it? All this fuss about unemployment figures. They're still saying it’s low, but I’m seeing it everywhere, proper lads and lasses struggling to find anything decent. My cousin, Liam, he’s been sending me messages, proper down in the dumps. Finished his apprenticeship in engineering, you know? Top marks, everyone said he’d fly. And now? Nothing. Agency work, if he’s lucky. It’s heartbreaking. Yeah, the headline numbers can be deceptive. They don't tell the whole story. It's the  quality  of the jobs that’s the issue, isn't it? And the sheer competition. There's just a tidal wave of graduates chasing a limited number of well-paid positions. It's a tough market out there. Liam, you say? Engineer? That's a good skillset. He shouldn't be struggling  too  much. He’s been applying for everything, love. Anything related to engineering, anything remotely close. Even warehouse jobs. He's feeling proper useless, gutted. Keeps saying “What’s the point, eh? All that effort for nowt.” It’s making me angry, you know? Proper furious at the system. And the government, naturally. I understand completely. That kind of sentiment… it’s corrosive. I remember feeling a bit of it myself, after finishing my masters. The job hunt felt endless. It’s the uncertainty that eats at you. Speaking of effort… you wouldn't believe the email I got today from the university bursary. Oh, don't tell me they're increasing fees again? Seriously? Worse, apparently. They’re suggesting a ‘premium’ for postgraduate courses. Something about ‘investment in research facilities’ and 'attracting top talent'. Basically, they want to charge more for people like me to carry on studying. It’s ridiculous. The government's supposed to be encouraging higher education, and this is how they go about it? Indirectly squeezing students… it’s just…  ugh . You’re havin’ a laugh, right? You're not actually serious? Where are they gonna get the money from, then? Drain Liam’s bank account? I wish. It'll be through loans, Student Finance. More debt piling up. It’s unsustainable. I’m thinking of writing a strongly worded email to the vice-chancellor. Just to make my feelings known. Aye, do! Send Liam’s details to the press too! Someone needs to highlight this. Speaking of highlighting… have you seen the new production of  Wicked ?

Right, so the badger’s wearing a tiny top hat. Do you  really  think that's necessary, Gran? It’s a bit… posh, innit? Oh, darling, it’s charming! It’s supposed to be a bit silly, a bit whimsical. This is Barnaby Badger, remember? He needs a bit of personality. Think of it - he’s off on a grand adventure to find the perfect berries! A little top hat shows he’s going somewhere special. Aye, Barnaby Badger sounds a grand wee character. Reminds me a bit of young Hamish at primary school – always wanting to dress up, that one. Though, his hats were usually made of paper and held on with sticky tape. Not quite as elegant as this, I must say. Are you thinking of doing a whole series with Barnaby, lass? That’s the dream, Mum! A whole series. I’ve got loads of ideas swirling around. Maybe Barnaby finds a lost puppy, or he helps a squirrel plant acorns for the winter... What about a dinosaur? Badgers and dinosaurs would be brilliant! They could be best mates. Now  that  is a good idea! A badger and a dinosaur… brilliant! See, Mum? He’s full of suggestions. He's a natural critic, bless him. We need to think about the family tree for the story, though. All the animals having families… Family trees are important things. Show those connections. Makes the story richer, doesn't it? Reminds you of your own. I’ve got a whole pile of old photos at home, you know. Pictures of my siblings, my parents... we could scan them and include some in the book as inspiration, a little behind-the-scenes peek. That would be lovely, Mum! Absolutely lovely. It would add something really special. I’ve been thinking about Barnaby’s family – he has a grumpy uncle, a very organized mother, and a younger sister who’s always getting into mischief. A bit like…well, a bit like ours, in some ways. Heh. Mum’s definitely the organized one, yeah. And my sister's always, like, hiding my socks. Don't you start! Speaking of siblings... Ben’s been asking about the family history again. He's really curious about his dad’s side. It’s tricky, isn’t it? Trying to explain the… complicated bits. Aye, relationships can be like that, can’t they? A bit tangled, like seaweed.

Right, another shift at the bakery done. Honestly, I'm knackered. Mrs. Higgins kept making me decorate these ridiculously elaborate gingerbread men. Little hats, tiny scarves… it was mental. Sounds stressful! At least you're earning, though. Still not hearing back about that internship application, are you? Nah, nothing yet. Just keepin’ me busy, that’s all. It pays the bills, well, part of ‘em anyway. I’m starvin’ now, mind. What’s for tea? I was thinking pasta. I picked up some pesto from the market earlier. Comfort food, you know? Speaking of comfort… I was just reading this article about body hair and societal expectations. It’s wild, isn't it? Body hair, eh? Where's this goin'? Don't tell me you're turnin' into some sort of activist. Not quite! But it got me thinking. We spend so much time, and frankly,  money , trying to get rid of it all. Legs, armpits, even eyebrows sometimes! Why is it such a big deal? Especially when loads of people are actively embracing it now. Well, I s’pose it's just… the norm, isn’t it? All over the telly, magazines… everyone’s smooth as a baby’s bum. I shave my legs, at least. Got a proper strop, dad got it for me for me birthday. Keeps 'em nice and close. Not much else, really. Armpits, yeah, but that’s mostly just 'cause I were wearin’ a vest top last summer and felt a bit self-conscious. Don’t get me started on eyebrows though. I’d look like a startled owl without a pluck. See, that’s what I mean! It's all about feeling self-conscious, isn’t it? Who decided smooth legs were the standard? My mum's always on at me to wax, says it’s 'just good hygiene'. But honestly, the expense! And the ingrown hairs! It's a nightmare. I've been leaving my legs a bit longer lately, just to experiment. Really? Like, actually hairy legs? Don’t tell me you’re going full-on Viking. No, not quite! Just... a bit more natural. Less stubble than you get after a weekend away, but… you know. It’s liberating, actually. Less hassle. And I’ve noticed people aren’t even commenting on it. Aye, I suppose. It’s just… I can’t picture myself not shaving. I’d feel… weird. Like I weren’t washin’ proper.

Right, so you're saying you’ve been alphabetising your research notes? Seriously, Liam? That’s dedication, even for you. I’m half expecting you to start colour-coding them by vowel sound next. It’s… therapeutic, Maisie. Honestly. You’ve no idea the chaos my data was. It was a right mess. And it helps me see patterns, you know? Like, I’ve noticed a bizarre correlation between articles using the letter ‘Q’ and… well, I won't bore you with that yet. It's still forming. And besides, the pub's a good place to organise thoughts – a bit of ale loosens the brain cells, doesn’t it? Loosens them, maybe. Drowns them, more likely. Though, I can appreciate the methodical mind. Reminds me of me Nan. She used to alphabetise her spices. Literally everything. Salt, pepper, cumin… all in order. Drove my Uncle Gary mental. He'd be lookin' for a pinch of paprika, and she'd be like, "Gary! It's 'P,' dear! Next to the parsley!" Sounds like a woman after my own heart. But tell me, the ‘research manager’ life – is it all spreadsheets and presentations, or are there moments of intellectual…release? It's mostly spreadsheets, to be honest. But I did have to present a report on consumer perception of flavoured gin the other week. That was a bit of a laugh. They were suggesting we market it to... teenagers. Teenagers and gin! Absolutely bonkers. Makes you wonder what else they're peddlin’. Speaking of peddlin’, did you hear about that fella down the road from me? Got nicked for… well, let’s just say less-than-legal herbal remedies. Less-than-legal herbal remedies? You mean… cannabis? The world's gone mad, hasn’t it? I mean, even my thesis supervisor said the arguments for decriminalisation are pretty strong. All based on evidence, of course. No dodgy spices involved. Aye, cannabis. Though he was tryin' to pass it off as “medicinal.” My mam always said if it smells dodgy, it probably is. Anyway, completely different topic, have you been watchin’ any boxing lately? Fury’s lookin’ pretty good, eh? Fury’s a phenomenon. The way he just… absorbs punishment and then comes back swinging. Reminds me a bit of the resilience you need for a PhD, to be honest. It’s just one punch after another of criticism and rejection, but you gotta keep gettin’ back up.

Right then, Penelope, let's tackle this St. Michael’s project. ANON’s initial brief was quite vague - "something sympathetic, something revitalising" – which, as you know, translates to 'give us a miracle on a shoestring!' What are your initial thoughts, given your experience with similar restorations? Sympathetic and revitalizing, yes. It’s the classic conundrum, isn’t it? St. Michael's is…challenging. That south wall, in particular, really worries me. The mortar’s crumbling something awful. We'll need a detailed analysis of the original composition to ensure any repairs are truly reversible, and that we're not introducing a new problem down the line. Have they commissioned a full materials survey yet? They’ve had a preliminary one, just a basic condition report. It flagged the wall, of course, but didn't go into granular detail. ANON hoped we could draft a proposal for a Heritage Lottery Fund grant to cover more extensive investigations. Frankly, I'm not optimistic. The competition is fierce, and their budget is... limited. HLF is a beast. They want impact, they want community engagement, they want demonstrable sustainability. And most importantly, they want to see a robust, realistic business plan. They’ll tear a hole in anything that smells of wishful thinking. You know, I remember when I was working on the restoration of the old mill in Datchet… Oh, do tell. You always have the best stories. …the council initially submitted a plan riddled with inflated figures for volunteer hours. They thought they could get away with it! Honestly, the reviewer practically spat out his tea. Lesson learned: be brutally honest about costs, and overestimate, rather than underestimate. And get everything independently verified. A qualified quantity surveyor is your friend. Absolutely. I’ve been trying to get ANON to understand that. They seem to think we can magic funds into existence. I’ve drafted a preliminary budget, but I'm hesitant to submit it without your input. I’m especially concerned about the stonemasonry. Replacement stone matching the original Cotswold stone is going to be astronomical. Cotswold stone, you’re right to be worried. Have they considered exploring locally quarried alternatives? It might not be a perfect match aesthetically, but with skilled pointing and careful application, it can be made to blend quite seamlessly. It's all about the detail. And it would significantly reduce the cost. We'd need to present a very strong justification, of course, explaining the reasoning openly in the application.

Right, that’s a proper brew, then. Strong enough to stand a spoon in, like me Grandma used to make. You still reckon that Earl Grey’s the dog’s bollocks, do you? Absolutely. It’s reliable. You know, a constant in a world of rapidly shifting linguistic landscapes. Though, I’m having a bit of a debate with Professor Davies about the impact of online slang on regional dialects. Online slang, eh? Is he still banging on about the death of Geordie? Because, honestly, that's just daft. It’s evolving like any language does, not disappearing. People are just finding new ways to be Geordie. Like, “canny” is still going strong, innit? You hear it on TikTok all the time. He argues that the sheer volume of standardised, often American, slang being adopted online is homogenising regional dialects. Fewer people are actively preserving or even  using  specific local phrases, he claims. He’s particularly concerned about Northern dialects losing their distinctiveness. Well, he needs to come up North for a weekend then, doesn’t he? A proper weekend, away from his tweed jackets and dusty tomes. He'd hear “bere” and “howay” before he could say "supercalifragilisticexpialidocious." It’s about more than just isolated phrases, it’s the rhythm, the intonation… it's a whole vibe, isn’t it? Trying to quantify that in a spreadsheet is ridiculous. I agree, of course. I’m just playing devil's advocate for him. He’s asking me to contribute a section to his upcoming book on the subject. To be fair, he’s more interested in the  mechanisms  of change, the sociolinguistic factors at play – influence of media, social networks, etc. He's less concerned with declaring a dialect "dead." Right. Still sounds a bit doom and gloom to me. Reminds me of that article I read last year about how millennials are forgetting basic geography. People always panic about languages changing. It’s what they  do ! Remember when everyone was in a right state because kids weren't using "shall"? Very true. It's the inherent fear of losing something valuable. Speaking of losing things, have you thought any more about our holiday? I was looking at flights to Iceland. Iceland! Reckon we could manage the cold? I’m a bit worried about the Northern Lights thing. It's a bit cliché, isn’t it? It is, but it’s a beautiful cliché.

Right then, operation ‘School Lunch Logistics’ begins. Honestly, it’s a minefield, isn’t it? Elsie, did you actually  eat  anything today? You look like you've been through a warzone. The carrots were orange. Really,  really  orange. And slimy. And Leo said they looked like worms. Worms! Yucky worms! I had chips. Lots of chips. Chips every day? That’s not exactly going to fuel your tennis tournament training, is it, Finn? You need more than just chips, love. Elsie, what  did  you have apart from the, apparently, traumatic carrots? Gravy. And some bread. I dipped the bread in the gravy. Dipping bread in gravy. That's… a choice. A choice I’m not sure is particularly nutritious. We really need to sort this out. Are you definitely happy with the packed lunches, both of you? It’s just… the cost, you know? Four days a week, it adds up. I like packed lunches! Mummy makes them yummy! She puts raisins in! See? He appreciates the raisins. Sometimes. Elsie, be honest, would you rather have a school dinner, even with the orange, slimy carrots? Granny makes much better dinners. Remember last Saturday? The roast chicken? And the Yorkshire puddings? Yes, Granny is a culinary genius. I’m not sure the school canteen can compete with that. But Granny can’t cook every day, can she? And we can’t spend a fortune on packed lunches. We need a happy medium. Maybe mixing it up? One dinner a week, and the rest packed? Can we have clowns at school dinners then? Like in the circus! Clowns at school dinners, Finn? Where did  that  idea come from? I want to be in the circus! I want to be a tightrope walker! Oh, darling, you'd be brilliant! Tightrope walking! You’re so graceful. Though, maybe stick to chasing tennis balls for now. Speaking of which, the tennis tournament’s next Saturday, isn't it? Have you both been practicing? I’ve been hitting the ball really hard!  Really  hard! That’s fantastic, love. But remember, aim is important too. Elsie, are you feeling confident? I’m a bit nervous. What if I miss the ball? You won’t miss the ball. You’re a brilliant player. And even if you do, so what? It's just a game. The important thing is to have fun, right? And you might even win! Now, about this school dinner situation... could we maybe talk to Mrs. Davies in the office?

That film was… something, wasn’t it? A bit much, perhaps, but visually stunning. Did you catch the historical inaccuracies, Dad? I was cringing a little. Inaccuracies? My dear, everything in those films is a bit… embellished, isn’t it? They need drama, don’t they? Though, I do agree, the costumes were rather splendid. Reminded me of that exhibition at the V&A. You remember that, Eleanor? Splendid is a generous word, Dad. It felt like they’d raided a fancy dress box and just slapped things together. As for the historical narrative, it was… questionable at best. I was more preoccupied with the CGI, frankly. Expensive, but occasionally distracting. Anyway, speaking of questionable narratives, did any of you attend that debate at King’s College yesterday? The one on teaching history? Matthew! Yes, I did. Quite heated, really. This professor from Oxford was arguing for a return to a purely chronological approach, source documents and all. So dry! I’m trying to encourage my students to really engage with the  why  of history, you know? Not just dates and battles. Think about it, they're approaching history with a different mindset, they need to engage with it in a way that makes sense to them now. Chronological, you say? That’s how I learned it. Dates and names. Worked well enough for me. Though, goodness knows, I haven't used much of it since. Dad, times have changed. These kids are growing up in a world saturated with information. They need to understand context, interpretation, bias… The current national curriculum is a mess, if you ask me. So much testing, so little room for critical thinking. It's churning out parrots, not historians. Exactly! And the pressure is immense. Trying to cram everything in, while also covering the demands of the exams… It leaves little time for the good stuff. I’d love to bring in more oral history, get them talking to people who’ve lived through significant events. That's a brilliant idea, Eleanor. Experiential learning is key. You know, I was talking to a recruiting manager at Unilever last week – they’re desperate for graduates with practical, industry-based experience. They’re finding that a lot of university degrees, even the prestigious ones, aren't equipping students with the skills they need on the ground. Degrees aren’t what they used to be. When I went to university, it was a serious undertaking.

Cor blimey, this drizzle's relentless, innit? Been coming down like cats and dogs since breakfast. Reminds me a bit of ’47, that summer. Never saw so much rain. We were all huddled indoors, reading comics mostly. Didn't have much else to do, ya see. Oh, darling, do stop comparing everything to 1947. You were five! Things weren't  that  bad. Besides, I’m trying to get this table looking decent. It’s a lovely piece, actually, though a bit scuffed. Your nephew John is coming round later, isn’t he? He'll appreciate the effort. Appreciate? John appreciates nothing beyond a decent pint and a football match, dear. Though, the rain is depressing. It's impacting deliveries, you know, at the gallery. Can’t get that new consignment of sculptures from the Cotswolds. Thankfully, I insured it. You learn to be cautious in business. Speaking of learning, remember that documentary on the Falklands? They were talking about the logistical nightmare of getting supplies across. The weather was just as awful as it is now. Imagine sending troops across the ocean in that… it practically beggars belief. Though, the police training they received… remarkable. They really had to be resourceful. Resourceful, eh? You lot talk about business and police training. I wouldn't know about that. My granddad, he fought in the Great War, you know. Didn't talk much about it, though. Just said it was “a dreadful business”. Came back quiet, he did. Never the same. Never understood a word of talk about logistics, or anything fancy like that. Just wanted a quiet cup of tea and to tend his roses. He sounds like a good man, Arthur. My own grandfather, he was a baker. Worked dawn ‘til dusk, six days a week. Never complained, though. Taught me the importance of hard work, he did. Though, I suspect he'd have hated John. All that time spent watching silly football… could have been learning a trade. Learning a trade? When John could be making money playing fantasy football? It's a different world now, Margaret. A completely different world. Honestly, the reliance on technology… it's staggering. I remember when you had to actually  talk  to someone to broker a deal. Face to face. No emails, no instant messaging… builds character, I tell you. Character is overrated, David. Efficiency is the modern currency. Although, I do miss the days when a telephone call felt more… personal.

Right, so, Northamptonshire. Officially leaving Bedfordshire behind. Feels…weird, doesn’t it? Like closing a chapter. Weird is a good word for it, lad. Bittersweet, too. Your mum's put a lot of memories into that house. You’ve got a lot of memories there yourself. Though, I reckon you’ll be making plenty more in your new place. I hope so. It’s just… a lot of boxes. And sorting everything. Did you manage to get those packing blankets from B&Q? Aye, got ‘em. Not the cheapest, mind, but worth it. Don’t want your precious books getting bashed up. Speaking of books, you still reading that Dickens you were on about last week?  Great Expectations ? Yeah, I'm enjoying it, actually. The language is… challenging, at times. I mean, the sentence structures! It’s brilliant for demonstrating to my students how English has evolved. They struggle with Victorian prose. Victorian prose, eh? Fancy that. Back in my day, you just read it and didn’t think about it. Different times, innit? Though, you’re doing good work, teaching English. Important stuff, making sure folk can communicate. Thanks, Dad. It’s rewarding, most of the time. Although, explaining the subjunctive mood can drive you mad. Have you heard anything from Uncle Barry? About the roof finally being sorted at his place? Spoke to him yesterday. Said the builders are starting on Monday. About time, really. The poor bloke was getting soaked every time it rained. He reckons it’ll be another two weeks before it’s truly finished. He’s worried about the cost, naturally. Yeah, I can imagine. Everything's so expensive these days. I’m still a bit stressed about the mortgage, to be honest. Trying to factor in moving costs and furnishing the new place and… Don't you fret about it, son. You're doing alright. Steady job, sensible head on your shoulders. We’ll help out wherever we can. Remember that time when you were about eight and you insisted on buying every single Mars bar in the shop with your pocket money? Oh god, don’t remind me! Mum was furious! I was bouncing off the walls for hours. I think she made me eat them all. She did! She absolutely did. Little tyke, you were. Always had a sweet tooth. So, you’re thinking of ordering a takeaway when you get to the new place, aren't you?

Right, let’s tackle this. Mum's birthday meal. We’re a decent size group this year, aren't we? Fifteen, I think? Yeah, roughly. Auntie Carol and her lot are coming, plus Uncle Barry and his daughter. And, of course, everyone else. Feels a bit much, honestly. I’m already picturing plates piled high. It does, but she’ll love it. She always says she enjoys having everyone together. Now, menu. I was thinking roast chicken, probably. Fairly safe bet. Potatoes, Yorkshire puddings… the usual. Sounds good! But maybe a vegetarian option? Gran's friend, Margaret, is veggie. We can’t just leave her with a sad salad. Absolutely. Right. Vegetarian option. Hmm… a butternut squash risotto? That’s nice and autumnal. And a bit fancier than just a mushroom stroganoff. Ooh, that’s lovely! Gran would like that. Salt, pepper, risotto rice...Forgot to grab some the other day. I've got some. Loads, actually. I went a bit crazy at Waitrose last week. Speaking of shopping, we need fish for tomorrow. Dad suggested salmon. Salmon's always a winner, isn’t it? Do you think we should get it from the fishmonger, or the supermarket? The fishmonger's always fresher, but more pricey, you know? True. Let's pop to the fishmonger. It's worth the extra few pounds. I'll go first thing in the morning. I’ve got that mental list going. Fish, candles - definitely candles, Gran loves a bit of atmosphere - and I need to rearrange the cupboards. There’s just no space for everything. It’s ridiculous. You're always rearranging the cupboards! Remember that time you moved all the teacups into the airing cupboard? Don't remind me! It was a temporary measure! But you're right, I do get carried away. It’s just… things tend to…accumulate. It’s a constant battle. And I want to make sure everything’s presentable for everyone. It will be lovely, honestly. You always do. Oh! We need to find a good spot for the photos. Gran gets so nostalgic looking at them. Yes, absolutely. Let’s put the albums on the coffee table. And maybe a selection of framed photos on the mantelpiece. Photos of her younger days, you know. Good idea. Should we include the ones from the holiday in Cornwall? She always talks about that trip. Definitely. And the one with her and Grandpa at the seaside.

Right, well, that’s been a right laugh, hasn't it? This whole wisdom teeth thing. I’m swearin’, I’ve got more holes in me mouth than a Yorkshire pudding. You're being a bit dramatic, Liv. It's just a bit sore, isn't it? And honestly, you were being a bit weird about the anaesthetic at first. "Are you  sure  it’s working?" You were peering at your tongue like you were expecting a rainbow to appear. Aye, well, I were nervous! I didn’t want to be chattin’ away while they were root canal-ing me head. And me mum, bless her, were on the phone every hour askin’ if I were alright. She’s a worrier, that one. Says I’m too thin, need more pudding. Typical. Your mum's just being a mum. Mine’s been asking if I've packed enough jumpers. France in July, apparently I'll freeze to death. Honestly, they haven’t changed a bit since we left. Are you feeling okay though? Really? No lingering numbness or anything? Nah, I’m alright, just a bit throbbing. Proper achey, like. And I can’t eat anything solid, which is a tragedy. I’ve been livin’ on ice cream and weird French yogurt. It’s a start, but it ain’t Yorkshire curd tarts, is it? No, it absolutely isn't. Speaking of moving back… did you manage to sort out the letting agent for the flat? I know you were saying it was a nightmare. Right pain, it were. They tried to charge me extra for ‘minor wear and tear’ on a flat that looked like it'd been used as a football pitch. I gave ‘em a right piece of me mind, I did. Had to get me dad on the phone. He sorted it, naturally. He's good with that sort of thing. Proper stubborn, like me. Like you. I’ve started looking at houses near uni in Norwich. Properly nervous about it all, though. It’s a big step, isn't it? Moving away from family... again. Aye, it is. But we’ll be alright. We always are. And at least this is closer to you than Doncaster. Though, I’ll miss having me mum on speed dial. Who's gonna worry about me on a daily basis now? You'll be fine. And you can always call.

Right, I’m thinking this lactose-free cake mix  might  actually work. Honestly, sometimes they’re a complete disaster. Last time I tried one, it sunk in the middle like a bog. Still, Leo and Elsie both adore cake. And Elsie’s been moaning about her tummy, poor love. Is it going to be chocolate, Mummy? Please, please chocolate! We'll see, sweetie. I thought maybe a vanilla with a berry swirl. Something a bit festive, given it’s nearly Chinese New Year. Look! Daddy said we can use these! Use them for what, darling? Don't tell me you're planning on paying for sweets with a rook! No! He said… he said sometimes, when you don't have proper money, you can use things that are special. Like these. We can give them to people who need… something. That’s a very clever idea, sweetheart. A very thoughtful idea. Your Dad's teaching you well. We can use them to do little acts of kindness, can't we? Maybe if we see someone looking sad, we can give them a knight. Or a pawn. A little something to brighten their day. Can I give someone a queen? Queens are the best! Absolutely, darling! A queen is a  very  generous gift. Although, we might have to be rather careful who we give them to. They’re quite valuable, aren’t they? Remember when Daddy was trying to teach us chess? It was a complete disaster, wasn’t it? You two kept trying to eat the pieces! I bit the bishop! And I tried to build a castle with the pawns! It fell down. It did! Okay, less talk about chess-based snacking. Let's think about kindness. We've got the chess pieces covered. What else can we do? Elsie, you’ve been doing a brilliant job helping Mrs. Peterson with her gardening. She likes the sunflowers I picked for her. She does! That was so lovely of you. Leo, you could draw pictures for the residents at the care home. They always enjoy seeing your colourful drawings. Can I draw dragons? They’re super powerful! Absolutely! Powerful dragons to bring good luck for Chinese New Year! Speaking of which, I was thinking we could make some red envelopes. And maybe bake some cookies to give out to the neighbours. Do you want to help me with that? Yes! Cookies!

Honestly, Mum, school was mental today. Mr. Davies went on and on about Victorian poetry. Like, who cares about Tennyson when I could be listening to Billie Eilish? Victorian poetry can be quite lovely, darling, but I completely understand. Billie Eilish  is  much more relevant to an eleven-year-old’s world. How was your ballet class afterwards? Did you work on the fouetté turns? Sort of. Miss Eleanor said my ankle still looked a little dodgy after… you know. Yes, after the accident. It’s amazing it recovered so well, really. The doctors were quite worried, you know. Honestly, I still have nightmares sometimes. Seeing the other car... It was awful. I know, Mum. I try not to think about it. Though, sometimes I catch myself staring at my knee, just… remembering. It's just a little scar now, barely noticeable. But it feels weird. It  is  weird. Your body's memory is a funny thing. Like that scar on my arm – you never knew about that, did you? I got it climbing a tree when I was about your age. Tried to reach a robin’s nest. Foolish, really. No, I didn’t. Can I see? Oh, it's pretty small. Does it hurt? Not really, just a vague ache if it gets cold. It reminds me of my childhood, the freedom we had. I used to spend all summer reading in the garden. Do you remember that old copy of ‘Alice in Wonderland’ I used to read you? Yeah! The one with all the wonky illustrations. I still have it! I’ve been reading it again. It’s so weird, but I love it. Makes me think about theatre. I wonder if they ever do a really cool, modern version? Like, with electro-music and neon costumes? That's a brilliant idea! Imagine the Mad Hatter's tea party with lasers! We should look online, see if there are any interesting productions coming up in London. You'd love that. We can use the Internet to find everything now! It’s a far cry from when I was a teenager and had to rely on the local newspaper listings. Honestly, it's a lifesaver. I was watching this amazing documentary on YouTube about the history of K-Pop last night. It was so interesting! K-Pop, eh? You certainly have eclectic tastes. You know, your Uncle David is bringing back that vintage record player he found at a car boot sale.

Honestly, Arthur, it's just exhausting. Last night’s meeting with the Sunbeam Valley group... all so earnest, so worried. They're fighting those solar farms like their lives depend on it. And you're right, the sheer scale of them, blotting out the landscape, seems… aggressive. I did my best to advise them on proper grounds for objection, referencing precedent cases, but it felt like trying to hold back the tide. It's the same pattern everywhere, isn't it, Margaret? Developers circling like vultures, seizing on perceived opportunities. Local councils, often pressured by central government targets, rubber-stamping proposals without proper consideration. They trot out the “green energy” mantra, but rarely address the actual impact on communities. The Sunbeam Valley people – did they mention the visual impact assessments? They need to be meticulous. And the impact on wildlife, of course. Meticulous is the word, Arthur. Absolutely. I dealt with meticulousness for years running Clarkson & Sons. Tidiness and precision were my watchwords. These planning committees, though… they’re a different breed entirely. They seem to thrive on obfuscation. I had a chat with the chap from the Northwood group yesterday evening - awful business, turbines practically on their doorsteps. Told him to zero in on the noise pollution, the potential impact on property values. Hard facts, you see. Facts sway committees more than heartfelt pleas. Precisely, Harold! Facts and figures. I spent hours yesterday researching case law around shadow flicker and bird migration patterns. Apparently, there’s a fairly robust precedent regarding the impact on migratory roosts. But the council’s report… just glossed over it. It’s infuriating! And getting a Planning Appeal granted… well, that’s a whole other battle. You need a QC for that, don’t you? Which, for a small rural group, is simply impossible. Quite. The imbalance of resources is staggering. The energy companies have battalions of lawyers and consultants. These local groups are relying on retired teachers and enthusiastic amateurs. It’s not a fair fight. I’m thinking the Sunbeam Valley group needs to push hard on the land contamination issues. Apparently, there’s a history of agricultural runoff there. Add that to the visual impact… Now, land contamination… interesting. That’s a potential pressure point. But here’s the thing, chaps: These renewable energy projects aren't going away. The world needs them. The real solution isn't just saying "no" to everything; it's about steering development towards  suitable  locations and demanding innovation.

Right then, love. So, this driving thing… you’re  really  sticking with it, are you? It’s a big responsibility, you know. Remember your Uncle Arthur? He prided himself on his driving, and ended up reversing into Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning rose bushes. The shame of it! Dad, please don't start with Uncle Arthur and the roses. It’s a classic story, but it doesn't help my nerves. Yes, I’m sticking with it. I’ve had three lessons now, and I’m getting the hang of clutch control. It’s still terrifying though, especially when people are beeping at me. Beeping is the British way of saying hello, love. Don't take it personally. And you’re doing well, aren't you, Annie? Three lessons is a good start. My Brenda took ages. She nearly gave the instructor a heart attack parallel parking. Thanks, Mum. It’s…a lot. The instructor seems alright, though. A bit monotone, perhaps. But he says I’m progressing. The biggest worry is the insurance. It’s absolutely outrageous! Have you any idea how much it’s going to cost me? Insurance. Don’t even get me started. It's a racket, pure and simple. I’ve been an accountant for near on fifty years, and I still can’t fathom the pricing. You’ll have to shop around, of course. Compare quotes. I can have a look at some comparison websites for you later. But being a young driver, it’s going to be hefty. Have you tried comparison websites, Annie? There’s one Brenda swears by - CompareTheThing. Silly name, but she says they found her a decent deal. You need to be careful though, read the small print. You don’t want to end up paying out when you need to claim. I've looked a bit, but it’s overwhelming! So many options. And it all feels like a scam. I’m seriously considering just sticking to public transport. It would be so much less stressful. Now, now. Don't give up already. Imagine the freedom! Popping to the shops whenever you fancy, driving to see your friends further afield… We’ll get you sorted. We'll find a reasonable quote. Remember that holiday we're planning for next year? Spain, wasn't it? You’ll need a car there, won't you? Exactly! The Costa del Sol is lovely. But the driving…  oh , the driving!

Right, Dad. So, Brighton’s still utter chaos parking-wise. Honestly, I spent forty minutes circling just to find a space near the seafront yesterday. Forty minutes! And then it was like, double what I usually pay. Daylight robbery, innit? Brighton, eh? Always was a bit flashy. Used to go down there with your mum, back in the sixties. Prices were a bit more reasonable then, of course. Everything was. Remember a decent cuppa and a biscuit cost tuppence. Now you’re paying a fortune for… well, not much more than that, really. Tuppence! Crikey. Makes you think, doesn’t it? I was thinking actually, maybe I should look at those self-employed jobs again. The flexible hours would be brilliant, especially with uni, but the income’s so unpredictable. Unpredictable, that's life, isn't it? Back in my day, we were all unpredictable. Nobody knew what tomorrow held. It was about survival, really. You learned to make do. Remember rationing? Not a lot of fresh produce around then. Everything came from tinned fruit and veg. I can’t even imagine. Although, with the way things are going now... I was reading about those food banks, Dad. It’s getting worse, isn't it? People I know, proper decent people, struggling to put food on the table. It is. Politicians, eh? All promise the world and deliver... well, nothing much at all, mostly. Blame Brexit, blame inflation, blame… whatever they can blame. It never seems to be their fault, does it? They’re all just lining their pockets, the lot of ‘em. Tell me about it. And the notifications on my phone! Drives me mad. Facebook pinging every five minutes, emails, uni alerts… Sometimes I just want to chuck the thing out the window. How did you manage before all this technology? Blissfully ignorant, love. Blissfully ignorant. We’d read the paper, have a cup of tea, and that was it. No constant bombardment of information. You had more time to… think. Speaking of tea, you want another? And I've got those biscuits you like. Yes please, Dad. Thank you. Actually, I’ve been trying to eat healthier, you know? Less processed stuff. It's so expensive though, getting proper fresh veg. Especially good quality fruit. It is pricey, that's for sure. But you're doing the right thing. Heard on the radio the other day that eating your greens is the key to a long life.

Right, so, Professor Davies  actually  said that Hamlet’s indecision was solely due to a poor breakfast. A  poor breakfast ! Can you believe it? I nearly choked on my Earl Grey. No way! Davies? Seriously? He's usually so… verbose. That’s brilliant though. Pure Davies. It's the kind of academic absurdity you just have to appreciate. You know, like when he spent fifteen minutes dissecting the use of the word "thee" in a sonnet. Exactly! Fifteen minutes! My brain started leaking out my ears. And the worst part is, he looked utterly serious. It was peak sarcasm, but he genuinely believed he was enlightening us. It’s a gift, really, the ability to be so unintentionally hilarious. He’s got that kind of professorial gravitas, doesn't he? He  has  to find something profound in everything. Reminds me a bit of my Uncle Barry, actually. Always trying to find the deep meaning in gardening. “The wilting of the petunias, my boy, is a potent metaphor for the ephemeral nature of existence…” Seriously. Oh, God. Sounds delightful. It’s fascinating how easily some people can weaponize seriousness, isn’t it? They use it to deflect anything that might suggest they're, you know, a bit daft. Like when I tried to explain to my grandma why I’m studying Shakespeare. It was like talking to a brick wall. Then she asked if I could learn to fix a leaky tap. Because  that's  a genuinely useful skill. The practical skills debate. My mum's the same. "Learn to code, dear, yes, but can you darn a sock?" You know, it’s funny – everyone’s obsessed with “winning” these days, getting that perfect career, the perfect life. But sometimes I think a really good skill is just… knowing how to properly load a dishwasher. That's a victory in itself. Absolutely! It’s the quiet victories, innit? I’ve been trying to get into golf, by the way. Utter disaster. I spent a fortune on clubs and I’m consistently worse than a toddler with a wooden stick. Golf? You? That's… unexpected. I always pictured you with a quill and a dusty book. Are you going to end up shouting at squirrels like my dad does when he's on the green? Pretty much! I swear one of them actively mocked me. Anyway, you? Last I heard you were slinging coffees at that place near the rugby ground.

Right, so, this week's conference… disaster. Absolutely a disaster. The keynote speaker pulled out, like, five hours before I was due to brief the hotel staff. Five hours! Can you believe it? Had to scramble, find someone else, rewrite the entire agenda… honestly, I need a holiday. A very, very long holiday. I’m proper knackered. Five hours? Blimey. That’s rough. You’re a star, though, sorting that out last minute. What happened to the original speaker? Apparently, a family emergency. Didn’t go into details. Not that I cared, t’be honest. I just wanted him gone so I could breathe again. Found some local chap who'd done a bit of motivational speaking, a retired accountant, bless him. He wasn’t exactly Barack Obama, but he didn't completely embarrass us. A retired accountant? That’s brilliant! Imagine the dreary motivational talk. "Spreadsheets: The Key to Success!" Exactly! Honestly, I was panicking. I thought I was going to have to cancel the whole thing! Anyway, how’s the construction site treating you, Liam? Still battling the elements? Yeah, still battling. Today we were trying to get this awning up, and the wind decided it liked playing with it. Nearly took out a poor bloke. Had to stop for a bit while we secured it properly. At least it's good money. Trying to save up for a deposit, you know? This Cambridge rent is criminal. Tell me about it! My flatshare with Chloe is lovely, but honestly, the estate agent was trying to pull a fast one with the damp patch. Said it was “character.” Character my foot! It's mold! I’m seriously thinking of moving out, but finding anywhere decent within budget in London is like searching for a unicorn. Aye, I know that feeling. Doncaster’s housing market isn't exactly booming, but Cambridge… it's ridiculous. I'm dreaming of getting a little cottage somewhere quiet… somewhere with a garden. A garden would be amazing. I’d grow tomatoes. And peppers. Actual actual proper home-grown veg. My mum keeps trying to send me jars of her chutney, which is lovely, but it’s taking up half my kitchen. Speaking of food, are you two still on those restrictive diets? I saw your Instagram, Amelia, you're only eating green things. Don't remind me. It's for a competition. "30 Days of Green."

Cor blimey, Brenda, you’re looking right chipper today! The light's a bit bright in your end, innit? Are you squinting? Just a bit, Arthur. Sun’s on me, see? Blooming lovely day though, eh? Better than watching the telly all mornin'. How's that Skype thing working for you? Still fiddly, is it? Hello you two! Arthur, you look positively crisp! And George, you're practically glowing! The sun suits you. Skype's fine, George, a bit glitchy sometimes, but it's good to see your faces. I’ve been out in the garden – it's just bursting with life. Bursting, is it? Well, that’s something. I was trying to get a decent view of that eclipse yesterday, but the clouds kept messing about. Did yous see any of it? Saw a bit. Dimmed a bit, like someone turned down the lamp, didn't it? Not as impressive as they make out on the telly. Still, a bit of a spectacle. Makes you think, don't it? About the cosmos and all that. Space and black holes... mind boggles! It does, doesn’t it? I was reading about black holes. Imagine, a place where gravity is so strong, even light can’t escape! Makes you wonder about the very beginning of space, doesn’t it? Aye, it does. Bit over my head, most of it, to be honest. I was more concerned about whether I’d need special glasses. Wouldn’t want me retinas fried, would I? Speaking of things that need looking at, have you two had any more bother with the neighbours and their fence? Still there, sadly. Still right on the boundary. They're being a bit awkward, they are. Claiming it was there before. Poppycock, I say! Been watching that boundary for fifty years, I 'ave. I tried to have a civil word with them, but Mrs. Higgins just sniffed and said they had paperwork proving it. Paperwork! Honestly. I think they're just being difficult. Anyway, I was pottering about and managed to get the owl box up. Hope we get a resident this year. Smart. Always fancied seeing an owl. Might even paint it to blend in. I've been watching that painting programme on the telly, you know. "Countryfile" had a chap doing landscapes. Proper clever, he was. Though, he went on a bit about being “politically correct” with his colours.

Honestly, this roundabout is giving me the willies. Three lanes, and nobody knows what they're doing! It's like a chaotic ballet of stressed-out drivers. You always exaggerate, Liv. It's just a fairly standard, albeit large, roundabout. Happens all over the place. Relax, we're practically there. Which reminds me, did you decide on that Italian place? "Bella Notte," I think it was called? Aye, it’s fine. Looks a bit… posh for us, dunnit? Like we’ll need to learn how to use a fork properly again. Remember that time we went to that French restaurant in Durham? I stabbed me chips accidentally. Mortifying. Oh, I remember! You looked like you were battling a particularly stubborn potato. It's fine, Liv, it'll be good. They have decent reviews. And besides, after that awful drive through Milton Keynes... we deserve a nice meal. Honestly, those roundabouts… they're designed by someone who clearly hates humanity. Where do they even  get  these planners? Milton Keynes is a concrete jungle! No offence to anyone who lives there, but it’s… it’s just bleak. It’s like they built it and then forgot to add the soul. Give me Sunderland any day, with its proper terraces and… well, at least it's  real . Did you see that house back there? The one with the ridiculous turrets? No, I missed it. Probably another new build trying to look like something it’s not. They always fail. They should stick to what they know - sensible squares and rectangles. At least then you know where you are. Speaking of knowing where you are, I’m still a bit lost when it comes to navigating this area. I used to take the bus to uni from Harpenden, never had to actually  drive  around. It was all predictable routes. See! Buses are the way forward! Reliable. Unlike this… . And they bring you right into the city centre. Remember when we went to Lincoln Cathedral? That was proper stunning, wasn’t it? It made you feel properly small. It was incredible. I took some photos, have you seen them? It's just so... imposing. All that history. It's completely different to anything we have up north. You barely have any proper cathedrals, just… churches. Aye, we’ve got churches, alright. But Lincoln’s different gravy. Grand, like. Proper awe-inspiring. You know, my nan used to tell me stories about her dad working on the bridges in the Tyne.

Aye, listen to that! Lovely, isn't it? Proper cheerful this mornin’. Sounds like a robin, I reckon. Though it’s a bit high pitched for a full-grown one. Could be a young’un, still learnin’ his song. It  is  lovely, Margaret. You always were the champion bird-identifier, weren't you? Me, I just hear ‘twit-twit-twit’ and assume it’s a bird. My hearing’s not what it used to be, you know. Though I do sometimes wake up thinking it’s the church bells, then realise it’s just my alarm clock. Dreadful things, alarm clocks. Why does nobody invent a gentle, gradual sunrise kind of wake-up? Gradual sunrise, eh? Now there’s an idea. Though I'd be late for my lectures every mornin’. You know, I was readin’ just the other day about a new study...apparently, consistent exposure to natural sounds, like birdsong, can actually reduce stress levels. Good reason to keep my feeders full, then! Got a new one, actually. A fancy squirrel-proof one. Though I doubt that’ll work for long. Those little blighters are cunning. Squirrels! Don’t even mention them. They raided my sunflower seeds last week. A veritable siege. I had to shoo them away with a broom. Speaking of sieges, I've got a dentist appointment next Tuesday. Dr. Harding. Not looking forward to it one bit. Ooh, Harding, eh? He’s a sharp one, that lad. Had a filling done by him last year. Didn’t feel a thing, which is always a bonus. Though I did get a nosebleed afterwards. Dreadful, right in the car! Had to grab a tissue and stuff it up me nose, lookin’ like some right old character. Nosebleeds are the worst. I had one the other day and nearly caused a scene in the supermarket. Felt like a geyser erupted from my face. Made my daughter, Emily, nearly drop her trolley. She’s worried about me, actually. Says I’m gettin’ too old to be chasing squirrels and getting nosebleeds. Well, chasing squirrels is good for the soul, love! Keeps you active, doesn’t it? Emily’s just bein' a typical daughter, fussin’ over her mother. She needs to remember we’re not all ready for the knitting circle yet! Though, mind you, Brenda from down the road turned eighty last week. Looked remarkably well, considering. Still pottering about in her garden.

Honestly, Sarah, it's just  lovely  to see you. It feels like ages, doesn't it? Since… what, Emily’s christening? It really does, doesn't it, Claire? Time just disappears, doesn’t it? Emily’s practically a teenager now. Where  does  it go? It was so nice to escape the chaos for a bit, you know? The kids are at my mum’s tonight, which is a small miracle. I can only imagine! My weekends are a constant battle against Lego and requests for ketchup on everything. How are things with you, really? You seemed a bit… stressed last time we spoke. Things are… different. Remember how I was looking into fostering? Well, that didn't pan out. Too many hurdles, too much paperwork. Instead, I ended up going down the adoption route. Adopted a little boy, Leo, just shy of two. It’s been… intense, to put it mildly. Beautiful and intense. Oh, Sarah! That’s wonderful! A little boy! That’s fantastic news. I’m so sorry the fostering didn’t work out, though. Adoption is such a big thing to take on. How are you finding single parenthood? Honestly? Sometimes it’s terrifying. Being responsible for this tiny human entirely on my own… but then he gives me the biggest, smiliest grin and it all feels worthwhile. It’s pushed me to my absolute limits, but it's also the most rewarding thing I've ever done. And, you know, I’ve started going to yoga. Three times a week. It’s honestly a lifeline. Keeps me sane. Yoga, you say? I’ve been thinking about trying that. My back’s been playing up something awful, especially since marking all those essays. I’d love a lifeline! Although, finding the time is another matter. What kind of yoga do you do? Hatha, mostly. Gentle, restorative. Perfect for de-stressing. They have some really good classes at the community centre. I’ll send you the details. Speaking of time, what about you? Still battling with Year Nines and Shakespeare? Still battling. Though, I’m seriously contemplating a career change. I’ve been secretly writing, you know. A novel. Terribly embarrassing to admit to, really. A novel! Claire, that's brilliant! What’s it about? Don’t be embarrassed! That's amazing. It's… a bit of a mess, to be honest. A historical romance set in Dorset. Very much inspired by my childhood, actually.

This is lovely, Anon. You’ve really made this place your own. Much nicer than that clinical show home we saw when you first moved in. Aye, that's right. Show homes are all the same, aren't they? Bleak and impersonal. Glad I could put a bit of life into it. You're enjoying the tea, then? It’s just a builder's brew, mind you, nothing fancy. It's perfect, thank you. Just what I needed after a particularly… energetic French lesson. Year nines, you know? Trying to explain the subjunctive? It's a battle every time. Education these days… it’s a different beast than when you were teaching, isn't it? Oh, it is. Radically different. I was a history teacher myself, you know. Secondary, mostly. And you’re right, it was a battle then too, just a different kind. Discipline used to be… well, it  was  something. Now, it's all about pastoral care and safeguarding and… well, you know. Wanting to be everyone’s friend rather than an authority figure. Makes it hard to get through the curriculum. Exactly! I feel like I’m spending half my time mediating playground disputes and the other half trying to get them to conjugate verbs. My mum, she’s a bit old-fashioned, says we’ve gone soft. She was a PE teacher, she’d have them running laps until they learned the difference between  être  and  avoir . Your mum sounds like a woman after my own heart. My wife, bless her, is more… diplomatic. Keeps me from saying things I might regret. Speaking of family, how's your little Leo doing? Last I heard he was obsessed with dinosaurs. He is! He knows more about the Jurassic period than I ever will. He’s started collecting them. The house is slowly being taken over by plastic T-Rexes. It’s cute, but… you know. A bit much. He’s also got a surprisingly good grasp of French, actually. Picks it up quicker than some of my students. Children are remarkable, aren't they? Mine's got a boy of his own now. Just turned fifteen. The teenage years. A whole new battleground. They’re fascinated with that… what’s it called? Tik Tok? Oh, don't even get me started. It’s a black hole of time and questionable content. I try to limit Leo's exposure to it.

Right then, this smells proper good. Proper good, it does. You sure this isn't some fancy Cambridge recipe, love? I'm used to proper Yorkshire grub, you know – meat and potatoes, gravy… none of this quinoa nonsense. Oh, stop it, Liam! It's just lentil shepherd's pie, alright? It's hearty, it’s vegetarian, and it’s not quinoa! You’ll like it. I’ve been trying to broaden my culinary horizons beyond Greggs, you know? Though, I do miss a good sausage roll. Smells… interesting. Is that the lentil thing, Anya? I’m starving. Just finished another marathon session on the structural analysis software – my brain feels like it’s been through a washing machine. Cambridge is certainly seeing an influx of engineers lately, isn’t it? Feels like we’re all huddled together, battling spreadsheets and concrete. Anya, anything edible yet? My stomach’s starting to rumble a protest. Nearly! Just needs a few minutes to bake. What were you lot up to, anyway? Besides torturing yourselves with numbers. I saw you heading out earlier, Ben and Tom. Ben was trying to convince me to watch the new Wes Anderson film. "Asteroid City." Apparently, it’s absolutely brilliant, meticulously crafted, aesthetically perfect… Utter rubbish, if you ask me. Don't waste your time. All style, no substance. Like a very expensive, very symmetrical sandcastle. The plot was… meandering. Sounds a bit poncey for me, that does. I’ll stick to a good action film, I will. Any recommendations, Tom? Something with explosions, maybe? "Extraction 2" was surprisingly good. Chris Hemsworth kicking serious backside. Pure adrenaline. Although, Anya, between the two of us, you probably wouldn't appreciate the nuanced character development. Oh, I’m sure I can handle a bit of action. It's not like you’re recommending Dostoyevsky, Tom. Though I did enjoy "Paddington 2." That was brilliantly nuanced. That’s fair! “Paddington 2” is universally loved. And Anya’s right, Tom. You're being a bit of a snob. I thought "Asteroid City" was cleverly veiled commentary on the anxieties of the Cold War era… It was a slightly longer advert for beige. Seriously, the colour palette was aggressively muted. It actively offended my eyes. Right, right, settle down, you two. This is actually banging, Anya! Proper good. See? Lentils can be decent! I'm putting this in my repertoire. Although… does it come with gravy?

Right, so, gyms. Absolutely mental. I tried to squeeze in a quick session at the PureGym near the uni before you guys picked me up. Packed like sardines, it was. Couldn't even get near the squat rack. Honestly, feels like everyone’s decided January’s the time to get ripped. Tell me about it! I went to the Fitness First near my flat yesterday. Similar vibe. All the treadmills were being hogged by people walking at a brisk pace, like they’re escaping something. Not exactly a sprint, you know? It felt…performative, almost. You're both exaggerating! I actually had a really good workout at Bannatyne's this morning. It was quiet, surprisingly. Maybe everyone’s still recovering from whatever festive overindulgence happened. I did almost drop a dumbbell on my foot though. That would have made for a less pleasant morning, wouldn't it? Bannatyne's is a bit posh, isn’t it? I just stick to my home setup. Less hassle. Plus, I can blast my music without bothering anyone. Speaking of which, what are you all listening to these days? I've been obsessed with this new synth-wave band, 'Neon Echoes'. It's proper atmospheric. Synth-wave? Sounds a bit too…neon for me, mate. I’m still on a classic Oasis kick, ironically enough. Bit cheesy, I know, but they never get old. It's the sound of my childhood. Oasis is timeless! I have to agree. But I've also been listening to a lot of Little Simz lately. She's incredible. Proper lyrical genius. What about you, Amy? Anything good? I've been diving deep into Fleetwood Mac. Don't judge! Their harmonies are just…perfect. It's relaxing for my brain after hours of editing articles about obscure fungal infections. You know, the glamorous life of an editor. Fungal infections? Blimey. That  does  sound glam. Anyway, speaking of things that aren't fungal, have you guys booked anything for the kids’ camp this summer? Little Leo is already asking about it and I’m starting to panic a little. Oh yeah, the camp! I completely forgot. We were talking about that at Christmas. Mum and Dad are probably on it, booking everything ages in advance. They’re like military strategists when it comes to holidays. Mum’s definitely on it. She's already got a spreadsheet, I bet. I need to call her later.

"Oh, come  on  ref! That was a definite foul! Honestly, you'd think they were blind, wouldn’t ya? Proper robbed, they are.” "Easy now, love. Don't get yourself worked up. It’s just a game. And to be fair, the wind's making things tricky for everyone out there. It's playing havoc with the flight of the ball.” “Just a game? Just a game?! This is the semi-final, Liam! This is  massive ! And the wind’s a rubbish excuse. They should've adapted, the dafties! Besides, it’s affectin’ both teams, isn’t it?" . "Alright, alright. Point taken. Still, they're holding their own. Look at that tackle from Davies – textbook. Solid defending.” . "Thinking of our Easter weekend plans though, are we? I was looking at that film festival in London – 'Cinema Paradiso Reborn' playing, you know? Might be worth a trek." “'Cinema Paradiso Reborn'? Liam, seriously? That sounds dreadfully… pretentious. I was thinking something a bit less…artsy. Maybe a proper action film? Saw the trailers for 'Apex Predators' - looks mental." "Mental in a good way, or mental in a 'this is going to be a cinematic disaster' kind of way?" He raises an eyebrow, a playful teasing glint in his eyes. "I do like a bit of cinematic artistry, though. Keeps the mind ticking. Plus, we haven’t been to London in ages." "Apex Predators is proper mental. Explosions, chases, genetically modified wolves...the lot. And we’ve been busy, haven’t we? Research reports piling up, you tryin' to finish that blasted thesis… Easter's about relaxin', not pretentious film festivals and stuffy audiences." She grabs a handful of crisps. "So, wolves it is then?" "Okay, okay. Wolves it is. Though, I maintain that 'Cinema Paradiso Reborn' would be a worthwhile experience. We could always compromise – Apex Predators on Saturday, a smaller, more manageable film on Sunday? Something a bit…less wolf-related." "Hmm, maybe. Depends on how mad the wolves are. Right, look! He's got the ball! Oh,  please  pass it to him! Don’t be a numpty!" . "Easter eggs, eh? Have you got any hidden around the flat yet? I reckon I’ll set a proper scavenger hunt this year, like when we were kids." "I have a few hidden, yes. Though, I'm not sure my hiding skills are as sharp as they used to be. You'll probably find them all in five minutes flat."

Jaysus, look at this wee fella. Liam, isn’t it? Absolutely covered in face paint at that funfair in Weston-Super-Mare. Remember that, Moira? Oh, bless him! He looks terrified, but also… thrilled. You could practically feel the sugar rush radiating off him. Weston-Super-Mare was a good shout, wasn’t it? A bit… chaotic, mind you, but good fun. Did he win anything on those games? Not a sausage. Tried to win him one of those giant stuffed animals. Spent a good twenty quid, the greedy little bugger. Ended up with a plastic spider and a very disappointed face. But the ice cream more than made up for it, I reckon. He practically inhaled three of them. Funfairs! They used to be something, back in my day. Glasgow’s Green Expo, that was the place to be. Real working-class entertainment. None of this health and safety nonsense either. You could win a real prize, not some shoddy plastic trinket. And the candy floss! Thick as clouds it was. What’s all the reminiscing about? Something interesting happening? Just looking through these old photos, darling. Remember Weston-Super-Mare? You were about eight, I think? Scared of everything except the carousel. Yeah, vaguely. I mostly remember being hungry all the time. And being told to stop hogging the chips. You did, love. You were a wee chip-gobbler. Still are, if I’m honest! Boys and chips. A universal truth. You know, reminds me of running the school fete. We always had a stall selling chips. Biggest attraction of the whole affair, you can bet on it. More popular than the bouncy castle, even! It’s funny, isn’t it? Simple things. Funfairs, chips… Makes you realise what really matters. Though, Weston-Super-Mare wasn't exactly the most scenic. More of a concrete jungle than a seaside resort. True enough. But Liam loved it. And that’s what counts. See, here's another one. This one’s from that trip to Iceland. Look at him, posing with a glacier like he’s conquered Everest. Wow! That’s…amazing. I never realised you’d been to Iceland. I’d love to go there sometime. Proper adventure. We should all go sometime. It was breathtaking, honestly. Expensive though, so... Maybe for a special birthday. Like, a big one. Iceland! Fancy that. Always wanted to see the Northern Lights. Never managed it, though.

That was absolutely lovely, Brenda. Honestly, your roast potatoes are still the best I’ve ever had - you’ve got some kind of secret. Oh, stop it, love! It’s just a bit of extra rosemary, really. And a good, hot oven. Your mum never could get them crispy, did she? Always a bit soft. Soft potatoes were perfectly fine. You didn’t want them snapping your teeth, did you? Back in my day, we were grateful for anything that came out of the oven! And speaking of days gone by, do you remember those little wooden dolls we used to play with, Brenda? The ones with the painted faces? Oh, Elsie! Yes! The peg dolls! We had a whole box of them, didn't we? You painted them all different colours and gave them fancy names. Mrs. Bumbleberry, wasn't one? And Captain Bartholomew! He was always sailing the high seas, rescuing damsels in distress... which were usually just Brenda’s teddy bears! That sounds wonderfully chaotic. I’m picturing a tiny, painted wooden man battling a very fluffy bear. We didn’t have those, did we? My toys were mostly… well, rather bland, actually. Lots of plastic building blocks and a rather stern-looking Raggedy Ann doll. Very sensible for my parents, I suppose. Sensible's boring, love! You need a bit of imagination sparking, don’t you? My mum always said, “A child with a box of sticks can have more fun than a child with a toy shop.” She was a wise woman. Though, she’d be horrified by all these eBooks now. Remember when books were  books , Elsie? You could smell the paper and feel the weight of them in your hands. Absolutely! And the library! Oh, the library was heaven. Miss Perkins, the librarian, knew everyone’s reading preferences. I used to spend hours in there, just browsing the shelves. I loved those collections of short stories. "The Wind in the Willows" was a favourite. Still is! I’ve tried eBooks, you know. But I find I just…zone out more. It’s harder to concentrate. Plus, I miss the actual turning of pages. There’s something so satisfying about that. Have you been watching "Call the Midwife," Brenda? Oh yes! Absolutely hooked. So moving, isn't it? It reminds me of some of the stories my nan used to tell me about working in the local factories.

Mmm, that's nice, that is. Proper pickle, this. Not that watered-down nonsense you get in the supermarkets these days. Remember Mrs. Higgins down the road used to make her own? Proper fiery it was. Could strip paint, that pickle could. Oh, I do remember. Nearly set your tongue on fire, didn't it? Though you always pretended you loved it. You used to brave it for a compliment from her. Bless her, she’s gone now, hasn't she? Years. Seems like only yesterday we were all chatting over the fence. Aye, a long time. Time does fly when you're... well, when you're not exactly doing much, does it? Still, not complaining. Got me sandwiches, got me telly, got you, haven't I? Can't ask for much more than that, can you? You're a lucky man, Arthur. And I’m lucky to have you. You know, Maisie's been asking about you. Wants to come visit next month. Maisie? Our little Maisie? Blimey, is she? Grown into a fine young woman, she has. Last time I saw her, she was still playing with those toy ponies. Remember those? She wouldn’t let anyone near ‘em, she wouldn’t. Fiercely protective of her ponies. She’s studying architecture now, can you believe it? All those blueprints and angles... It’s quite clever, really. I sent her some photos of the old windmill. Thought she might appreciate that. The windmill? That’s a good shout, that is. Shame about the state it's in now, though. Used to be a grand sight, you know. Wind blew right through it, kept the whole village powered, practically. My grandad used to work there. Said it was a right noisy place. All that clatter and whirring. It must have been. They're talking about restoring it, apparently. Some heritage group. Seems like a lot of money, though. Wonder if it'll ever actually happen. Money, eh? Always a problem, isn't there? Never had much of that myself. Still didn't starve, mind. Always managed. Had a good mum, I did. Taught me how to stretch a shilling further than anyone I knew. Remember her making soup from practically nothing? Carrots, potatoes, a bit of onion... tasted like a feast, it did. She was a wonderful woman. She taught me a lot too, about looking after children, about making do.

Right, so, tell me everything! Last time we spoke, you were interviewing for that new role at St. Hilda’s, weren't you? Did you get it? I did! I actually started last week. It's brilliant, honestly. Smaller class sizes than my last school, much more supportive leadership, and the kids are just… lovely. A bit boisterous, of course, but lovely. It feels like a proper fit, you know? That’s fantastic, Liv! Congratulations! I’m so pleased for you. St. Hilda’s has a good reputation. It sounds like a weight off your shoulders, finally finding somewhere you feel settled. You looked absolutely knackered last time we met. I was! The constant job hunting was draining. Anyway, how's the copywriting going, Chloe? Last I heard you were working on a campaign for some fancy organic dog food. Don't remind me! It’s surprisingly complex. The creative director is obsessed with conveying ‘authenticity’ in a way that doesn’t sound completely ridiculous attached to kibble. It’s been a battle of wills. I’ve practically written three different taglines that all involve talking about "wholesome, tail-wagging goodness." I’m starting to see dogs everywhere. Oh, bless you! At least it's interesting. I’m still slogging away with phonics and fractions. Little Tommy drew a picture of a unicorn eating a calculator yesterday, and declared it was ‘helping with his maths.’ Honestly, at this point, I'll take any help I can get. Sounds chaotic, in the best possible way though, doesn't it? Speaking of chaotic, my mum’s convinced she’s going to win the lottery and is already planning a trip to the Maldives. She keeps asking me if I want a twin suite. Your mum's always been optimistic! That's brilliant… and slightly terrifying. Mine’s stressing about Christmas presents already. She's got a spreadsheet, you know. A  spreadsheet  for Christmas presents. I swear, she's single-handedly keeping the paper industry afloat. Oh my god, mine too! She's on the phone to distant relatives asking what everyone's "subtle hints" are. It's mental. I think she’s got a present sorted for my cousin’s cat this year. The cat?! That’s dedication! Although, knowing Margaret, it’ll probably be a hand-knitted cardigan. Seriously. I got a ceramic gnome for my eighteenth birthday. Still have it. It stares at me from the windowsill.

Right then, so this street… Lark Lane. Lovely, isn't it? A bit bohemian, always has been. Much nicer than that bit down towards Granby Street, eh, Annie? Too much trouble down there, you know. Always something going on. Aye, it is, Karl. Lark Lane's alright. Got the little shops, the cafes... used to love wandering down here when I was a kid. Though, it's changed a bit, hasn’t it? Used to be proper independent shops, now it’s mostly chains, innit? Still, better than Granby, like you say. Heard some awful stories. It's got a good vibe, doesn't it? I sometimes come here after work to grab a coffee. It's a bit more... pleasant than where I work. The office is all beige and stressful. It's good for Quidditch practice, Dad. Loads of space if you imagine it. Quidditch, eh, Liam? Always thinking about your games. That's good, son, good to have an imagination. Though, I was hoping you'd be more interested in the Brontës at your age. Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights... proper classics. Leave him be, Karl. Letting him read Harry Potter is much better than forcing Dickens down his throat. And anyway, it’s proper storytelling, that is. Good characters, good plot. I actually really enjoyed  Harry Potter  when I was growing up. Still do, if I'm honest. It’s proper escapism. More escapism than I need most days, mind. Escapism… a dangerous thing. Keeps you from confronting the realities of the world. Though, I suppose a bit of magic now and then doesn’t hurt. Tell you what, Annie, it reminds me of that article I read the other day about ISIS using children to recruit. Dreadful, just dreadful. Need to keep people grounded, eh? Don’t go bringing ISIS into it, Karl. That’s a bit much, isn’t it? We’re just having a bit of a chat. My nephew’s been having a right time with his asthma lately. That’s the only horrors I need to worry about, thanks. Asthma's a nightmare. My grandma had it. Always wheezing and struggling to breathe. GP keeps telling her to lose weight, but… it’s easier said than done. Hermione Granger had asthma. She used this thing called an inhaler. It helped. See? Even in the world of magic, medical innovations play a part. Speaking of innovations, how's your new job going, Emma?

Nepal, really, Brenda? It's ambitious, isn't it? At our age? Though I must admit, the photographs I’ve seen… the Himalayas... simply breathtaking. Are you seriously thinking of trekking? Ambitious? Perhaps! But why not? I’m fitter than I was last year, and I’ve always wanted to see Everest, even if it’s just from a distance. And it’s not  all  trekking, dear. We'll have plenty of time in Kathmandu, exploring the temples and the markets. I’ve started a little scrapbook already, gathering information. What do you think, Margaret? You're the sensible one! Nepal… well, it sounds lovely. Expensive, though, I imagine. Remember that trip to the Dordogne? That was a revelation, wasn't it? The food, the countryside… we ate so much duck confit! And proper sausages, not those watery things you get in the supermarket these days. Speaking of which, have you been to the Farm Shop lately? Their pork sausages are divine. Better than anything you’d find at the Village Shop, that’s for sure. Oh, the Village Shop… it’s gone downhill, hasn’t it? They stopped stocking decent Earl Grey. And the bread… perpetually stale. The Farm Shop is a treat, though, isn't it? Though the prices! Still, you pay for quality. I'm trying to be better about having everything gluten-free. It's a nightmare sometimes, finding something I can actually enjoy. Gluten-free, that’s a whole new world, isn’t it? My grandson, little Finn, is coeliac. It’s so important to be careful. My husband, George, he’s become quite the whiz in the kitchen. He makes a brilliant gluten-free shepherd’s pie. Honestly, a revelation! It’s put his skills to the test. He used to just grill sausages and call it a night. Oh, George! My Edward was hopeless in the kitchen until he retired. Now he makes a mean risotto! It’s marvelous, seeing men take on that role properly. It’s a world away from my father’s time, wasn’t it? All rationing and ‘make do and mend.’ He used to tell stories of his mother’s cooking during the war, stretching a single chicken across a week. And my mother-in-law... goodness. Her family fled Siberia during the war, went all the way to Africa… imagine! No fresh food for months, relying on whatever they could forage or barter.

Right, phew! That was a mad dash from the station. Cambridge is proper bustling today, innit? It’s lovely though, this place of yours, Anon. Really cozy. Glad you think so! It needed a good tidy, admittedly. You look knackered, Chloe. Long day at the conference centre? You have no idea. We had a VIP speaker pull out this morning, total last minute thing. Had to rearrange seating, re-print name badges, brief the AV team… Yorkshire puddings were nearly forgotten! It were a right kerfuffle, I tell thee. Honestly, sometimes I feel like the entire event hinges on me and a copious amount of tea. Sounds stressful! I’m just glad I don’t deal with panicked speakers and logistical nightmares.
