And is there anything I can do to mitigate it? Mitigate, eh? Always a clever word, that. Right, so, inheritance tax. Officially, it's called ‘Inheritance Tax’ or IHT. And the threshold, as of now, is £325,000. That’s the amount you can inherit tax-free. Your Aunt Margaret’s cottage… is it worth more than that, roughly? I think so. Possibly around £450,000, maybe even more, depending on the market. Alright then. That means you’d be looking at a tax bill. But hold your horses! There are several things that can reduce that. One, your annual gift allowance – you can give up to £3,000 a year to anyone without it counting towards your inheritance tax. Okay, annual gift allowance... right. And what else? Well, if your spouse or civil partner inherits, that’s their allowance, not yours. And any unused portion of your partner's allowance often can be passed on to you. There’s also the Residence Nil Rate Band. That’s a bit of a mouthful, isn't it? It is! Explain. It’s another allowance, specifically for your main residence. Currently, it’s £175,000 per person. So, if your Aunt Margaret leaves you the cottage, that £175,000 is tax-free on top of the standard £325,000. That’s a grand total of £500,000 you can inherit tax-free. So, if the cottage is worth £450,000, I wouldn’t pay anything? Near enough, love. Unless it’s worth significantly more than that. Above £500,000, then yes, you'll be paying a rate of 40% on the amount exceeding that figure. Now, there's more to it, of course. Gifting large sums in the seven years before death can complicate things… but we’ll worry about that if it comes to it. Right. Seven years… that’s good to know. What about all this talk about the government changing tax policy?

Honestly, Mum, this project is eating my life. It's just… relentless. Deadlines are shifting every five minutes, and Brenda in Marketing keeps changing her mind about the colour scheme. Mauve for the website, apparently. Mauve! Who even  likes  mauve? Mauve, love? That’s a bit… bold, isn’t it? Sounds like Brenda's got a bit of a creative streak. Don't you worry yourself sick over it though. You’re doing brilliantly, you always do. Remember that time you organised that village fete when you were, what, twelve? You got everyone involved and raised enough money for new swings. Mauve's a drop in the ocean compared to that. Okay, okay, you're right. But the fete didn't involve a PowerPoint presentation to the board every other day. And it certainly didn't require me to learn the nuances of brand consistency. It was just bouncy castles and a cake sale. Well, things have moved on a bit since then, haven't they? Tell you what, are you coming for Sunday lunch? I’m making your favourite – roast chicken with all the trimmings. A proper sit-down meal, you deserve it. Oh, Mum, that sounds  amazing . Seriously. I think I might need the mental reset a roast chicken can provide. Is Dad helping with the potatoes again? Last time he nearly set the oven on fire. He tried, bless him. He thinks he knows best, the clever clogs. I had to wrestle the potato peeler out of his hands. He’s on salad duty this time, which should be safer. How’s your little flat? Are you still battling with that leaky tap? Don't even remind me! I called a plumber, obviously, but he said it's a "complex issue" and quoted me something ridiculous. I’m trying to get a second opinion. It's dripping  constantly , Mum. It's driving me mad. Sounds like a tiny waterfall in my kitchen. A tiny waterfall! Goodness me. Those plumbers, eh? Always trying to take advantage. I’ll have a word with Barry down the street. He’s a retired engineer, knows a thing or two. Might be able to take a look for you for a decent price. That would be absolutely brilliant, Mum. You're a lifesaver. Seriously. Anything to avoid another conversation with that man in the overalls who told me I needed to replace the entire plumbing system.

Right then, lass. That chilli was champion, it really were. Proper warming after that wind we had earlier. Better than that watery stuff you tried to make last Christmas, eh? Oh, come on, Dad! It wasn't  that  bad. And it's good you enjoyed it. I was trying a new recipe. Speaking of trying new things, have you had a look at that link I sent you about voluntary work? Voluntary work? Aye, had a gander. All seemed a bit… fancy, love. Sorting paperwork at a posh charity shop. Not my cup o’ tea, that. I've spent enough time sorting paperwork in a lab, thank you very much. Hello! Smells fantastic in here. Is that the chilli I keep hearing about? And Dad, about the voluntary work – remember what we talked about? Maintaining a routine is good for you, for your mental health. It doesn’t have to be ‘fancy.’ Plenty of opportunities for practical help around here. Practical help, eh? Like what? Picking up litter? I’m not a street sweeper, son. I’ve got a degree, for heaven’s sake! Dad, don’t be like that. There’s a community garden that needs volunteers - help with planting, weeding… even just chatting with the regulars. It wouldn't be strenuous, and it’s fresh air. Plus, Jamie mentioned they could use someone with a science background to help with the soil analysis. Soil analysis? Well, that’s a bit more like it, isn't it? Using my skills, even if it's just a bit. Better than staring at the telly all day, I suppose. Still, it feels a bit demeaning, doesn’t it? After a career… It’s not demeaning, Dad. It’s contributing. And Jamie's right, they'd genuinely appreciate it. Speaking of contribution, did you ever get around to sorting out those old iPods? Mum’s been asking about them. She wants to put some of her old music onto them for her walks. I tried, but they're being awkward. They need some updating, and I haven’t quite figured out how to do it. Keeps giving me error messages. It's like archaeology, trying to get technology that old to work. Archaeology, you say? That's a good one. I remember when those things were the bee's knees! Spent a fortune on wee tunes for them back in the day. Fancy that – data stored on something smaller than a fingernail.

Honestly, Lizzie, I’m drained. Absolutely drained. Another double lesson of teenage angst today. They’re convinced TikTok is more important than, you know, understanding the difference between ‘their,’ ‘there,’ and ‘they’re.’ It’s a constant battle. Tell me about it! Though my lot are slightly older, they’re just as bad with the grammar. They think ‘like’ is a verb. A  full  verb. It’s… demoralising. So, how was the conference yesterday? Did you pick up any brilliant teaching strategies? Oh, the conference. Don't even get me started. It was a… experience. Lots of powerpoint slides, lots of jargon, and a surprising amount of talk about mindfulness for teachers. Mindfulness! After a day wrangling hormonal teenagers, the idea of  meditating  just makes me want to hide under my desk. I can imagine! Did any of it actually feel useful? I’m still processing the keynote speaker’s ideas about “culturally responsive pedagogy.” It sounded lovely in theory, but applying it practically felt… complicated. Especially when you have thirty different cultures in one classroom. Complicated is an understatement. It was mostly just… vague. Lots of nodding along and pretending you understood what they were going on about. The best part was the coffee, to be honest. And the bacon butty at breakfast. That was a proper highlight. Did you manage to get a bacon butty? I did! One on arrival, and another mid-morning when I was desperately flagging. I think I spent half the day just fueled by bacon. The workshop on using AI in the classroom was surprisingly interesting, though. They showed a tool that could generate lesson plans based on specific learning objectives. AI? Honestly, it’s terrifying and exciting all at once. I'm clinging to my whiteboard and old-fashioned methods. I worry about them becoming too reliant on technology. What happens when the internet goes down? Chaos! Absolute and utter chaos. The students would riot. You're dramatising a bit! But I get your point. It's about balance, isn’t it? Using it as a tool to enhance teaching, not replace it. Though, that lesson plan generator  did  look rather tempting. Thinking about all that marking… Don't even mention marking. I have a mountain of essays to grade. They’re all essays about dystopian literature. Which, ironically, is exactly what my life currently feels like. I swear, if I read one more paragraph comparing my classroom to the Panem arena, I’m going to scream.

Honestly, this is just lovely, isn’t it? So much…green. Cambridge feels perpetually grey, doesn’t it? Even when the sun shines. Aye, it’s smashing. Proper countryside. Much better than the M6, I’ll tell you that for nothing. You’ve hardly moved since we left Tarnow, though. Are you alright? You seemed a bit…pensive earlier. Oh, just thinking. About…well, everything, really. I saw a picture of Amelia the other day, you know, my niece? On Facebook. She’s absolutely sculpted now. Pilates, apparently. And protein shakes. I feel like a crumpled cardigan next to her. Amelia’s always been a bit…intense about the fitness thing. Don't you let it get to you, love. You're fine. You look good. Besides, you're on holiday! That’s got to be good for the soul, hasn't it? And less time obsessing about calories probably. Easier said than done, darling. It’s a lifetime habit, isn’t it? Though I  did  try that Zumba class in the village. Briefly. Let's just say, my coordination isn't exactly suited to Latin rhythms. I can imagine! Right, I'm thinking we should pull off soon, check the map. Are we still on track for Rzeszow before dark? This GPS is being a bit temperamental. I think so. It said something about a service station somewhere around… Oh, goodness, I can’t remember the Polish name. Sounds like "Szczepanów" or something. Dreadful to pronounce! Perhaps if we had a television to look at whilst you drive. A telly? In a campervan? You’re joking! Space is already tight enough as it is. Besides, half the fun of travelling is disconnecting and just… experiencing things. Remember that book you were reading? The one about the woman cycling through Scandinavia? Oh,  The Long Way Round . Yes! It was utterly captivating. I'm halfway through it, actually. She's so wonderfully independent. I wish I had some of that independence... some sort of purpose, really. That volunteering thing I mentioned… I’m still dithering about it. You should do it! Seriously. Helping out at the animal shelter sounds brilliant. It’d be good for you, getting out and about, meeting people. You’re always saying how you miss having a routine. I do, don’t I? But… the confidence. It’s a challenge. And the men… Honestly, the dating scene is just a minefield anywhere.

Right then, ANON, so you were saying about feeling a bit overwhelmed by it all? All this… stuff we were rattling on about - Vikings, telomeres, pyramids… it's a lot to take in, isn't it? Especially when you’re juggling a toddler, poor you. It is, isn’t it? I mean, kayaking with the Vikings sounded  amazing , actually. But then you mentioned telomeres and suddenly I was thinking about… well, everything. My mum's been having a bit of trouble with her joints, and I just… I guess I started thinking about ageing in general. And feeling like I should be doing something, anything, to slow it down! Ridiculous, isn't it? Not ridiculous at all. It’s natural. We all grapple with it, even us IT types who spend our days staring at screens hoping to unlock the secrets of the universe. The telomere bit is fascinating, though. Think of them like the plastic tips on your shoelaces. They fray over time, causing the 'rope' – your DNA – to shorten. Aging, in a way, is just controlled shortening of those tips. Some studies suggest things like plant-based diets and exercise can help maintain them. Not a fountain of youth, mind you, but every little bit helps, aye? Exercise… right. Between nap times and tantrums, exercise feels like a distant memory. But you're right, a plant-based diet… I could probably manage that. My mum keeps going on about turmeric having magical benefits. Turmeric's got antioxidants, so there's something in it. Listen, let's not get lost in the science. What  really  got you thinking, beyond the aging stuff? Was it the bit about global warming and the energy resources? Because that’s a proper bugger, isn’t it? That, and the pyramids. Honestly, how did they  do  that? Given their tools… it's mind-boggling and also slightly frightening. It feels like we haven't even scratched the surface of understanding how clever people were back then. It makes you wonder about the Vikings too, really. They navigated vast oceans using surprisingly simple tools. Absolutely. And you know, there's growing evidence some of those ancient cultures understood things about tectonics – the earth's plates – that we're only just catching up on now. Look at the precision of some of those stone structures, aligned with celestial events… it suggests deep observational skills. It’s humbling, isn’t it?

Right, so, about this voucher for Casa Roma. Mum, you said you'd checked if they were doing that seafood pasta I like? Because last time we went, they'd taken it off the menu. Ruined my whole evening, it did. Yes, darling, I called this morning. They confirmed they have it. And they’ve got a new chef, apparently. Italian, from Sicily. So, hopefully, it’ll be even better than before! Though, really, how can they improve on that garlic and chilli sauce? Garlic and chilli sauce, eh? Reminds me of the time I tried to make that myself. Ended up needing a fire extinguisher! Burnt the pan solid. Your mum wouldn't let me near the kitchen for a week. Oh, Dad! You’re hopeless in the kitchen. Anyway, the voucher’s got to be used by the end of the month, hasn't it? I was thinking next Saturday? Would that work for you both? Before it rains again, because honestly, this weather… Next Saturday is lovely. Gives me time to finish this massive pile of paperwork. Speaking of, did you see I got a call from the bank about some automatic payments? I was wondering why my account was getting so low. Need to look at that later. All those little expenses add up, don’t they? Aye, they do. Remember when everything was cheaper? You could get a loaf of bread for tuppence! Not that I'm feeling particularly nostalgic. These fruit trees I planted are looking rather pricey with the fertiliser and everything. Hoping I get a good crop of apples this year, or I'll be eating them all myself! Speaking of money, have you seen those sunglasses at Oliver Bonas? The tortoiseshell ones? I’ve been looking at them online, but I really need to try them on. Think I deserve a treat after all this Sixth Form stress. Go for it, love. You’ve earned it. Although, maybe wait until after Casa Roma. We don’t want to blow the voucher money. By the way, I saw a beautiful baby chair in JYSK the other day. I thought of Sarah and Mark... maybe as a little gift, for when the little one arrives? A baby chair, eh? Time flies, doesn’t it? Seems like only yesterday your mum was complaining about me leaving muddy footprints on the freshly mopped floor. Speaking of yesterday, saw a load of chickens free-ranging down near the beach.

Right then, love. Honestly, this tree is giving me the willies. It’s lopsided already, isn't it? Remember last year? We had that whole fiasco with the star nearly falling on the cat. Sparky didn't like that one bit. It's not  that  bad, Mum. Just needs a bit of tweaking. Are you sure you haven't just got a wonky eye? And Sparky’s a dramatic little thing, honestly. He’d act scared if a feather landed on him. Wonky eye? Don't be daft. I've got perfectly good eyesight, thank you very much. It’s the tree! And speaking of Sparky, have you seen Mrs. Higgins’ new puppy? A little French Bulldog, all wrinkles and snorts. Absolutely adorable. She's been letting it wee on everyone's lawns. Honestly, the cheek of it. Mrs. Higgins and her little doggy adventures. Classic. I saw Maisie the other day, remember her from school? She's doing really well with her pottery business. Posted some gorgeous mugs online. You should take a look. Maisie! Good for her. It’s lovely to see people pursuing things they’re passionate about. Reminds me, I need to get my nails done. They’re looking a fright. I keep catching them on everything at work. You still doing those gel things, then? It lasts ages, doesn’t it? Saves me having to go back every other week. Yeah, I am. And they look amazing. I’m thinking of getting a Christmasy shade this time - maybe a sparkly red? What about you? Any exciting shifts coming up at the hospital? You were moaning about that new student last week. Oh, bless him, he's trying. Just a bit clumsy, poor thing. Took three attempts to put a drip in. Three! Anyway, yes, I’m on the night shift Christmas Eve. The usual chaos. But you'll be out with Liam, won't you? Probably. He’s trying to book a table at that German restaurant in town. He’s really gotten into German history and culture lately. Keeps spouting facts about Bismarck and stuff. Liam, eh? Always had a thing for the serious stuff. German history? That’s a bit niche for a December date, isn't it? Though, I suppose, the Christmas markets are lovely. I went to Cologne once, years ago. Beautiful city. So much history crammed into every cobblestone. Did you know it was a Roman settlement for centuries?

Right, well, here we are. Sussex. Officially home, I suppose. Bit bare, innit? Feels like a showroom, not a place to  live  yet. It’s lovely, honestly! Loads of light. And the garden looks like it could be amazing. Though, yeah, showroom vibes are definitely present. Needs personality. So, internet? That’s priority number one, surely? Absolutely. I tried to book something with Virgin, but their engineer can’t get out until Thursday. Thursday! We’re stuck with our phones for a few days. I rang Sky, but they’re even worse. The joys of rural broadband. Thursday? Seriously? That's ages! Right, needs a massive spreadsheet of things to do while we're disconnected. Okay, first, we need to unpack properly. I'm starving, though. Anything in that box of ‘essentials’ you brought? Essentials, apparently including half a roll of duct tape and three different kinds of screwdriver. No food, sadly. I was too preoccupied with ensuring the TV would work. Purely practical concerns, you know. Of course, you were. Proper gentleman teacher. Right then, Operation Grocery Shop commences. Honestly, I'm craving something seasonal. Remember those amazing plums we got at Borough Market last year? Vaguely. I remember the mess you made eating them. All over your face. It was glorious. Sussex markets are probably different though. Any chance they'll have decent sausage rolls? That's my fallback. You and your sausage rolls. I'll see what I can find. While I’m out, do you want me to grab something for dinner? I was thinking maybe a roast chicken – easy, fills the flat with a nice smell. Although, I wouldn't want to trigger the neighbours… The nursery? Yeah, probably best not. Little Timmy’s already been peering over the fence. I think he was trying to identify the strange noises of us lugging furniture. Oh dear. Well, chicken's out then. How about pasta? I could get some courgettes and tomatoes – they’re lovely at the moment. And pesto. Always pesto. Pasta sounds fantastic. You’re a lifesaver. Just… maybe not too spicy. My stomach’s still adjusting to the move. Speaking of adjusting, have you thought about setting up a direct debit for the council tax? I need to get that sorted. Council tax. The bane of everyone’s existence. I’ll do it tonight. My bank’s a nightmare with their online security, but I’ll persevere.

"Liv! Honestly, it’s so good to see you! You look amazing! Sorry, I nabbed a table already - this place is always packed on a Saturday, isn’t it?" "Daisy! You too! It's brilliant to see you. Yeah, it always is. Thanks for grabbing a table, I was dreading the queue. I'm starving, to be honest. The placement agency interview went on  forever  today." "Oh, blimey! Tell me about it. What did you end up interviewing for? Still looking at marketing, then?" "Yeah, mostly marketing, but this was a slightly different angle - digital marketing and social media for a new tech startup. Sounded really interesting, actually. Lots of talk about influencer campaigns and data analytics. My brain feels like mush now, to be perfectly honest. Fancy a drink while we look at the menu? I need something strong." "Definitely! I'll go grab us some drinks. I was thinking a prosecco, maybe? It feels like a celebratory catching-up kind of day. So, the startup – where were they based?" “In Birmingham. Which is a nightmare to get to. It’s a shame, because I’d really like to move out of Brum, eventually. My mum keeps saying I need to settle down, get a proper job, and find a nice boy. Typical mum, you know?" She laughs, rolling her eyes playfully. "Absolutely typical. My dad’s the same! He keeps asking when I’m going to ‘start a proper family’. As if project coordinating isn’t a proper job! Honestly, sometimes I want to scream. So, how's your mum doing? Still glued to the telly watching Bollywood films?" "She is! And convinced that every actor is her long-lost soulmate. She’s actually been trying to teach me some Bollywood dancing. It’s… an experience. What about yours? Still driving him crazy with her endless gardening?" "Always! The prize-winning roses are her pride and joy. Actually, she's planning a trip to Cornwall next month. Wants to see the Eden Project. I'm thinking of tagging along, it would be nice to have some proper mum-daughter time." “Oh, Cornwall! That’s lovely. Remember that disastrous family holiday to Devon when we were kids? The one where it rained for the entire week and Dad got stung by a jellyfish?” “Oh my god, yes! And Gran ended up buying us all those ridiculously oversized buckets and spades because we were so bored.

Honestly, you wouldn’t believe the look on Professor Davies’ face when I mentioned parmo. Like I’d just uttered a curse word! He was all, “A…parmo? What  is  a parmo?” Proper mortified, he was. Davies, eh? Typical. He probably thinks anything north of Watford is wilderness. I remember trying to explain Balti to my nan once. She just looked at me with this confused pity. "Why would you want bread swimming in curry, love?" Aye, it's a constant battle, isn’t it? People just don't  get  it. They think the North East is all pit villages and rain. Which, alright, there’s plenty of rain, but there's so much more. Proper food, for starters. You should bring your mum up for a weekend. She'd love it. I’d love to. She's been saying she wants to visit somewhere different. Though, you know her – she’ll probably insist on going to a cathedral. She's obsessed with them. Right, the cathedral fanatic. We could find a nice one in Durham, then we’re already sorted for the day. And then, after, parmos. Proper, loaded, cheesy parmos. Sounds like a plan. So, tell me more about this Davies incident. Was he actually being rude? Not intentionally, I don’t think. Just… clueless. We were talking about regional differences in culinary traditions for my research, and I brought up parmos as a prime example of a dish deeply rooted in a specific area and with a unique identity. He just stared blankly! I had to explain what it was, all the layers, the chicken, the cheese, the sauce... it was mortifying and hilarious all at once. Brilliant. You should have just left him there, baffled. How's the research going otherwise? Still drowning in data? Drowning is putting it mildly. I'm trying to map regional identity through food preferences, and apparently, people are  incredibly  protective about their chips. There's entire mailing lists dedicated to chip thickness and frying methods. Chips? Seriously? People are that passionate? That’s amazing. It’s just like the arguments in Birmingham about Balti spices. Everyone has their favourite combination, and they'll defend it to the death. It’s bonkers! I’ve had people swear that only certain chip shops in their hometown can make a “proper” chip. It's fascinating, really. It’s a window into a whole load of other things – history, social class, tradition… Absolutely.

Alright, Gran, you still reading that paper? It’s like, ancient history already. Don't be cheeky, lad. It's only Tuesday. And this isn't just "ancient history," this is important stuff. About that… that Sunak, is it? Honestly, the man's got no backbone. Sunak’s alright, I reckon. Better than Truss, defo. Remember how ropey things were with her? Proper mess, that. Alright? Alright? He's selling off the country bit by bit! Privatising the NHS, I heard. Selling it to the Americans! Mark my words, it'll be all gone before you're my age. Come on, Gran. That’s a bit dramatic, innit? The NHS is safe. Everyone says so. It's just… needing a bit of sorting out. Long waiting lists, you know? My mum’s been trying to get a dentist appointment for ages. "Needing a bit of sorting out"? They've been chipping away at it for years! Thatcher started it, you know. Slowly, slowly, weakening it until they can swoop in and take it over. I remember when you could just walk into your GP, no appointment needed. Doctors looked after the community, cared about their patients. Not like these days, all about profits and targets. Right, well, I'm gonna have a quick look at what the news says about the NHS then. Just to see what’s going on. Loads of articles... most of them say it  is  struggling. Staff shortages, funding cuts... See! I told you! You young ‘uns, you trust everything you read online. They spin it all, you know. But I’ve lived long enough to see how things change. Used to be, a man’s word was his bond. Now, it’s all about bending the rules and lining your own pockets. It's not all bad though, is it? I mean, we've got loads of technology now, loads of things people couldn't even dream of back in your day. Technology! Hmph. Technology that keeps you glued to that infernal phone, forgetting how to talk to your family! We used to have conversations, real, proper conversations. Round the kitchen table, with a cup of tea. Not typing away at a screen. And we didn’t need the news on our phones to tell us what was happening. We knew our neighbours, we looked out for each other. There was a sense of  community , lad.

That was a grand feed, Mary. Proper roasted chicken, just like you used to make at home. Though, honestly, Liam, must you wave your fork about like you’re conducting an orchestra? Keep it on the plate, lad. But I was just trying to get the last bit of gravy, Dad! It was good gravy. Leave him be, Sean. He's a growing boy. And besides, a bit of enthusiasm never hurt anyone. You were the same at his age, Liam. Remember all the splashing at Fitzgeralds Park? Yeah! And Dad got soaked trying to chase me! I’ll never forget that, will I? You were a slippery wee thing. FitzGerald's Park is lovely, mind you. Should take the wee ones again soon. Granny, are you enjoying yourself? You haven’t touched your Brussels sprouts. These sprouts… they're not like the ones we had back in Glasgow. These are… softer. A little too soft for my liking, dear. But the chicken! The chicken is lovely, Sean. Just lovely. Reminds me of when I used to bake for the staff at the school. Always had a roast on Fridays. That's lovely, Granny. So, Sean, did you see anything about that blood moon tonight? Apparently, it's supposed to be quite spectacular. A blood moon?! Really? Will I be able to see it? It's a lunar eclipse, Liam. The moon passes into the Earth’s shadow, and it turns a reddish hue. They say it’s a bit eerie, but it’s a brilliant sight, proper. We might take a wee walk to the park after, if the clouds behave themselves. Eerie, is it? Reminds me of tales my grandmother used to tell. About werewolves and witches and all sorts of mischief happening under a blood moon. She used to say it was a time when the veil between worlds was thin. Werewolves?! Real werewolves? Granny's just spinning a yarn, love. It's just a bit of fun. Though, you’ve got to admit, it  does  sound a bit spooky. Now, now, Mary. Don't go scaring the boy with stories of mythical beasts. He’s barely eleven. But it's a good story, Granny. Tell him about the fairy rings you used to see in the fields near Glasgow. Oh, aye. There was a field behind the school, all wild and overgrown. Used to see perfect circles of mushrooms there.

Dreadful business, this whole Scottish referendum thing, isn't it, Arthur? Utterly dreadful. Feels like the whole country's on edge. I've been trying to explain it to my Year Nines – bless their cotton socks, they’re mostly interested in TikTok. But trying to get them to grasp the nuances of constitutional law… it’s a challenge. Aye, a challenge indeed, David. It’s more than just TikTok, isn't it? It's fundamental to the whole setup. I read an interesting piece in the Argus about the economic implications for Brighton if Scotland breaks away. Could be a bit of a knock-on effect, you know, with the tourism. Though, to be honest, I’m more concerned about the principle of it all. A united kingdom… well, that’s something to cherish. Reminds me of when I was a lad, volunteering at the pier. All sorts came down, from all corners of the UK. Precisely. Though, you can't ignore the underlying frustrations, can you? Decades of feeling unheard… So, how's the shop doing? Still battling the online retailers? Battling is the word for it. Online’s a beast. I had a job interview for a young lad yesterday, applied to be a stock assistant. Bright enough, seemed keen, but lacked experience, naturally. Had a bit of a stammer, poor chap. Reminded me of my younger self. Oh dear. Did you offer him the position? I told him I'd be in touch. I'm leaning towards it, actually. Gave him a bit of encouragement, you know? Said everyone stammers a bit when they’re nervous. I remember getting tongue-tied interviewing for my first job at the hardware store – nearly babbled on about pigeons! But he seemed like a good lad, willing to learn. What about you? Any turbulence at school? A bit. One of my colleagues, Mrs. Davies… she’s threatening to retire early. Apparently, the paperwork alone is driving her mad. Said she’d rather knit tea cosies than fill out another Ofsted form. Can’t say I blame her. Teaching used to be about inspiring young minds, now it's an administrative nightmare. Sounds familiar, doesn't it? Running a business these days... it's all numbers and regulations. Barely time to actually  do  anything. How's your daughter doing, by the way? Still in London? She is. Absolutely thriving, actually. Just got promoted at her firm.

Right, so, Luton airport, then straight to…where exactly are we headed again, Dad? My brain feels like mush after wrestling with those bloody colour palettes all morning. Portugal, Aaron. Algarve, remember? We talked about it for weeks. And mush? You’re an art worker, you deal with colours all day! It’s your profession, not a punishment. It’ll be lovely, Aaron. Sunshine and Pastel de Nata! And remember that little kennel we saw online? We could look into fostering a Portuguese Podengo while we’re there. They're adorable, those little fellas. A Podengo? Seriously? I’m barely managing my succulents at home. A dog, especially a Portuguese one, seems a bit…ambitious. They’re actually incredibly intelligent, Aaron. Easily trained, energetic, but also fiercely loyal. A challenge, but a rewarding one. Like teaching a particularly stubborn group of Korean students, really. Want to hear about my lesson on the subjunctive mood? Please, Liam, no. I’m actively avoiding education at the moment. My student loans are haunting my dreams. Tuition fees are ridiculous, aren't they, Dad? Absolutely ridiculous. Tell me about it. They keep going up and up. Back in my day, you worked part-time and covered everything. Now, it's like a lifetime debt sentence. Speaking of money, I saw a shocking article about pension schemes the other day... apparently, a lot of people are woefully underprepared. Oh, don't start on pensions, John. Let’s enjoy the sunshine and cheap beer first. I was thinking we could get some of those pre-made paellas from Aldi when we get back. Saves all the faff, doesn't it? Aldi’s paella is… questionable. It tastes vaguely of tomato soup and regret. We’re getting a proper seafood restaurant, Mum. I'm serious. It’s the least I deserve after another week of battling corporate fonts. You know, there's a world record for the largest paella ever made. It was in Valencia, if I recall. Something like 120 tonnes of rice! Honestly, it's mind-boggling to think about cooking that much food. 120 tonnes! I can barely manage a simple shepherd’s pie without setting off the smoke alarm. Reminds me of that disaster with the custard I tried to make for your birthday, Aaron. You wouldn’t touch it. That was traumatic, Dad. A solid, rubbery mass of... something. I think the cat refused to go near it too.

Right, alright. So, Grandad, are you sure you’re alright back there? Seems a bit…quiet. You usually have some comment about me driving like a lunatic. Lunatic, eh? Aye, lass. You've got a bit of lead foot, that's for sure. Reminds me o' my Elsie when she first learned to drive. Nearly took out a postbox, she did. This road's a bit narrow, mind. Watch out for those sheep. Sheep? Are we passing a farm? I didn't see any on the satnav. Though, satellites don’t exactly pick up livestock, do they? Aye, a farm’s just up ahead. Big one. Always loads o' animals wandering about. Makes your life interesting, it does. Especially when you're trying to get to ANON’s for dinner. Now, sheep’s not the only thing to worry about, pet. You got cows as well, and sometimes pigs escape. Saw a pig once, right in the middle of the A560. Caused chaos, it did. Absolute mayhem. Pigs on the A560? Seriously? That sounds like something out of a sitcom. Aye, that's Grandad. He's full o' stories like that. Most of 'em are probably embellished, mind. But it makes for a good laugh. And he's right, you gotta be careful. Saw a cow once, stood smack-bang in the middle o' the lane. Nearly gave meself a heart attack. Heart attack, you say? Elsie’s sister, Mildred, had a heart attack. Right in the middle o’ Blackpool Illuminations. Can you imagine? Surrounded by flashing lights and all. Awful business. But she recovered, thankfully. Strong woman, Elsie’s sister. Strong. Grandad, while I admire your storytelling… perhaps we could focus on the current driving situation? It’s rather lovely countryside, though. Makes a change from London. All concrete and glass. Do you often come out this way? We do. Mum always likes a good ramble, and this is on the way to her favourite tea rooms. She’ll have a right moan if we don't stop for scones. Speaking of which, Grandad, you alright for scones? Fancy a jam and cream? Scones? Now you're talking! Elsie used to make the best scones. Light as a feather they were. Not like the ones you get nowadays. All hard and dry. Rubbish, they are. I actually quite like a dry scone. You can really taste the flour. It’s textural.

This butternut squash soup is lovely, isn’t it? It's just what I needed after that walk. My knees are protesting a bit today, I must admit. Though, the scenery was worth it. Absolutely breathtaking up near Ullswater. It really is delicious, Mum. You’ve outdone yourself. And yes, I completely agree about the scenery. I took some photos earlier, I’ll show you later. How far did you walk exactly? You shouldn’t push yourself too much, especially with your knees. Push yourself? That’s Mary for you. Always off traipsing about the hills. Remember when she insisted on hiking up Scafell Pike, even with that dodgy ankle? Oh, don't remind me, Arthur! I was younger then. And the view  was  spectacular, even if I did spend the next three days hobbling. It just proves, you see, that a bit of exercise, even if it’s a bit painful, is good for the soul. The choir helped too, of course. Rehearsal went well tonight – we’re really starting to gel for the Christmas concert. That's brilliant, Mum! I'm so glad the choir's going well. Are you singing your usual solo? I’d love to come to the concert, I’ll put it in my diary. Though, finding the time these days is… a challenge. Editing deadlines are relentless. Speaking of schedules, your Aunt Carol called earlier, Mary. Apparently, she's still fuming about you being late for her birthday lunch last month. She blamed it on the "Millennial lack of respect for punctuality.” Honestly! Oh, Carol! She'll be alright. She just likes to hold a grudge. Though, you  were  rather late, dear. Three-quarters of an hour, I believe. It put a real dampener on her roast beef. I know, I know! I’m truly sorry. A last-minute rush job with a client threw everything off. I promise it won’t happen again. Aunt Carol can be… intense. I’ll send her a nice card and a box of chocolates to smooth things over. Chocolates are always a good start. So, about family plans… We’ve had a few calls about that Anderson Foundation gala next month. Apparently, they're raising money for underprivileged children's education. Seems a worthwhile cause. Yes, I saw something about it online. I think it’s wonderful, the work they do. A good education is vital. I spent my life trying to impart a little understanding of mathematics, and the frustration of seeing so many bright children held back due to circumstance...

Right, so, parents’ evening. It was…an experience, wasn’t it? Mrs. Davies seemed quite concerned about Leo’s maths. Said he was really struggling with fractions. Fractions are hard! Like, really, really hard. Can I have more pasta? Please? It’s yummy! Of course, darling. Yes, they  are  hard, aren’t they? But Leo really needs to put in some extra effort. Mrs. Davies suggested we get him some extra worksheets, and maybe a tutor. Bit drastic, I know, but… A tutor? That sounds boring. Can't we just, like, practice fractions while watching cartoons? That’s…not quite the approach Mrs. Davies had in mind, love. Although, maybe a little bit of fun practice wouldn't hurt. We'll see. Speaking of fun, World Book Day is next week! Have you two decided what you’re going as? I'm going as a lion! Roar! A magnificent lion! And you, sweetheart? I'm going as Hermione! I’ve got the wand and the scarf and everything! I’m going to read a really loud bit from  Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban . Brilliant! You’ll be fantastic. Speaking of characters in books… Mrs. Davies mentioned Leo was distracted during a lesson yesterday. He told her he was thinking about a character in a book eating… well, I can’t quite repeat what he said. He said it smelled like cooked… people! Yes, dear, that's precisely it. Apparently, in this book he’s reading, there's a character who eats people. He was trying to describe what it supposedly smelled like. I had to gently explain that eating people is  very  wrong and that we don’t talk about such things. Eww! That’s disgusting! Why are books even allowed to  say  that? Well, they're trying to create a vivid picture of a… somewhat unpleasant character, I suppose. It’s probably quite gruesome, isn’t it? Anyway, moving on! After school tomorrow, I’m picking you both up and then we're heading to the circus! Remember? The circus! With the elephants and the clowns! And the trapeze! I want to see the lions! Are they real lions? They are, darling. But they’re very well looked after. And please, let's try to avoid discussing the aroma of cooked human flesh near the elephants, alright? Okay! But it  was  a really weird thing to think about! It certainly was.

Right, so, the curtain shop is booming, apparently. Saoirse tells me they’re practically swamped. Did you hear about that, Moira? They’ve had to take on another lad. No, I hadn’t! That's brilliant for them, isn't it? Saoirse always had a good head for business. Though, having Finn helping out must be a good thing too. He seems to be settling in well. Finn! Finn! That's him, soldier! And settling in grand, he is, the wee rascal. He’s actually quite handy with the measuring tape, apparently. Seems the retail gene skipped me and landed squarely on them two. Oh, retail, eh? Good honest work. My Jimmy, bless his soul, he used to say there's nothing more satisfying than a customer leaving happy with their purchase. Reminds me of teaching, really. Seeing that little spark of understanding light up a child's face… precious. That’s lovely, Nan. Speaking of sparking, have you thought about the birthday party, Liam? Oisin's getting on, practically a big boy now. Should we do something bigger than just a few friends around? Aye, I've been having a think. The rugby match is on the Saturday. I was thinking a trip to Páirc Uí Chaoimh. There's a good atmosphere, and Oisin'd love to see the lads playing. Though I’m not sure if it’s suitable with his wee legs. What do you reckon? That sounds a bit ambitious, maybe. He’s still a bit small for a massive crowd. What about a bouncy castle in the garden? We could invite all his friends from creche and a few from down the road. Easy, fuss-free, and he’ll adore it. A bouncy castle… That's a grand idea, Moira. Easier than wrestling tickets and explaining to him why he can't be on the pitch. Right, bouncy castle it is. I'll have a look online. Do you think we need to do fairy cakes as well? Fairy cakes are always a good shout! A bit of sugar never hurt anyone. Though you need to watch those colours, eh? Don't want his wee teeth turning green! Green! Like a dinosaur! Exactly, Oisin. Dinosaurs! Right, Moira, maybe just regular vanilla then. And speaking of regular, I'm dreading these charity calls. They’re relentless this week. Half of them are scams, I swear. Tell me about it!

Right then, you two. I'm still convinced your “Palindrome Panic” was a cheat, Finn. Honestly! "Detartrated"? Who even  uses  that word? It's a perfectly legitimate word, Maisie! And as a consultant engineer, I deal with quite a lot of chemistry. Detartrated wine is a serious business, you know. It prevents precipitation. It’s vital for clarity. Let the man have his fun, Maisie. It  was  clever. I mean, birkenhead isn’t exactly a hotbed of winemaking expertise, but even  I  know detartrated is a thing. Though, I admit, using it in a word game is peak Finn. Peak Finn is finding a loophole, that’s what. And I’m fairly certain you two conspired. You probably practiced this ages ago, didn’t you? While I was battling spreadsheets and linguistic anomalies. Conspired? Maisie, that’s outrageous! I was researching corrosion inhibitors, thank you very much. Not plotting world domination through palindromes. Besides, you’re the language expert here. Shouldn’t you be able to conjure up some obscure, symmetrical wonder? Alright, alright, don't rub it in. It’s harder than it looks! Especially when you’re limited to, like, common English. You're tempting me to pull out something from Old English just to win. Oh, please don't. That’ll just confuse everyone even more. Remember when you tried to explain "wyrd" to Aunt Carol last Christmas? It did  not  go well. Don't remind me. Carol thought I was inventing words. Anyway, what about you, Liam? You’ve been suspiciously quiet. Got any brilliantly obtuse palindromes up your sleeve? Hmm... let me see. Nothing quite as… specific as "detartrated," admittedly. But I did find "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama." Classic, I know, but I always thought it was rather nicely constructed. The Panama one? Honestly, Liam, that’s like showing up to a chess tournament with a pawn. That's practically cheating with its fame. Fair point. It’s a bit of a default. But it demonstrates the principle, doesn't it? The neatness of perfect symmetry. Aye, it does. But it's lackin’ a bit of… spark. I need something with a bit more grit, a bit more… Sunderland. Sunderland? Are you suggesting there’s a uniquely Sunderland-esque palindrome? Well, not specifically. But a word that reflects the spirit of the place, you know? Something a bit rough around the edges, a bit resilient… Maybe a word related to shipbuilding?

Honestly, Liam, you look like you’ve been hit by a bus! Seriously, what have you been doing? You’re practically melting into that armchair. Don’t even start, El. I’ve been engaging in a vital, crucial, and frankly, heroic activity. Oh, let me guess... conquering Mount Laundry? No! Napping. Serious napping. After that lecture on post-structuralist theory, my brain needed a full system reboot. It was like wading through treacle. Post-structuralist theory? Sounds thrilling. I had Contemporary Poetry, which was marginally better, mostly because the lecturer kept accidentally calling Wordsworth 'Woody'. Woody Wordsworth! You’re having a laugh! Did anyone correct him? Nah, everyone was too polite. He’s a bit of a legend, you know. Bit eccentric. But, seriously, you look wrecked. You’re normally buzzing around like a caffeinated hummingbird. I’m conserving energy, El. Big plans for the evening. Gig at The Ropewalk. You going? Stone Roses tribute band. Stone Roses?! You know that’s not my thing, is it? All that jangly guitar... I’d rather listen to a vacuum cleaner. Come on, don’t be like that! It'll be good fun, atmosphere will be buzzing. Plus, remember Gaz and Chloe are going. Gaz and Chloe, always dragging me into things. And last time Chloe tried to teach me how to do a windmill. Nearly broke my arm. Oh god, yeah! That was a disaster. Right, speaking of disasters, have you seen the pictures Anon sent? The ones from that holiday in Skegness when we were, like, twelve? Don't you dare! Please tell me I don’t look like a baby seal wearing a floral swimsuit. Worse, I reckon. You've got that suncream on your nose like a giant beacon. And Anon's got this ridiculous perm. It looks like a poodle exploded on his head. Oh my god! You’re right! This is mortifying! Look at me! I was so tanned! And that swimsuit… horrific. Were we really twelve? Twelve and supremely confident that we were on the cusp of world domination. Remember how we vowed to become famous pop stars and move to LA? And we’d all have matching chihuahuas. Oh, bless! Anon’s perm is actually worse than I thought. It’s… sculptural. It is. It really is. We need to send this to everyone in the group chat. Just to remind them of our... glory days.

Right, so I’ve gone over this submission for the planning committee again. It still feels… insufficient. Honestly, I’m having second thoughts about even presenting it. Morning. More second thoughts, eh? You've been fretting about this for weeks, love. What’s the sticking point this time? Is it the visual impact assessment again? Part of it, yes. But it’s more than that. It's the entire structure. They’re going to grill us, you know they will. Mr. Henderson practically sneered at the feasibility report last time. And the residents' objections are, frankly, relentless. They genuinely think a small eco-village is going to invite hordes of tourists and ruin their views. It's ridiculous. Right, ridiculous. Yes, they're always delightful, aren’t they? But we just need to demonstrate that we’ve considered everything, addressed every concern. Walk them through it logically. I've been reviewing the finances here - I think we need to hammer home the long-term economic benefit to the area. Local jobs, increased footfall for existing businesses… it’s about showcasing the positives. I've got the economic projections, of course. And the sustainability report. But it feels like shouting into the void. They’re already predisposed to dislike it because it’s  different . It challenges their idea of what the area  should  be. That's their problem, not ours. Our job is to present a well-reasoned, thoroughly researched proposal. Okay, let's look at the structure. We open with the community need – the lack of affordable housing, the need for sustainable practices. Then we move onto the design, highlighting the eco-friendly features, the blend with the natural landscape. Then financials, then address the resident objections head-on… What are their biggest gripes, specifically? Mostly traffic, noise, and light pollution. And they're concerned about the impact on the local wildlife – the badger set nearby, particularly. Right. Okay, we need to preempt those. We've got the traffic management plan, the noise mitigation strategies… have you included those detailed schematics showing the shielded lighting? Yes, they’re in Appendix B. But I'm still worried they'll dismiss them. They're so entrenched in their position. Then we make them  understand  them. Use visual aids. Maybe even a simple 3D model of the village showing how it integrates with the surroundings, demonstrating minimal impact. I can help with that, I've got some basic skills in SketchUp.

Honestly, Chloe, the price of avocados has gone completely mental. Mental! Five pounds for  one ? Are they solid gold now? Tell me about it! I saw a cauliflower the other day that was practically knocking me over with its price tag. It’s ridiculous. Did you get any decent tomatoes though? The ones last week were like little watery sponges. Managed to find some that  looked  respectable, yeah. We’ll see. I’m thinking pasta tonight, maybe with a pesto and some roasted veg. Unless you’re feeling something else? You looked like you needed a massive carb load after your shift. That actually sounds amazing. My brain feels like mush after dealing with Mr. Henderson all afternoon. He convinced himself the squirrels in his garden were government spies. Honestly. Oh god. That's… a lot. You’ve got a saint's patience, you know that? Remember Sarah from sixth form? She used to insist the pigeons were drones. Sarah! Oh my god, I'd completely forgotten about her! The one who wore all velvet and smoked roll-ups in the library? What ever happened to her? No clue. She vanished after A-levels. Apparently, she was going to be a famous poet or something. Probably ended up running a chain of vegan cupcake shops, knowing her. Probably! Speaking of disappearing, have you noticed Mrs. Higgins hasn’t been putting her bins out? It’s been weeks. I'm starting to think something’s up. I saw a removals van parked outside last Tuesday, but I couldn’t see much. Really? That’s weird. I thought she was just getting more reclusive. She’s always been a bit odd, hasn’t she? Remember when she put those flamingoes in her front garden and refused to take them down? Don’t remind me! Peak Mrs. Higgins. Anyway, pasta sounds good. I'm utterly exhausted. Did you see that film, "Anyone But You?" It’s on Netflix? Oh, I did! It was terribly cheesy, but oddly enjoyable. Sydney Sweeney is gorgeous, isn't she? Though, I didn't believe a single thing they said. Rom-coms have totally lost the plot. Exactly! It was like they were trying to mimic "When Harry Met Sally" but completely missed the point. Still, escapism, right? I swear, all the men I meet are like, Mitchell . Absolutely zero spontaneity. Don't even get me started! I went on a date last week, and he spent the entire time talking about his cryptocurrency investments.

Blimey, this advert’s a right load of rubbish, innit? Like, who buys a vacuum cleaner based on someone jumping around in a sparkly jumpsuit? It's designed to grab your attention, Liam. It’s advertising 101. Emotional appeal, manufactured aspiration… all the fancy NLP stuff they teach us about. NLP? You’re applying psychology to a Hoover ad? Seriously, love? Well, yeah. Think about it. It’s triggering feelings of wanting a clean house, wanting to impress guests, wanting to feel… in control. Subliminal messaging all over the place. And the music’s brilliantly manipulative too. You’re taking the mickey, aren’t ya? Right, I'm changing the channel. This rubbish is giving me a headache. Ooh, look! Big car boot sale down at the Wirral Showground on Saturday. Fancy a look? Might find a bargain. Saturday? Hmm, I do have that meeting with Mr. Henderson about the new patient intakes. Might be a bit tight. What are you hoping to find? Nah, just a poke around, y'know? Always good for a laugh and a bit of rummaging. Maybe some old vinyl, that'd be dead on. Thinking of trying to flog some of my old trainers too. Got a couple of pairs I barely wore. Be careful what you buy. I read an article in the Journal of Consumer Behaviour about the psychology of impulse purchases at car boot sales...it's a minefield. They design the layouts to encourage maximal browsing - clustering similar items, creating a sense of urgency... Here we go again! You and your brain. Right, so, what are your plans for the week then, other than analyzing the shopping habits of bargain hunters? Anything exciting happenin' at work? It's been fairly busy actually. We're seeing a noticeable spike in anxiety amongst younger clients, particularly those relying heavily on their mobiles. The constant comparison, the fear of missing out… It's pretty draining to witness. Yeah, I get that. I barely put mine down, to be honest. Even when I'm supposed to be marking essays. Speaking of which, gotta get some of that marking done this week. The students are proper clueless about Dickens. Dickens? Still teaching that? Bless 'em. Have you considered incorporating some multimedia elements? Maybe a short film adaptation? It might engage them more. I've tried, but they all just look at their phones and complain about it bein’ too long.

Honestly, this weather is just ridiculous. One minute sunshine, the next a downpour. It's messing with my students - they can’t concentrate when it changes so drastically. I had to cancel their outdoor speaking practice today. Proper dreary. Tell me about it. The golf course was a swamp this morning. Had to call it quits after nine holes. Still, at least it makes for decent conversation, right? What have you all been up to? I swear, feels like ages since we properly all got together. Work’s been manic, as always. The BBC’s gearing up for a big series on local history, so I’ve been buried in research and content planning. It’s fascinating stuff, actually - digging through archives. Did you know Birmingham used to be a centre for button-making? Fascinating, Tom. But my brain is fried from chasing a story on property prices. Honestly, it's terrifying. My editor wants something splashy, but all I can find are depressing statistics about affordability. It's making me seriously question ever buying a place in London. Property's a nightmare everywhere, isn't it? I was looking at a small cottage near Harrogate the other week, and the estate agent was practically laughing at me for suggesting the price was a bit steep. Apparently, they're offering incentives like freezers and TVs just to get people to sign. Madness. Incentives? Seriously? That's… desperate. It does make you wonder, doesn't it? I'm still renting, but I’m starting to look around Hertfordshire a bit. The prices are ridiculous there too, but at least I know the area. Speaking of insane prices, has anyone tried that new Korean place, 'Han's Kitchen,' down the road? Apparently, their bibimbap is legendary. But the reviews also mention the wait. Could be hours. I've heard good things! I'm always up for trying new food. I've downloaded this app, 'Tasty Trails', that recommends restaurants based on your dietary preferences. It's surprisingly good. I used it to find a proper curry house last week – haven’t had a curry like that in ages. Apps! Don’t even get me started. My phone's practically overflowing with them. I’m trying to be better about limiting screen time, but then I find something new to download. There’s this writing app, ‘Scrivener’, a friend recommended it, but I don’t know if I have the discipline to actually stick with it.

It’s lovely to have you all here. It's been far too long since we've all been together properly. Remember how daunting it felt moving here in '67? Completely alien landscape compared to Gloucestershire. Daunting is a good word, Penelope. Absolutely daunting. I arrived in Ramsgate for an interview, fresh off the train, thinking I’d landed in the Mediterranean! The sea air, the… well, the general atmosphere. Though, truth be told, the interview didn’t go spectacularly. You? Spectacularly? Arthur, you were always a model of calm composure! I remember you talking about it – the interviewer kept asking about your knowledge of Wordsworth and… beetroot farming! Honestly! It was a grammar school, David! Apparently, beetroot farming was considered a crucial skill for a classics teacher! Though, I did manage to land a job at the secondary school down the road. The real challenge was finding somewhere to live. Tell me about it. Birmingham was…compact, shall we say, in the sixties. Finding a place as a newly qualified dentist was a trek. Ended up renting a room in a house owned by a rather eccentric widow who collected porcelain dolls. Hundreds of them, staring down at you from every shelf. Gave me the shivers. Oh, goodness. I had better luck, actually. Managed to find a tiny cottage just outside the village. Needed a  lot  of work, of course. Leaked like a sieve in winter, and the garden was entirely overgrown with brambles. But it was mine, and it was affordable. It was all about pottering rather than pride back then. Speaking of affordable, Penelope, you mentioned renovating. My first flat in Manchester was… well, ‘renovation’ is a generous term. ‘Structural intervention’ is probably more accurate. The floorboards sloped alarmingly, and I'm fairly certain the entire building listing. But it was £5 a week! Those were the days, eh? We were living on air and enthusiasm. I eventually bought a small terrace house in Cliftonville. Took me years to save up, though. My wife, Margaret, she was the one who really pushed me. Said I needed to stop living in a glorified cupboard. It's funny, isn’t it? How much our wives shaped our lives? I met Eleanor at a teacher’s conference in York. Dreadful conference, actually. Absolutely freezing. But he was charmingly awkward trying to offer me a biscuit. And then… well, that was that.

Well, this is lovely, isn't it, Penelope? A proper cuppa and a good natter. Haven't had a proper natter like this in... well, ages, truth be told. Taunton's been a bit quiet lately, you know. More dust than customers, mostly. It  is  lovely, Marion. Thanks for having me. And I completely understand about quiet towns. Sydney was bustling, of course, always something happening. But it had a frenetic energy that, frankly, I didn’t miss when I finally retired. This pace is much more agreeable. You mentioned dust in your gallery – are you still specializing in those delightful porcelain figurines? Oh, the figurines! Yes, still clinging on to them, I am. Though the market’s a fickle thing. People want the ‘shabby chic’ now, you see? Not pristine Victorian beauties. Makes a body wonder what the future holds for a girl like me. My father, bless his soul, he'd have known what to do. He was a farmer, you know. Solid, dependable. Nothing flighty about him. Always said "A field well tilled is a life well lived.” Didn’t quite apply to selling little shepherdesses, did it? No, I imagine not. My father, he was a shipbuilder. Quite different, I suppose. A world of metal and rivets, not soil and crops. He wouldn't have understood my career either, really. Speech and Language Therapy... it was quite unconventional for a woman back then, even in Australia. Did you always know you wanted to be an artist, Marion? Not always, dear. Started out wanting to be a proper actress, you know. Got as far as RADA, I did. Just a short stint, mind. Realized quickly it weren’t for me. Too much… fuss. Too much performing and not enough…  being . Art felt more truthful, somehow. More honest. I could capture a feeling, a moment… without having to say a word. Did  you  always gravitate towards helping people with their voices, Penelope? It wasn’t a sudden decision, no. As a child, I was terribly shy. Utterly tongue-tied, really. Couldn't speak properly in class. Absolutely mortifying. My mother took me to a wonderful speech therapist – Mrs. Hawthorne, a formidable woman with a twinkle in her eye. She unlocked something in me, you see? Gave me the confidence to  find  my voice. I suppose it was only natural, eventually, that I wanted to do the same for others.

Right, so, parsnips are done. Carrots next. Honestly, this roast dinner is gonna be epic. You reckon Liam will eat all that gravy? He’s a gravy fiend, that one. Liam will inhale the entire vat, yeah. He practically lives on gravy. And don’t even get me started on the stuffing. Did you remember to get those chestnuts? Sorted. Got the good ones too, not those watery ones you sometimes get. Honestly, the quality of chestnuts can make or break a stuffing. It's a serious business. Thinking of adding a bit of apple this year, add a bit of sweetness. What do you reckon? Apple's a good shout. Balance out all that savoury. Ooh, I was thinking about doing a cranberry sauce with orange zest. Bit fancy, innit? Might need to pop down to that little deli on Portobello Road. They do the best dried cranberries. Fancy is good. We’re embracing the Christmas spirit, aren't we? Speaking of which, have you even  started  on the decorations yet? My flat looks like a bomb site. I need a serious injection of tinsel and fairy lights. I’ve got a few bits, but nothing major. Been a bit busy with the bakery. Apparently, everyone wants gingerbread men with glittery icing this year. The demand is insane! I’m even thinking about doing a limited-edition Christmas cake – a dark chocolate and cherry one with gold leaf. Got a client already, a bloke from Mayfair. Gold leaf! You're going proper high-end. Good for you. So, is Chloe coming over tonight? I was hoping to get her thoughts on… well, on something rather important. Yeah, she said she’d be here around seven. Promised to bring her famous mince pies. Don’t tell her I told you, but she’s been trying out a new recipe with star anise. Apparently, it's a game-changer. Speaking of the devil! That'll be her. Right, oven's on, veggies are nearly ready. Operation Christmas Roast Dinner is a go! Hi guys! Sorry I'm a bit late, train was delayed. Oh my god, this smells incredible! What are you making? Roast dinner! Full Monty. And Chloe, darling, you look fantastic. What have you got there? Mince pies! The experimental ones with the star anise. Let me know what you think! Business is absolutely manic at the cafe, you wouldn't believe.

Blimey, Mum, this is nice. Proper peaceful, innit? Not like dodging tourists and dodging pigeons back in London. It is lovely, darling. A bit of countryside does wonders for the soul, doesn't it? You seemed a bit… frayed around the edges when I picked you up from Cambridge. Thesis getting you down? Yeah, a bit. It’s just… the final chapter feels monumental. Like the whole thing's gonna collapse if I don’t get it right. I’m going back and forth on the arguments. Doubt creeping in, you know? It’s a right pain. It always is, at that stage. The culmination of all that work. You’ve put in a phenomenal amount, Liam. Remember when you first told me you wanted to do your thesis on post-colonial representations in early modernist poetry? People thought you were mad. Yeah, Professor Davies nearly choked on his Earl Grey. But I'm convinced it’s a solid bit of work now. Just need to nail this ending. What about you? How’s the new author you were telling me about? She’s brilliant. Absolutely brilliant. Young woman, writes historical fiction with incredible depth and sensitivity. I’m already envisioning her having a very bright future. It’s… invigorating, working with new voices. It reminds me why I do it. Speaking of futures, have you given any more thought to what you’ll do after you graduate? I've been trying. It's just… daunting. Academia feels like a slog. Endless applications, competing for tiny positions… I don't know if I’m cut out for it. There’s that internship with the literary agency, though. Might be worth a shot? That’s an excellent idea, darling. Getting a foot in the door in publishing would be invaluable. And it's a world away from dusty seminars and grant applications! Though, don't rule out academia completely. You’re intelligent and passionate. People underestimate your abilities sometimes. Maybe. But I'm also thinking about… buying a place. Proper ridiculous, I know. When am I ever going to be able to afford a flat in London? It  is  a challenge, no doubt. But it's not impossible. Have you been looking at anything? Remember that area near Clapham Junction? Prices are starting to soften a little there. Yeah, I had a look. Tiny studios, mostly. Cramped as anything. It's just… I want somewhere with a bit of character, you know?

Oh, hello! Didn’t realize anyone else was lingering in this rather splendid corner of the Law Faculty. Lovely building, isn't it? So much history practically radiating from the walls. It really is. I was just admiring the stained glass. Alumni Day 2 is certainly proving busier than yesterday. I’m Eleanor, by the way. Imogen. Nice to meet you, Eleanor. I'm coordinating language research at the university, and I’m finding it rather fascinating – all the connections you can draw between language, history…it's endless, really. Are you an alumna? I am! Just finished my postgraduate degree in Linguistics last year. Now I’m a Research Administrator, mostly wrangling data and chasing funding. Less exciting than actual research, perhaps, but necessary! What about you? Did you study here? No, I studied at UCL, but I’ve been at Cambridge for a couple of years now. Fascinating to see how different institutions approach things. I’m particularly working on a project mapping the evolution of regional dialects in England – back to Roman times, ideally. Wanting to see how invasions and migrations really re-shaped language. Excuse me, ladies. Forgive my eavesdropping, but that’s a most intriguing topic. Dialectal shifts...absolutely vital for understanding population movement. I’m Professor Davies, from the History department. I spent a good portion of my career excavating deserted medieval villages in Shropshire. Amazing how much the land remembers, if you know how to listen. Professor Davies! It’s a pleasure. I've read some of your work on the Shropshire settlements. The pottery analysis, particularly impressive. It’s fascinating how everyday objects can tell such compelling stories. Absolutely! It's all intertwined, isn't it? Landscape, language, material culture… You know, it reminds me somewhat of my work on ancient Chinese. The sheer number of loan words coming into Classical Chinese from various nomadic groups… it’s a tangible record of trade and conflict, all embedded in the lexicon. Ah, Chinese! A monumental undertaking. I haven't touched it myself, but I’ve always had a keen admiration for the complexity. My sister, bless her heart, dedicated her life to Arab culture and language. She taught at the American University in Cairo for nearly thirty years. Learned fluent Arabic, of course, but she also became incredibly knowledgeable about the history and poetry. Said it was like uncovering a hidden world. That sounds incredible.

Right, so, another week done. Honestly, this dissertation is trying to actively give me grey hairs. I swear, Professor Davies is just… picking apart every sentence. Tell me about it. My boss at the bakery is being massively picky about the sourdough starter this week. Apparently, it's not “vibrant” enough. Vibrant bread! Who even says that? Sounds stressful, both of you. At least you have something tangible to show for your efforts. Running a café is just… constant firefighting. This morning, the espresso machine decided it wanted a vacation. Right in the middle of the breakfast rush. Classic. Machines hate you when you need them most. Though, you know, that's kind of a universal truth, isn’t it? Speaking of universal truths, have you guys seen that video of the squirrel waterskiing? It's gone properly viral. No, haven’t! Send it over. I need a serious dose of absurdity after deciphering the nuances of post-structuralist theory all day. Seriously, I’m starting to question if I even understand what I’m writing about. Sometimes I think dyslexia makes things ten times harder. I know I’ve always struggled with dense text. Yeah, having dyslexia definitely adds another layer of complexity. I remember in uni, I'd have to read passages three or four times just to grasp the main idea. It’s frustrating when people assume you’re just not trying hard enough. Absolutely. It’s not a lack of intelligence, it's a different way of processing. My little cousin, Liam, has it too. He’s brilliant at building things, absolutely spatial awareness, but reading is a real battle. He’s really into coding now, which is brilliant, it plays to his strengths. It’s amazing how education seems so fixated on a traditional, text-based model. Films, photography… visual storytelling is becoming more and more important. And it’s accessible to so many more people. You don’t need a degree to have a voice. Which is good, because the cost of education now… it’s ludicrous. Honestly, I feel guilty sometimes, having a decent degree and now doing alright as a producer. Were things always this hard for your parents, anyone? My mum did a degree in Classics, but she had to work part-time to fund it. She always says it nearly broke her, but she wouldn’t trade it for the world.

Honestly, David, this whole NHS thing is just… unbearable. I spent three hours on hold yesterday trying to get a referral for Mrs. Peterson. Three hours! And the woman's in genuine pain. I know, love. It's awful. Saw an article online this morning – waiting lists are extending again. Apparently, they're predicting a winter crisis even worse than last year. Typical, isn't it? Typical is an understatement. It’s actively distressing for the students, seeing their parents struggle to access even basic care. They’re stressed enough as it is with essays and exams, and now this adds another layer. I had a student in my office yesterday practically in tears because her mum's been waiting months for a scan. It's the same everywhere, isn’t it? Even with private insurance, you can feel the strain. My aunt’s been trying to get an appointment with a specialist for ages. Thankfully she can afford it, but it shouldn’t be like that. It shouldn't be a postcode lottery or dependent on your bank balance. Exactly! And the government... don't even get me started. Their rhetoric is all about 'strengthening the NHS' but it feels like they're actively dismantling it piece by piece. Did you see the latest figures on the funding cuts? Vaguely. I try to avoid the news these days, it’s just relentlessly grim. Easier on the blood pressure, you know? Although, avoiding it entirely isn't really an option when it impacts everything, is it? What about that article about the proposed changes to inheritance tax? Apparently, they’re thinking of lowering the threshold even further. Oh, brilliant. Just what we need. Another way for the wealthy to avoid paying their fair share. We’d need to restructure our finances again, wouldn't we? It wouldn't impact you and me drastically, thankfully, but it's the principle of the thing. It feels utterly unfair. It is. It’s just… infuriating. Honestly, I’m half tempted to move to somewhere with a slightly more sensible government. New Zealand, perhaps. Although, leaving Norwich… that’s a big ask. New Zealand, David? Don’t be daft. We’re not moving to New Zealand. Besides, who would teach Victorian literature to all those lovely Norfolk students? They adore you, you know. They do, don't they? Alright, alright, you’ve convinced me. Stay put it is.

Honestly, this quiche is absolutely lovely, ANON. You’ve really outdone yourself this time. Much better than that shop-bought one we had last month, remember? Dreadful it was. All soggy and…and lacking in flavour. It really is good, Gran. ANON’s been experimenting with different cheeses. This one’s got a lovely tang, don't you think? And the pastry’s perfect – not too thick, not too thin. Aye, it’s canny good, it is. Proper job. Reminds me of my mum’s, this does. She used to make a cracking quiche Lorraine. Never wrote down a recipe, mind. Just knew it by heart. Lost it all when she went. Shame that. Your mum was a marvel, Arthur. Such a reliable woman. Always a pot of soup on the stove, even in July. Do you remember that summer we all went to Cornwall? That picnic on Fistral Beach? Oh, I’ve seen the photos! You all look so tanned. And Dad's wearing that awful Hawaiian shirt. Seriously, Gran, where  did  you dig that out? It was a gift, darling. From Aunt Mildred, of all people. She had a penchant for tropical prints. Though, I must say, the beach was divine. Truly, a memory to cherish. Did you ever get around to finishing that documentary on the Hubble telescope, Arthur? Not yet, love. Got rather distracted by the football, didn’t I? Leicester did alright this week. Didn’t they? Proper shocker, that win against Man City. Never thought I’d see the day. Still, it’s a long season. Don’t want to get ahead of ourselves. It was incredible, Dad! I actually stayed up to watch it. All that data they're collecting… it's mind-blowing, really. I was reading about exoplanet atmospheres the other day. They’re starting to identify biomarkers, organic molecules that  could  indicate the presence of life. Good heavens, dear! Life on other planets? Do you truly think that’s possible? It’s quite astounding to consider. It reminds me of H.G. Wells, actually.  The War of the Worlds . Remember that? I used to read it to my students. Terrified them, I'm sure. H.G. Wells. Always a doom and gloom merchant, that one. Give me a good nature programme any day. David Attenborough. Now  that’s  a proper show. Saw a documentary about the puffins on the Isle of May last week.

Right then, so Finn, you were telling us about this…  Roblox  game? It sounded a bit mad, to be honest. Like, building your own worlds and fighting… what was it, zombies? It's not  just  zombies, Dad. It’s a survival game. Me and Liam were building this massive fortress, see? Like, three levels, with traps and everything. And then, this other player kept trying to raid it. It was intense! A fortress? Sounds complicated. Is it hard to learn? I've always been hopeless with those sorts of games. Remember trying to play  Sim City  once? Ended up with the entire population living in sewage. Nah, it’s not that hard. There are tutorials. And you can find loads of videos online showing you how to build stuff. Liam's really good at the engineering bits, like, making the walls super strong. I’m better at the defense, setting up the traps. Sounds like a good partnership. So, Liam… Is he a relation? Another friend? He’s from the holiday camp. He’s here for the week. He’s really good at building. Way better than me. Honestly, he's practically a Minecraft god. A Minecraft god, you say? Well, that’s a title. Little Ronan here, is he showing any interest in your digital kingdoms? "Dino! Roar!” Ah yes, the dinosaur. He’s much more interested in the tangible world at the moment, aren't you, lad? "Rawr! Dino eat zombies!” He’s got the priorities straight! At least he's playing with  something . I'm worried about him just staring at screens all day when he’s older. Maybe we should get him some more soft toys? We’ve got a pile already, but… I build some stuff in  Roblox  that looks like toys, actually. Like, a giant teddy bear you can climb on. It's a bit glitchy though. It keeps clipping through the floor. Clipping through the floor. Only in the digital world. So, Finn, what's the biggest challenge in this… fortress building, then? Beyond dodging zombie raids, of course. Resources! You need wood, stone, metal… everything. And it all takes time to gather. Someone keeps stealing our wood, too. It’s really annoying. We think it's that player who keeps trying to raid us. He must be lurking around, waiting for us to be low on supplies. A digital wood thief! Goodness, it sounds like a proper soap opera.

Cor, this is reet nice, innit? Proper cozy. Feels like Christmas already, even though it's only November. Though, November’s gettin' closer to Christmas every year, it feels like. It does, doesn't it, Arthur? ANON’s put up some lovely decorations. Much better than last year's wonky fairy lights. Remember those? Nearly gave me a fright. Wonky fairy lights are a hazard, definitely. Speaking of hazards, how’s the car, ANON? Ready for the journey up to Mum’s on Christmas Day? That A45 can be a beast in the snow. The car's fine, Dad. ANON got it serviced last week, remember? It's got new tyres too, so it should be okay. Although, I'm hoping we don't  have  snow. Please, no snow. I have this amazing outfit planned for Christmas dinner, and it's definitely  not  snow-appropriate. Orange is not a good snow colour. Orange? Never thought about it like that. Still, if it snows, it snows. Gives the countryside a proper bit of sparkle, it does. Used ta love buildin’ snowmen when I were a lad. Not got the knees for it now, mind you. You and your knees, Arthur. Always moaning about your knees! Speaking of Christmas dinner, are we having brussels sprouts again? I still have that dream about being chased by a giant one. Brussels sprouts are a necessity, Brenda! Though, perhaps we can offer a sprout-free option for the younger generation? Any preferences, girls? I’m okay with sprouts, actually. But can we have parsnips  and  carrots? Like last year? Yeah, parsnips are good. And a giant Yorkshire pudding. Like, a  really  giant one. Big enough to hide in. Hidin’ in a Yorkshire pudding! Now there's a thought. Reminds me of a joke I 'eard down the pub. What do you call a lazy kangaroo? Oh, here we go... Pouch potato! Classic, Arthur. Absolutely classic. You haven’t changed a bit. So, ANON, you were saying something about a boy friend for Amelia? Dad! It’s embarrassing. Let the girl breathe, Richard! It’s her life. Go on then, love, tell us about him. What’s he like? Well… his name is Liam. He’s in my art class. He’s really good at drawing horses. Like,  really  good. Better than me, even. Horses? Does he ride? He does! He has a stable down near his house.

Right, nearly ready. Smells lovely, doesn’t it? Bit of a comfort food kind of evening, I thought. After that shift I had... honestly, the things you see. Still, at least it's Friday. Comfort food is exactly what's needed. That funding meeting this afternoon was a right old slog. Mrs. Henderson went on and on about spreadsheets. Spreadsheets! Like we haven’t got enough to worry about. So, tell me about your shift, love? Anything exciting? Though knowing the NHS, exciting probably means someone nearly needing resuscitation. More like a lovely elderly gentleman deciding he wanted to re-enact his days as a merchant sailor, complete with sea shanties. Took a good half hour to convince him that calling me “matey” wasn't entirely appropriate. Though he did have a cracking story about a hurricane in ‘67. It was nice just listening, you know? Sometimes it’s more about the chats than sticking drips in. Smells amazing! What is it? And are you two gossiping already? Just recounting the usual tales of bureaucratic madness, darling. And your mum was telling me about a sea shanty-singing patient. You wouldn't believe it. A sea shanty patient? Seriously? Only you, Mum. What’s cooking? It’s a shepherd’s pie.
