Honestly, I’m not sure if it’s a bad thing. He's passionate about  something , at least. Passionate’s good! Better than moping around. He’s a good lad, Liam. Proper gentleman, when he wants to be. What about Emily? Is she still battling with quadratic equations? Don't even mention them! Emily's convinced she’s failing maths. I’ve been trying to help, but you know how it is – teenage logic, it's a different planet. She says Miss Davies hates her. I’m trying to find out if there’s actually something going on, but she clams up the moment I start asking questions. Teenagers, eh? Like herding cats. My Chloe's the same. Doesn’t want me poking my nose in anything. Though she’s been buzzing about going to see Maisie and her friends next weekend. You know, the ones they got on the bus with last month? Oh yes! I remember. I'm a little wary about that group to be honest. But it's good for her to socialize. I’ll have to check with Mark, see if he's free to drive them over. I've got that consultant appointment next Tuesday, remember? Aye, the scan. How are you feeling about that? No point pretending everything's dandy. Honestly? Terrified. Trying to stay positive, you know? Focusing on work, the kids, keeping busy. But the fear…it’s there. I keep thinking about what happens if… well, you know. I've been looking at some financial stuff, actually. Re-evaluating everything. Just in case.

Right, spill. You lookin' proper stressed, Liv. Another essay due? Worse, actually. I've got an interview next week. Proper terrifying. An interview? For what, then? Not another internship at that awful marketing firm, is it? They seemed to think "synergy" was a personality trait. No, thank goodness. It’s for a bar job. Down in Manchester city centre. It's a gastropub, apparently really trendy? Called "The Velvet Fox." The Velvet Fox? Blimey, that's a posh name. Sounds like a place that’ll want you to know the difference between a stout and a porter. You know your beers, don’t you? I try. I've learned a hell of a lot just listening to you at the pub back home. You’ve practically given me a degree in ale. But... gastropub is a different beast, isn't it? It's not just pouring pints for lads after a footie match. Aye, it's not. They'll want you to know about food pairings, be able to describe the notes in a whisky, maybe even make a decent cocktail or two. But you're bright, Liv. You'll be alright. What's got you so worried, then? Is it just the fanciness of it all? It’s partly that, yeah. I’m used to the busy, loud, sometimes chaotic atmosphere of a regular pub. This sounds… refined. And I’m terrible at small talk. The interview description explicitly said they’re looking for someone who can "engage with customers and build rapport." My brain just goes blank! Right, that’s a common problem. Honestly, most folk don’t want you to be a chatty Cathy, just… approachable. Ask them about their day, comment on their meal, say "lovely weather we’re havin'!" - simple stuff. I’ve been doin’ it for years. It's like… it’s just bein’ a friendly face, innit? Easy for you to say, you’re a natural! You could chat the bark off a tree. I’m more the type who hides behind a textbook. Honestly, it's a skill, like anything else. You practice. Tell me, what sort of questions do you reckon they’ll be askin’ you? The usual, I guess. "Why do you want the job?" "What are your strengths and weaknesses?" "Tell us about a time you dealt with a difficult customer." The last one genuinely terrifies me. I once dropped a pint down a bloke’s back

Right then, holiday planning officially underway, I reckon. Feel like I’ve been dodging questions about it for weeks. People just  assume  you’ve booked something. Tell me about it, Liam. I’ve had Mrs. Henderson practically interrogating me about my intentions for August. As if I’ve got a villa in the Bahamas just waiting for me! I'm thinking Blackpool, honestly. Simple, cheap, and the kids will be happy. Blackpool, you say? Och, bless your heart, Margaret. Blackpool’s grand if you like dodging seagulls and trying to find a lukewarm chip, but it's not exactly a tonic for the soul, is it? I'm off to County Clare again. The sea air always does a grand job for me. County Clare, Moira? Lovely choice. I envy you the peace and quiet. I’m battling with the family holiday situation at the moment. My daughter’s decided she  absolutely  needs to go glamping in Cornwall, and my son wants to spend two weeks playing video games in a cabin in the Lake District. A compromise is proving...challenging. Glamping? Is that still a thing? Seems like an unnecessarily expensive way to rough it. Honestly, give me a caravan and a flask of tea any day. My mum’s been trying to convince me to come with her to Skegness. "It's got everything, Liam!" she says. Everything except, well, charm, probably. Skegness! Oh dear. Margaret, that’s a bold move. Caravans are fine, though. At least you've got a kettle, right? My husband’s got his heart set on a cruise this year. A cruise! Can you imagine? Buffet dinners and shuffleboard. It's not exactly my idea of a relaxing getaway. He says it’s all about the ‘experience’. I say it’s about being trapped on a floating city with a thousand other people competing for the last bread roll. Cruises… Full of fancy folk and organised fun. No, give me a little cottage, a good book, and the sound of the waves. Last year, I saw a seal sunbathing on the rocks. Now  that ’s an experience. Better than any musical production on a cruise ship, I'll tell you that much! A seal! Now that's something. My daughter's already got a Pinterest board dedicated to ‘rustic woodland vibes’ for her glamping trip. Think fairy lights, log burners, and a miniature copper bathtub.

Honestly, Liam, how many times can they clear the ball without actually  doing  anything with it? It’s like watching paint dry, but with slightly more running. Patience, Maisie. Patience. It's early days yet. And look, they’ve shifted Wilson to the left wing. That might open up some space for Gallagher. Aye,  might . He’s been invisible for the last twenty minutes. Honestly, I’m starting to think I should have stayed in Sunderland tonight. At least there’s a good chippy there. A good chippy? You're willing to miss a Premier League match for a battered sausage and chips? That’s devotion to your local cuisine, I’ll give you that. Divotion? Nah, it's common sense! This is depressing. All this possession, zero goals. I’m proper peckish, too. I could murder a doner kebab right now. A doner kebab? You’re going from a chippy to a doner? That’s quite the culinary leap. And, ambitious considering it’s nearly ten o’clock. Well, a girl's gotta dream, doesn't she? Plus, I'm thinking Wembley next week – need to stock up on energy somehow. You wouldn’t deny someone vital pre-Wembley fuel, would you? Absolutely not. But maybe something a  little  less… intense than a doner? How about we order some pizza? I know that little Italian place down the road does a decent one. Pizza's always a winner. But it’s not quite the same, is it? There's something about that greasy, slightly questionable meat in a doner… it’s an experience. Like… a comforting betrayal. A comforting betrayal. You truly are one of a kind. Right, let's compromise. Pizza and then… we’ll see. Perhaps a sneaky packet of chips when the action picks up. Now you're talking! You're learning my ways. Though, chips are  essential , Liam. Not a "maybe." It’s a crucial supporting player in the overall late-night football-watching experience. It's practically a national requirement. You know, it’s funny. I spent years studying behavioural economics, trying to understand consumer decision-making, and you’ve managed to convince me that chips are an integral part of Premier League enjoyment. See? My North Eastern logic prevails. It's simple, really. Dizzy from lack of goals, need salty goodness. It’s science! Speaking of, do you reckon that tackle was a foul?

Right then, Grandma, this tea is lovely. Proper Yorkshire blend, isn't it? Mum, you've done well. Yorkshire? Nah, lad. It's Lancashire tea, honest. My Elsie, bless her, always got it from Ainsworth's down the road. Best cuppa in Withington, it were. Proper builder’s tea. Strong enough to stand a spoon in. Mum, don't start going on about Ainsworth's again. They closed down decades ago! And it definitely tastes like Yorkshire Tea to me. Honestly, you remember everything differently. Aye, well, memories play tricks, don’t they? Especially at my age. Still, Ainsworth's were good, I'll give you that. Remember their gingerbread? Lovely, lovely gingerbread. Speaking of lovely things, did you see that new film, 'Coronation Mayhem'? The one with Olivia Colman? Oh, yes! I went last week. Absolutely hilarious! I cried laughing in the cinema. Olivia Colman is brilliant, isn’t she? Such a natural. Films, eh? Back in my day, we'd go to the Astoria. Monopol cinema it were then. All those black and white pictures. You had to hold onto your hat when they showed the war films! Scared the living daylights out of us kids. Crikey, Grandma! I can’t imagine. I used to love going to the cinema. Remember that 4x4 I was looking at, Mum? The Land Rover Defender? You and your cars! Always thinking about your next car. It’s a bit much for a city, isn’t it? Where on earth would you park that thing in Manchester? But it's a proper vehicle! I could take it out to the Lake District, go off-roading… It’s an experience, you know? Plus, they're bringing back the old ones, restoring them. It’s a bit of a classic. Land Rovers? Always trouble, those. My Arthur had one once. Spent more time fixing it than driving it, he did. Always something breaking down. Honestly, a good bicycle’s best. Simple, reliable. You and your bikes, Grandma. You’re wishing you were thirty again! She did cycle everywhere when she was younger. Used to deliver telegrams all over Withington, she did. In all weathers! Aye, I did. Dressed in my best coat, too. Didn’t want to look scruffy delivering telegrams. Though some of them weren't very cheerful news, mind you. Weddings and funerals, mostly. Mum, how's that lemon drizzle cake coming along?

Honestly, this pancake chaos is exactly what I needed after that school assembly this morning. Little Leo was meant to be representing our class with his reading, and he just… froze. Wouldn't say a word. Just stared at the microphone. Poor love. Was he scared, Mummy? Did he drop his paper? Did he?! He  did  drop his paper, actually, Thomas. And well, yes, he was probably a bit scared. It’s a lot of pressure for a seven-year-old. It reminded me a bit of how I used to be, utterly terrified of public speaking. Remember Mrs. Higgins in Year Five making us recite poems? I practically fainted. I don’t like talking in front of people. It's alright, darling. You don't  have  to. Some people find it hard. But Leo just needed a bit of a pat on the back, you know? He’s a brilliant reader, really. Just had a moment. It’s made me think even more about how different kids’ experiences are though. Some of them haven’t even got a proper breakfast this morning, let alone practice reading in front of a crowd. It's heartbreaking. Why wasn't he hungry this morning? He said he didn't want pancakes! Sometimes people aren’t hungry, love. Maybe he wasn't feeling like pancakes, or maybe he was a bit worried about the assembly. It doesn’t matter. More for you two then. Are you both washing your hands before you have another one? Yes, Mummy. Nooo! I’m still building my tower! Thomas, towers need clean builders! And remember what Mr. Finch said in assembly? About germs. Seriously, before you cause a pancake-induced disaster, clean those hands. We’re going to the Science Museum on Saturday, remember? We need to avoid any extra bugs. I want to see the rockets! You absolutely will. And maybe we can catch a show about space. It's been ages since we've been somewhere exciting. We could even plan a trip to Paris one day! Imagine, croissants and the Eiffel Tower! Paris has snails. Ewwww! Some people like snails, Thomas! Different countries have different foods. Remember that story about Peter and Flora going to Green Knowe? They tried all sorts of unusual things. Did they try snails? I don’t think so, darling. But they were definitely brave about trying new things. Like brushing your teeth properly!

This sweet and sour chicken is… aggressively sweet. Honestly, I think they’ve added a whole extra cup of sugar. Nah, it’s good! You're just being dramatic, Elsie. Besides, we needed something cheerful after… well, everything. Ben's right. It  is  good. And yeah, the funeral was… heavy. Poor Aunt Carol. At least she had a good innings. Did you hear what Uncle Derek said about her knitting skills? Something about a wonky cardigan that resembled a sentient slug? I definitely heard it. He was trying, bless him. Trying to find a levity, I think. Though, honestly, his humour is… specific. Specific is putting it mildly. It’s like he actively  tries  to be awkward. Still, you're right, it was a lovely send-off. All those pastel colours… Mrs. Higgins went all out with the flower arrangements. Right? And the slideshow! So many photos of Carol dressed as a pirate at that village fete. Hilarious! Speaking of photos, did anyone manage to get a picture of Daniel trying to balance that massive plate of sandwiches? He looked like he was about to topple over. I did! I'll send it to you. He’s got that expression like he’s questioning all his life choices. Seriously, that boy needs to eat a proper meal instead of just cramming things in his mouth. He'll be alright. He's got that "glamourous starving artist" thing down. Anyway, did you guys see the news about that cricket match? England totally choked! Don't even  start  me on cricket. It's just… baffling. Why are they standing around for so long? It’s like a really slow, strangely dressed game of tag. Hey! Don’t knock it. It’s a classic. Though, I’ll admit, they didn’t play brilliantly. Still, at least it’s something to complain about besides Aunt Carol’s funeral. Speaking of complaining, how's the housemate situation going, Elsie? Still having issues with Liam leaving his socks everywhere? Don’t even. It’s reached a new level. This morning I found a pair nestled  inside  the toaster. The toaster! I’m starting to think he’s doing it on purpose. That's… concerning. Have you had a proper sit-down with him? Maybe explain how unhygienic it is? I’ve tried! He just shrugs and says, "They’re just socks, Elsie." Just socks! They're breeding in there, I swear!

Right then, who remembers old Mrs. Higgins next door in our old house? The one who kept pigeons? Honestly, the sheer number of them! They’d leave… well, let’s just say the garden required frequent attention. Higgins, you say? Ah, yes, Margaret Higgins. A good woman, actually. A bit eccentric, perhaps, with those pigeons. But she always had a kind word and a slice of Victoria sponge for the children. Wolverhampton didn’t have pigeon ladies, mind you. We had butchers and bakers, really. Proper tradesmen. Not like these… supermarkets. You’re right, Dad. Mrs. Higgins was a character. I remember once, I was about ten, and a pigeon flew into our kitchen window. It was flapping around frantically. She came rushing over, a net in her hand, looking utterly distraught. She rescued it, of course, babied it for a day, and released it back into the flock. She was utterly devoted. She really was. And you know, even though it was a nuisance at times, when we sold the house, I felt a bit sad seeing all those pigeons gone. It felt like a little piece of the neighbourhood’s character had flown away. It’s funny how you get attached to things, isn't it? Attached? I was attached to my accounts! Being an accountant, you know, everything had to be precise, balanced. Pensions, tax returns, you name it. This modern world, though…it's all just algorithms and things. Where's the skill? Where's the thought? All this ‘Scan As You Go’ in the supermarkets, that’s a prime example. It’s just asking for mistakes! Tell me about it. I tried it last week. Ended up paying for three boxes of rice krispies instead of one – apparently, I hadn’t scanned it properly. Took ages to sort out at the checkout. Honestly, I miss just handing your items over and having someone actually  look  at them. At least you knew they were counting correctly! Absolutely! And the queues at the checkout now are ridiculous. Everyone’s fumbling with their phones, trying to get the app to work… it’s chaos. Though, on the upside, at least we've got rice krispy cakes! I made a batch this morning. Rice krispy cakes, eh? Now you’re talking! Nothing like a bit of sugar to brighten the day. Reminds me of my wife, Millie. She made the best rice krispy cakes you ever tasted.

Right then, operation Chinese New Year feast is officially underway! Poppy, Leo, are you two behaving yourselves while Mummy tries to conjure up some deliciousness? Almost finished, Mummy! My dragon has extra sparkly scales. See? I used gold and silver! Mine’s got fire coming out of its nose!  Makes roaring noises  Brilliant, both of you! They’re looking very impressive. Poppy, yours looks like it could fly to the moon! Speaking of which, did you learn about the planets today at school? Yes! We learned about Jupiter. It's REALLY big! Bigger than Earth! And it has a big red spot. Miss Davies said it’s a massive storm. I like Saturn! It has rings! You two are little scientists! It’s wonderful. Alright, little astronauts, could you scoot away from the table for a moment? I need space to chop these spring onions. Oh, and Leo, please stop breathing fire at Poppy! Sorry, Mummy! My dragon needs a princess! Can I draw a princess for it, Mummy? Absolutely! Draw away. This reminds me, we watched  Barbie and the Great Adventure  last weekend, didn’t we? You both loved it. Such a lovely film. Do you remember how Barbie travelled through the portal? Yeah! She went through a sparkly thing! And she had to save that king! It was exciting! It was! Right, noodles are nearly ready. Poppy, what's happening with your piano lessons this week? Are you working on that tricky bit of ‘Für Elise’ still? Almost! It’s hard. Mr. Henderson says I need to really put my shoulders into it. But it sounds pretty when I get it right! Leo is doing really well with his drums, though! Bang! Bang! BOOM! I’m learning a song about dinosaurs!  Starts tapping a rhythm on the tabletop  That’s fantastic! You’re a little rockstar! And you're both so excited about your activities. Sometimes I just can’t believe how quickly you’re growing up. Now, is anyone else feeling a bit peckish? I've got some prawn crackers. While I'm getting those, Leo, please don't climb on the chairs. But I want to see the noodles! In a minute, darling. Safety first. Poppy, are you still drawing your princess? What’s she wearing? A sparkly dress, like Barbie! And she’s got a crown! And she’s riding my dragon! Sounds like a fantastic story!

Blimey, this is lovely, innit? Proper sunshine. Thought Rome’d be all drizzle and grey from the pictures. I know, right? It's so much nicer than the photos implied. And the Aperol Spritz is absolutely essential. First thing I did when we landed, needed one. That AirBnB was a bit of a trek from the station though, wasn’t it? A trek is putting it mildly, Poppy! It was like a scavenger hunt, wasn’t it? Three flights of stairs, a wonky lift, and a concierge who spoke entirely in gestures. Honestly, I thought I was going to collapse. At least the view is decent once you're up there. Tell me about it! I had to lug my espresso machine up four floors in Florence last year. Nearly threw my back out. This place… … this is a welcome change. Quiet too. You can actually hear yourselves think. Yeah, it’s a lot less manic than the tourist traps we walked past earlier. So, Poppy, how’s your Italian coming along? You were saying you wanted to brush up a bit. It’s... patchy, to be honest. I can order a coffee and ask for directions, barely. My Duolingo streak is currently defunct. I feel like I should’ve put in more effort. My mum will be mortified. Don't worry about it! Half the people here don't actually speak properly either. It’s all about pointing and hoping for the best, isn't it? I managed to order a panino earlier by just miming eating a sandwich. Brilliant. That's fair enough. I’m Australian, so my language skills are mostly limited to shouting “G’day!” and asking for a flat white. Which, by the way, they don’t seem to  get  here. They look at me like I've got two heads. A flat white? Seriously? That’s just a latte with no foam. Don’t be ridiculous, mate. She's trying to disrupt the Italian coffee scene, you know. Shut up, Liam! I like a decent coffee! Anyway, so, dinner tonight. What's the plan? I'm starving. I was thinking somewhere near the Pantheon? Pantheon sounds good. I saw a place earlier with amazing reviews for their pasta cacio e pepe. It’s just around the corner, actually. Should I book something? Book it! I’m in. I’m craving carbs. This heat just drains you. Are there any decent veggie options there?

Right, okay, so I’ve been looking at venues for the hen do. It's proving…challenging. Honestly, I’m starting to think a weekend in Brighton is the only sane option. Everywhere else feels either ridiculously expensive or… well, a bit naff. Brighton’s a good shout! Loads to do. But naff? What have you been looking at? Don’t tell me you’re considering that "Medieval Mayhem" weekend again? Remember how Sarah cried because they made her wear a plastic crown? Oh god, Medieval Mayhem! That was a disaster. I'm still finding bits of felt in my hair from the crafting session. No, definitely steer clear of anything involving pointy hats and bad historical reenactments. Brighton is solid. Easy to get to, good nightlife, and decent cafes. I second Brighton! Plus, we could do a vintage shopping trip! There’s that amazing little shop on the North Laine, “Re-Loved Treasures,” remember? We could all get matching…something. Like, slightly ridiculous hats! Matching ridiculous hats… I’m loving it. Okay, Brighton it is. Now, about activities. I was thinking maybe a cocktail making class? Or a spa day? Obviously, we need something crafty, too, because, well, you two and I are practically professional crafters at this point. Cocktail making sounds fun, but a spa day feels a bit…sedate, doesn't it? For Chloe? She'd last five minutes before starting a water fight. I’m leaning towards something a bit more lively. Maybe axe throwing? I know, slightly terrifying, but it would be a story! Axe throwing?! Absolutely not! I’d spend the entire time convinced I was going to accidentally chop off a finger. Let’s stick to something slightly less lethal. How about a pottery painting class? We could all paint mugs with ridiculous faces on them. Chloe would adore that. Pottery painting is brilliant! And we could get personalised aprons to wear… with Chloe’s face on them! That’s guaranteed hilarity. Speaking of personalised things, I’ve been trying to perfect my sugar cookies. I finally got the royal icing consistency right! I was thinking, for the hen do, I could make a batch with little Chloe-themed decorations. Oh my god, that’s amazing! Chloe would be obsessed. You truly are a baking goddess, Ali. Seriously, you should be selling these things. I’m rubbish at royal icing, it always ends up looking like… something a toddler did.

Right, so, I’m thinking this chilli needs a bit more…oomph. What d’you reckon, Liam? More paprika? Or maybe some chilli flakes? I’m feeling a bit peaky, to be honest. This cold is proper lingering. Paprika, definitely. Chilli flakes are a bit much when you’re already feeling rough. You sound worse than yesterday. Are you taking anything for it? You know Mum'll have a right go if she finds you haven't. Yeah, yeah, I've got some paracetamol. Doesn't seem to be doing much though. I just feel…fuzzy. Makes concentrating on, like, a decent colour palette for this agency job a proper nightmare. Anyway, did you sort the hotel for that conference in Manchester next week? Almost. I was looking at a few. There's that Premier Inn, pretty standard, you know? Reliable, clean-ish. Or there's this boutique thing, ‘The Silk House’, a bit pricier, but supposedly really nice. Got good reviews. Thought we could treat ourselves, seeing as we're both working. The Silk House? Sounds a bit fancy for us, doesn't it? I mean, I’m used to a Travelodge, innit? Though, hand on heart, that Premier Inn last year in Milton Keynes  was  pretty decent. Remember that dodgy stain on the carpet though? Gave me the heebie-jeebies all night. Okay, fair point about the MK carpet. But this place is different. Apparently, they have a really good restaurant and proper comfy beds. And it’s right in the city centre. Saves on taxis, saves on hassle. Think of the early mornings for the conference – you'll need a good kip. True, true. The early mornings are brutal. Alright, send me the link. Let me have a gander. What are we eating with this chilli anyway? Rice? We’re proper short on rice, aren’t we? I think I used the last of it last night with that dodgy microwave meal. I picked some up from the shops earlier. Basmati. Fancy, I know. Wanted to elevate the chilli experience slightly, you know? It's not just a load of beans in a pot. You practically inhaled the last microwave meal, by the way. Definitely not helping your recovery. Don't start, Liam! I was hungry! And feeling awful. Speaking of which, you’re really not helping my immune system with all that food-shaming. I need fuel, not lectures.

Right then, Marjorie, let’s get this shopping list sorted. We need to be organised, don’t we? That calendar fob order needs to go in soon. I saw some lovely ones online – little felt animals, you know. Would you like a fox? Or perhaps a badger? A badger! Oh, you are a card, Penelope. A fox would be smarter, wouldn’t it? More cunning. And yes, please, let’s get the list done. My memory's not what it used to be. Are we still needing that vanilla extract? For the shortbread? Absolutely. And a new sponge. The last one was a frightful disaster. Remember when we tried to bake that Victoria sponge for Mother's birthday? It collapsed like a souffle! Dreadful. Speaking of birthdays… did you ever sort out those birthday cards? I need to put the ages on. It’s getting trickier every year, isn’t it? Looking at the numbers… Yes, isn't it? I got started, but then I got distracted remembering those awful birthday cards Mrs. Hawthorne used to make us in primary school. All glitter and scratchy felt. Honestly, she thought she was crafting a masterpiece. Remember the art and craft afternoons? We usually ended up melting the glue guns and making a right mess. Oh, goodness, yes! The glue guns! And remember having to rush out to the field for hockey? Those dreadful old hockey boots! They always pinched horribly. I never could master the game, even though the PE teacher, Mr. Davies, tried his best. He was a good man, though. Always encouraging. He was. And do you remember Miss Perkins, our teacher in Year Three? She was fascinated by local history. We'd do projects on the old Margate seafront. I was always convinced that understanding history was the key to understanding everything. That’s probably why I ended up teaching it, I suppose. What about you, Penelope? What did you fancy doing when you were little? I was obsessed with sound, actually. Recording everything. I used to spend hours with my dad’s old tape recorder, capturing bird song in the garden or the sound of the waves crashing on the beach. I even tried to record a proper interview with Mrs. Higgins next door about her prize-winning roses! It was awful, naturally. But the idea… fascinated me. I did briefly consider sound recording at university, you know.

Right then. This is lovely, really lovely. Much more… settled than that flat you had in London, eh? Feels like a proper home already. Though, Holsworthy... bit of a change from Southend, wouldn't you say? It is, Dad. But a good change, I think. And it’s gorgeous here, isn't it? The countryside is stunning. The neighbours seem really friendly too. Mrs. Treweek, next door, popped over with a Victoria sponge yesterday. You can’t complain about that! Oh, Mrs. Treweek! She's a treasure, that one. Makes the best scones I’ve ever tasted, honestly. And she’s got a prize-winning rose garden. You’ll be getting gardening tips off her in no time, Anon. Gardening, you say? I've got a bit of an idea about that, actually. Used to have a small allotment back in the day. Tomatoes, mostly. Always fancied a marrow though. Never quite managed one big enough to win a prize. Well, there's plenty of room for a marrow in the garden now, Dad. Anon’s already planning on building a little shed. It's quite ambitious, though. A shed? Sounds like a bit of DIY, doesn't it? Hope you’re not planning on doing it all yourself, Anon. Don't want to see you fall off a ladder! He’s got it covered, Dad. He's found a local handyman, apparently. Seems reliable, from what Anon’s told me. And he’s also signed up for a woodworking course at the community centre. Oh, brilliant! That's a lovely idea. They have some really good courses there. Remember when I took the pottery one? Made a rather wonky vase that looked like a collapsed soufflé. I remember! You tried to pass it off as ‘modern art’. Well, it  was  modern! It was expressing… the fragility of the human condition. You always were a fibber, Margaret. Still, good on you for trying something new. This new job of yours, Anon – what’s it actually like? You’ve been so vague about it. Something to do with data analysis, wasn’t it? It is, Dad. It’s with a company that tracks consumer behaviour for local businesses. It’s surprisingly interesting, actually. Lots of spreadsheets, but it's helping small businesses understand their customers better. They’re really keen for me to come in and do the Christmas planning, which is a bit daunting.

Aye, it’s mental, isn't it? How many new trainers they’re bringin' out every week. Just looked at Foot Locker, and they’ve got three new colourways of the Air Max 95s. Three! And they’re all sellin' out within minutes. Seriously? You’re still on that? You were moaning yesterday about being skint. Don’t go tempting yourself, Liam. Focus on the job search. I  am  focussin'! It's research, right? Gotta know what's hot. Gotta stay on the pulse of the trends. If I get a job in retail, I need to know what people are wantin’. Strategic market analysis, basically. Right. Strategic market analysis. Sounds fancy for lookin' at trainers online. Mum's got an interview tomorrow, you know. At that care home in Cleator Moor. She does? That’s brilliant, lass! Proper brilliant. Fingers crossed for her then. She deserves a bit o' luck, poor lass. She’s been hustlin' for ages. Better than I have, anyway. Don’t be like that. You’ve applied for loads of things. It’s just… nobody’s got back to you. But this one feels better. She actually had a proper chat with them yesterday. Aye, but they all feel "better" until you get that rejection email, don't they? It's always the same. "Thank you for your interest… unfortunately…" Proper kick in the teeth it is. I was lookin’ at some online courses, mind, to boost my CV a bit. Digital marketing, they were callin’ it. Digital marketing? That sounds...useful. But is it free? Because we need to be sensible. Remember what happened last time you signed up for something "free" and they started takin' money out of Mum and Dad's account. Don’t remind me about that dodgy online guitar lesson course. I’ll never live that down. This one’s different, I swear. It’s through the Citizen’s Advice. Government-backed, apparently. Right. Well, check it out then. Anything’s gotta be better than endlessly refreshin’ Foot Locker. Have you seen that new show on Netflix, 'The Fall'? 'The Fall'? Nah, haven't watched it. Is it any good? I’ve been stickin' to 'Taskmaster' mostly. Alex Horne is a genius. The way he phrases things... It’s just… comedy gold. It's brilliant! It's a proper thriller, set in Northern Ireland. Gillian Anderson’s in it, you know.

Right then. This place is… well, it’s certainly got character, hasn't it? A lot more character than that soulless flat in Southend. Though, I do miss the sea sometimes. Still, Holsworthy's not bad. Quiet. Peaceful. Just what I need after… everything. It  is  lovely, Dad. Much more space. And the light’s brilliant here, especially in the afternoons. You’ll love the coastal path, honestly. I’m so glad you moved down. Are you feeling alright about it all? Settling in? Settling in fine, love. Bit of a culture shock, I suppose. Used to the grey skies of Essex, isn't he? No colourful Cornish flowers for him! But he’s got a good view now, plenty of fresh air, and company. Eat your sandwiches, girls. These are proper Devon ham, not that processed stuff you get up north. Thank you, Margaret. These are lovely. And you’re right, the light  is  fantastic. Reminds me a little of holidays we used to take in Greece, you know. All that sun reflecting off the white houses. Though, Greece doesn't have quite the same dampness, does it? No, Dad, I doubt it. So, about this walk tomorrow… I was thinking we could do the stretch from Clovelly to Bucks Mills. It’s not too strenuous, the views are incredible, and there's a rather delightful little pub in Bucks Mills for lunch. Bucks Mills pub is fine, Sarah. A bit touristy now, mind you. Used to be a proper smugglers' haunt. Still, the fish and chips are decent. We’ll need to check the tide times, though. Wouldn’t want to be wading through ankle-deep water. Smugglers, eh? Goodness. Always thought Devon was all rolling hills and cream teas. Never figured it for a smuggling hotspot. This house, too – you wouldn’t believe the things I found crammed in the attic when I was clearing out. Old maps, a dusty telescope… Oh, do tell! Did you find a pirate’s treasure? Not quite. Mostly old gardening tools and a rather alarming collection of porcelain dolls. Gave me quite a fright, they did. They were staring at me! Men! Always exaggerating. Probably just a few chipped teacups and some moth-eaten blankets. Now, about the furniture… you said you wanted to go to that showroom in Bude? Yes, that's the one. Saw their catalogue online. They've got a lovely oak dresser I've had my eye on.

Right, that was glorious. Proper Sunday roast. Mum would be proud. It was lovely, wasn't it? Honestly, sometimes I feel like I live on coffee and supermarket sandwiches during the week. This was a treat. You barely touched the Yorkshire puddings, though. You’re supposed to  love  Yorkshire puddings! I did! Just… feeling a bit blah after that grant proposal. It’s been hanging over me all day. Didn’t really want to push myself to enjoy a mountain of carbs. Oh, that’s the one for the wellbeing project in the NHS, isn't it? The one you’ve been working on for months? What’s the news? Don't tell me they rejected it. Not rejected, not yet. But the feedback... it's a bit lukewarm, you know? They're saying it’s good, solid research, but lacks… 'impact'. Apparently, just demonstrating a correlation between social isolation and mental health isn't groundbreaking enough. Impact? Seriously? So, what, they want you to single-handedly solve loneliness in the elderly? That's a bit much to ask of a postdoc, isn’t it? I’ve had days where I feel like just proving a kid can read the clock is groundbreaking. Exactly! I argued that demonstrating a strong link  is  impactful. It justifies further resource allocation, pilot programs...but they wanted something more… tangible. One reviewer suggested a randomized controlled trial showing a direct causal link between a specific intervention and a measurable improvement in mental health outcomes. A full-blown RCT? That’s... significant. And expensive. Funding for those is like hen's teeth. Tell me about it. It would basically mean rewriting the entire proposal, finding new collaborators, securing a huge amount of funding… and then waiting two years for results. Which is fine, theoretically. Except… I'm up for tenure review next year. This proposal was supposed to strengthen my case. Oh, darling. That’s awful timing. Look, it’s just one panel of reviewers, isn't it? Plenty of others will see the value in your work. Have you spoken to Professor Davies about it? She's always been a champion of your research. I have. She suggested pivoting. Focusing on a smaller, more specific cohort – perhaps focusing on carers, who are notoriously vulnerable to burnout and isolation. A targeted intervention, more easily quantifiable results. That sounds sensible. Narrowing the scope might make the impact easier to demonstrate.

Right, this stew's nearly ready. Bit of rosemary in it, just like Mum used to make. Smells lovely, doesn't it? Though I still think it needs a bit more Worcestershire sauce. Smells alright, love. Though, you know, your Mum always added a spoonful of Marmite too. That’s what gave it that…  something . Marmite? In stew? Seriously? That sounds absolutely horrific, Uncle David. Don't knock it 'til you've tried it, love. Back in the day, everyone put Marmite in everything! My Nan swore by it. Said cleared up a cold faster than anything. Though, fair to say, she also swore a lot in general. Your Nan was a character, Gary. I remember her telling me a story about trying to train a parrot to say "Good morning, sunshine." Ended up teaching it to yell "Bloody awful weather!" instead. Oh, I remember that! She tried for weeks, didn’t she? All that gentle encouragement. Then that parrot just let rip. Typical. Speaking of animals, has anyone heard from Chloe about the kitten? She said she was looking at shelters. Not yet, Auntie Sarah. I messaged her earlier, she said she's still browsing. Apparently, they've got a tiny little tortoiseshell that's won her over. She sent me a picture; it’s adorable! All fluffy and ringed tail. Tortoiseshell, eh? Always lucky. My Grandad used to say they brought rain if you kept one in the house. Ridiculous, of course. Still, never hurt to have a bit of luck, I suppose. Speaking of luck, I had a right old blinder yesterday. Took on a job in Chelsea – decorating a whole flat. Proper posh place, all parquet flooring and Italian tiles. Made a decent bit, I did. Though the client was… particular. Wanted the skirting boards painted exactly three shades lighter than the walls. Three shades! Who even notices that? Some people, eh? It’s good you earned some, Gary. Things have been a bit tight lately, haven’t they, Sarah? A bit. The extra shifts at the hospital haven't been helping. Trying to save up for Maisie's university fees. It’s frightening, the cost of everything these days. You’ll manage, Auntie Sarah. Maisie’s brilliant; she’ll get some sort of scholarship, I reckon. She's such a hard worker. Are you still teaching her sign language? Trying to! It's slow going. She's a right handful, that one.

Right then, Grandad, you were tellin' us about that trip to Italy, weren’t ya? I was just dyin’ to hear more. It sounds a world away from a damp Tuesday in Horsington, that's for sure. Italy, aye. Lovely country. Lovely. Wasn't quite the same as it is now, mind you. 1968, it were. Fresh off the boat, me and Margaret. Can’t imagine you young folks would recognize it. No mobile phones, no fancy tourist traps… just proper Italian life. 1968? Wow. That's... a significant chunk of history. What was Italy like then? Culturally, I mean. Were the cities very different? Different? Stone's throw different, lad. Rome was still recovering from the war, you know. There were piles of rubble in places, not just grand ruins. And the Vespas! Everywhere you looked, a swarm of Vespas. The noise alone was something else. Margaret loved 'em, wanted one desperately. Never got one, though. Too practical, she were. Aye, sounds like Gran. Always practical. Did you eat well? That's what I really want to know. Italian food's the best, innit? I had a proper carbonara last week, nearly cried it were that good. Eat well? Lass, we ate like kings! Fresh pasta every day, of course. Tomatoes you could taste the sun in. And the wine… goodness, the wine! It wasn't like these bottled things you get nowadays. It was served in simple pitchers, often straight from the vineyard. One little trattoria in Florence… I can still taste their bistecca alla fiorentina. Absolutely divine. Fiorentina? That sounds incredible. I’ve read a bit about Tuscan cuisine, all about simple ingredients and letting the quality shine through. Do you think restaurants today overcomplicate things? Overcomplicate? Absolutely! All these foams and drizzles and reductions... it's all a bit much, isn't it? Back then, it was about the produce. Good olive oil, good tomatoes, good meat. And a chef who knew how to cook it simply. Less is more, I’ve always said. So, what was your favourite part, Grandad? Besides the bistecca, that is! Did you do any sightseeing? See the Colosseum or anything like that? Of course, we saw the Colosseum. Magnificent thing, even back then. But my favourite part… wasn’t the sights. It was the people. The Italians. They were so warm, so welcoming. We didn’t speak much Italian, just enough to get by, but they were always happy to help.

Right, so, the feedback on Module 3 was... robust, wasn’t it? A lot of students struggling with the post-structuralist interpretations of Woolf. Honestly, I suspected as much. They seem to be equating it with just…general negativity. Robust is one word for it. I'd say ‘confused’ is more accurate. They’re latching onto the critique without grappling with the build-up. Did anyone actually  get  the connection between the Bloomsbury group’s social experiments and her stylistic choices? A handful, bless them. Mostly the ones who’ve obviously done the pre-reading. But the majority… it’s just a wall. And the essays are full of phrases like "Woolf seems to just be saying nothing is good.” Ugh. Right. Typical. We need to rethink our approach. I was thinking, perhaps a more concrete example? Something less overtly theoretical to start with. What about dissecting ‘Mrs. Dalloway’ a little more closely, focusing on the stream of consciousness technique? Start with the  how  before the  why  of the critique. That’s… brilliant, actually. A ground-up approach. I was going to suggest dividing them into smaller groups for discussion, but you're right. The theory feels very abstract to them currently. It needs a solid foundation. Do you think we should scrap the entire introductory lecture on post-structuralism and revisit it after a deeper dive into the text? I think so. We can frame it as a skill-building exercise, showing them  how  to analyse rather than overwhelming them with concepts they can't apply. Maybe some exercises where they identify the techniques and then we move onto analysis? What do you think about using that short clip from the BBC adaptation of 'Orlando'? It visually demonstrates the fluidity of identity she was exploring. Excellent. That’s a fantastic idea. I’ll pull that up. And we could couple it with a short writing exercise – just one paragraph, describing a single moment in the scene focusing on Woolf’s techniques. Low-stakes, gets them thinking. By the way, have you started planning the assessment for Module 4 yet? I’m completely stuck on how to make it engaging. Nearly. I was thinking a creative response, tying into the theme of memory. Something like, “Imagine you are a character in one of Woolf's novels writing a journal entry.” That encourages them to inhabit the world and perspectives, doesn’t it?

Honestly, this thing is a menace. It promised to make a decent cappuccino, and all it delivers is lukewarm, milky water with a pathetic dusting of foam. I miss my old percolator. Simpler times. Simpler machines. It’s a bit fussy, I’ll grant you that. You just need to fiddle with the settings, Mum. It does make a good flat white, actually. And we couldn't exactly lug your percolator up here to Hunsonby, could we? It's practically an antique! Flat white, eh? Sounds fancy. Not like a proper cuppa. Anyway, speaking of lugging things, have you had a chance to look into those removal and storage quotes yet, love? These boxes are starting to take over the whole house. I can barely get to the telly without tripping. I have, Michael. And they’re extortionate! Absolutely extortionate! One company wanted nearly £800 just to  store  the furniture for six months. Six months! It’s daylight robbery. Removals on top of that? Forget about it. I’m starting to think we should just sell everything. Mum, don't be dramatic. £800 is steep, yes, but it's not the end of the world. I’ll keep calling around. I found one yesterday that was slightly more reasonable, around £550, but they had a waiting list. I'm on it. We need somewhere safe to keep everything until we decide what to do with it. You know, with… everything. Everything being politics, I presume? Can’t escape it, can you? Even up here in the Lake District. Saw something on the news this morning - more chaos with the Tories. Absolutely shambolic. Shambolic is putting it mildly, Michael. It’s an utter disgrace. It makes you long for a bit of… decency, doesn’t it? Someone with integrity. Someone with a plan. Well, the Labour leadership race is heating up. It’s a bit of a mixed bag, to be honest. Rebecca Long-Bailey’s got some good ideas on housing, but I worry about her association with Corbyn. And Wes Streeting seems a bit... aggressive. Corbyn! Honestly, Sarah, don’t even mention him. He did more damage than good, I think. Though, there was something admirable about his… idealism. Even if it was utterly unrealistic. Idealism’s a dangerous thing, Mary. Always has been. Gets you trampled on. I used to be a bit of an idealist myself, you know.

Right, so we’re committed then? “Barnaby Butterfield” for me? Sounds like a posh bloke who owns a lot of tweed. It’s brilliant, Liam! Honestly, the best pseudonym so far. I'm sticking with "Rosalie Rivers," though. It just  feels  right. I've always been fascinated by rivers, massively. My dad used to drag me canal boating in the Midlands when I was a kid. Not exactly glamorous, but… peaceful. I like yours, Rosie. Mine's a bit… predictable, I suppose. "Penelope Pike." At least it rhymes! Honestly though, I'm more bothered about this lunch. It's practically deserted in here! Picked a dodgy spot, didn’t we? Nah, it's alright, Penelope. Gives us space. Much better than cramped in, eh? So, "Penelope Pike," that’s good. Got a ring to it. I'm going with "Jasper Jett." Simple, yeah? Like a quick getaway. Jasper Jett! Loving it. Right, food. This menu is promising. Loads of pasta, obviously. Should we get a load of different things and share? Italian always tastes better when you're sharing. Definitely! I'm thinking the linguine with clams. And maybe something with a really good ragu. I’m proper hungry. Though, I did have to sneak a few croissants from the bakery this morning… a baker's prerogative, innit? Always! I'm going for the carbonara. Though I’m trying to avoid too many creamy sauces, you know? My cafe has been doing a breakthrough with lighter, fresher Italian, inspired by all those Aussie salads you’ve been raving about, Aussie. Yeah, man! Gotta keep it fresh. Australian cuisine is all about that. Although, a proper creamy carbonara is hard to beat… What about drinks? They got Aperol spritzes? Those are top. Aperol spritzes are essential. Although… I wonder if they have any decent hot sauces. I’m obsessed. Last time I was in Rome, I practically lived on chili oil and balsamic vinegar. It's the perfect combo. Balsamic vinegar and chili oil? Liam, you’re a madman. I think I’ll stick to lemon and olive oil, thanks. Honestly, you’d think you were trying to flout kosher law or something! You need a bit of restraint. Rosie's got a point, Liam. Do you even  like  kosher food? It just feels very… specific. My auntie Sheila keeps trying to get me to go with her, but it’s just not for me.

Right then, listen to this. Absolute state of Liam. He messaged me on Tinder, said he was a ‘massive foodie’. Foodie! Turns out, his idea of fancy dining is chips and gravy. Chips and gravy, honestly! Oh, you're having a laugh! That's classic, though. You can't trust Tinder bios, love. They’re mostly lies. Did he at least  offer  to buy you chips and gravy? That’s a decent gesture, innit? Honestly, the guys on Tinder are something else. I had one who said he was a ‘world traveler’ who'd been to Skegness. Skegness! That’s hardly the Amazon, is it? Skegness! My grandad went to Skegness once and said it was the most disappointing thing that’d ever happened to him. He was a miner, mind, so he'd seen a few things. Still, you'd think they’d put some effort into their profile. Seriously! It's like they don’t even  try . Speaking of trying, did you see Chloe tried to cook lasagne last night? The kitchen still smells like burnt cheese and despair. Oh, Chloe, bless her. I offered to order a pizza, but she was having a ‘culinary moment’. Ended up microwaving a bean and cheese burrito. Felt bad for the poor burrito. Chloe's attempts at cooking are legendary. Remember that Yorkshire pudding incident? The one that practically glued the ceiling to the extractor fan? Oh, God, yes! It was like a giant, misshapen, eggy cloud. Took us three hours to scrape it off! We should’ve just let her stick to making tea. You lot are ruthless. But, speaking of housemates, I’m having a right nightmare with Sarah. She leaves her dirty dishes piled up in the sink for  days . It's breeding a whole ecosystem in there. Tell me about it! I had a flatmate who used to leave coffee cups with crusty grounds in them for weeks. They’d practically fossilise. You have to have a flatmate intervention, don't you? Definitely. A passive-aggressive Post-it note campaign only gets you so far. You need to sit her down and have a proper chat. Maybe a chart. A cleaning schedule. With colour-coded boxes. A chart! That’s brilliant, 5! She'll think you’re bonkers, but at least she’ll know you’re serious. I once made a shared Spotify playlist titled "Dishes Done" and added pop songs every time someone cleaned.

Honestly, Maureen, this lot in Parliament… It's just a shambles, innit? Another day, another crisis. They're fiddling while the country burns, I tell you. Don't start moaning again, Arthur. You say that every morning. It’s become your breakfast routine. And what's the crisis  now ? Did they run out of biscuits in the House of Commons? No, no, serious this time. This business with the Universal Credit payments… Apparently, a lot of folk are going without. Folk who  need  it. You know, people like us. Universal Credit, eh? Always a mess, that. Never worked right since they brought it in. Remember when we had the old system? At least it was predictable. Exactly, Bernard! Predictable! This swings around like a weathervane. One minute you’re alright, the next you’re facing eviction. And they talk about helping working families… Where's the help for those of us who haven't worked in a while? Alright now, both of you. Don't get yourselves in a state. They’ll sort  something  out. Eventually. Sometimes it just takes a bit… oh, a lot, really… of pushing. And complaining. Like you are, Arthur. It's not just complaining, Maureen! It’s about fairness. It's about the country looking after its own. I spent thirty years building bridges, for goodness sake! Bridges that are still standing. And now… Speaking of bridges, did you see that documentary on BBC Four last night? About the Roman aqueducts? Brilliant engineering, that. Still standing after two thousand years! Shows you what they knew, doesn’t it? Far superior to some of these modern monstrosities. Roman aqueducts, eh? Well, yes, impressive stuff. But it doesn't change the fact that this government… Bernard, stop trying to steer the conversation away from politics. It'll give you a headache. Have a biscuit. Thank you. Though I can’t quite get my head around how they built those things without JCBs and concrete mixers. Amazing, really. Actually, reminds me of that old 'Dad's Army' episode with the German prisoner... Here we go again. Dad's Army. Always Dad's Army with you, Bernard. Can't we talk about something serious for once? Arthur, dear, it  is  serious. People are worried. Bernard is just trying to lighten the mood. It’s a coping mechanism. And honestly, 'Dad’s Army' is a classic. Some things never get old.

This is lovely, love. Really lovely. You’ve outdone yourself. Though, honestly, I’m still stuffed from that afternoon tea with Penelope. Penelope and her scones. Always a dangerous game engaging with Penelope's afternoon teas, isn't it? You knew you’d be struggling to eat this, didn't you? Well, I didn’t want to be rude. And she’d been so excited about the new floral china. It  was  rather pretty, I’ll grant her that. But four scones? Four! And clotted cream piled like little snowdrifts… She does like to impress. How was the charity meeting after that? Did you manage to escape without offering to bake for a jumble sale? Just barely. Apparently, they’re short on volunteers for the craft fair. I managed to steer the conversation towards you. Told them you were a whiz at face painting. Face painting? You know my artistic abilities extend to drawing a passable stick figure, at best. They’ll be running for the hills! They don’t know that. It’s all about encouraging participation, isn’t it? They seemed quite keen. Said it would attract families. I think Mrs. Higgins, the chairwoman, has a rather over-optimistic view of your hidden talents. Right. So, I’m facing a weekend of tiny children covered in blue glitter and weeping because I’ve painted their noses green. Wonderful. Did you mention my considerable fundraising experience? Because that’s  slightly  more useful than a patchy clown. Of course I did! But she kept going on about how vibrant and fun you are. Apparently, you used to be quite the dancer in your youth. That was one drunken wedding, Sarah. One drunken wedding and a couple of questionable attempts at the Macarena. Let's not exaggerate. How was work today, then? Anything exciting happening at the library? Slow. Very slow. We had a major influx of people wanting to return books on time because of the storm warnings. Feels like everyone's trying to get their affairs in order. A bit morbid if you ask me. I did have a lovely chat with old Mr. Henderson about his rose bushes, though. He’s having terrible trouble with aphids. Aphids, eh? Right. I’ll have a look on the internet tomorrow. There’s that organic spray thing you can get… less harmful to the bees. Do you think Leo’s coming home for the weekend?

Honestly, this weather is dreadful. Just grey, relentless grey. Tarnow’s not exactly known for its sunshine, is it? Though, I suppose it’s a bit better than Cambridge has been recently. Everything’s damp, clinging. Makes you feel…oppressed, doesn't it? Aye, it's a bit miserable, innit? Proper Lancashire weather, though. Reminds me of home, in a way. Except at home, you can at least smell the countryside on a damp day. Here… it just smells…well, like Tarnow. Which isn't a bad smell, mind, just a...distinct one. Feel alright now, though? You were looking a bit peaky earlier. A bit. That cough's still lingering. Think it finally settled in my chest. Stupid Polish plumbing – I swear the dampness is the culprit. At least it’s something to distract me from… everything else. Going back to Bury, for Uncle George's funeral... ugh. It’s all a bit overwhelming. I know. It’s awful about your uncle. Bury'll be…well, it’ll be Bury. Loads of faces you haven’t seen in ages. And all the awkward small talk about the weather and when you’re coming back “for good.” Exactly! "Coming back for good." As if I have a choice. Or a place to come back to, really. This flat… it’s…fine. It’s somewhere. But it’s not  home , is it? Is anywhere, really, anymore? I keep scrolling through Instagram, seeing everyone's lives, all so perfectly curated. My cousin's posting pictures of her garden in Henley, looking all idyllic and…established. And all I feel is… adrift. Don't do that to yourself, love. Social media's a highlight reel, remember? No one’s posting pictures of their overflowing laundry basket or their existential dread. It’s all filtered sunshine and forced smiles. I catch myself doing it too. But you've got something they don't – you're living abroad! That's… adventurous. Adventurous? It feels more like… a prolonged gap year I can’t afford to end. I do enjoy the TEFL, though. The students are lovely. It's just... the security. The feeling of purpose. That’s what’s missing. I always fancied being a librarian, you know. Surrounded by books, quiet… I can see that. Something calm. You were always a reader. So, you ever considered online tutoring? You could do that from anywhere. And then… well, then you could really go anywhere.

Honestly, this Earl Grey is a bit weak, innit? You’d think a London pub could manage a decent cuppa. Still, beats the rain outside. How's the programming going, Liv? Still wrestling with those surveys? It's...a process. Less wrestling, more... gentle negotiation. The logic gates are proving particularly stubborn today. Actually, I think I finally cracked one of the particularly annoying data validation issues. Feels almost criminal to be celebrating over survey data, though. Criminal? Come on, that’s dedication. I’m currently battling a client who wants us to sell organic dog biscuits using the emotional power of sunsets. Sunsets! It's peak copywriting madness. I’ve suggested we focus on the fact that dogs  like  biscuits, but they’re not showering me with praise. Organic dog biscuits and sunsets. You’ve landed yourself in a right pickle, haven’t you? Still, at least it’s… creative. I'm mostly dealing with endless rows of numbers and dropdown menus. Do you want to grab something to eat while we're here? I'm famished. Their chips look alright. Chips sound amazing. I'm starving, actually. This copywriting gig is draining. All the ‘passion’ and ‘synergy’ talk just sucks the life out of you, you know? I skipped lunch completely today trying to convince them a golden retriever wouldn't understand a haiku. Trust me, I understand the draining part. All the ‘critical analysis’ and ‘theoretical frameworks’ they throw at us can be pretty exhausting. So, chips it is? What about a side of onion rings? Definitely onion rings! My treat. Don’t want you bankrupting yourself on student loans  and  supporting my bad copywriting choices. Speaking of which, have you heard from Chloe and Finn? They were supposed to meet us here, weren't they? I texted Chloe earlier. She said they were running late. Finn’s apparently had a mini-crisis trying to find matching socks. Typical. You know, I was thinking, maybe we should all get together next weekend to check out that new Korean place in Shoreditch? Ooh, that sounds lovely! Korean food always hits the spot. Although, knowing Chloe, it'll involve a twenty-minute debate about which kimchi is the most authentic. Remember that time she spent an hour arguing with the waiter in that tapas place in Barcelona? Oh god, how could I forget? She's relentless. But, it’s part of her charm, isn’t it?

Oh, honestly! What time is it? It feels like I just closed my eyes. Mmm… five minutes, Mummy! Five minutes 'til breakfast! Are we having pancakes? Five minutes… massively exaggerated, I suspect. It's more like seven-thirty. And pancakes… tempting, but maybe slightly ambitious for a Saturday. How about toast and jam? Less sugar rush, more manageable clean-up. Toast is boring! I want pancakes with sprinkles! Like a rainbow! Yeah! Rainbow sprinkles! And syrup! A  lot  of syrup! Alright, alright, little negotiators. We'll see. Breakfast is toast and jam for now, but we  might  be able to conjure up some sprinkles later. Now, what are we planning for today? I was thinking we could head to the park this afternoon. Can we practice my juggling? I almost got three beanbags up! I can do a handstand! A  really  good one! See? Okay, maybe not right now. I’ll bet. We’ll save the handstands and juggling for the park. Speaking of skills, I saw an advert for a “Neon Moon” event in Cambridge tonight. It’s a circus skills workshop with a light show. Ooh! A light show? Can we go, Mummy? Please? Circus skills! Like… tightrope walking? Are there tigers?! No tigers, thankfully. It’s more plate spinning, juggling, maybe a bit of aerial hoop. It looked really fun, and a good chance for you two to show off any skills you pick up at the park. I’d be a brilliant juggler! I just need to practice more. I'm going to be the best handstand-er  ever ! Wonderful ambitions! Now, let's get downstairs and I’ll make that toast. Oh! Something popped into my head. I was reading something the other day about Australian slang. Did you know they say "arvo" instead of afternoon? Arvo? What’s an arvo? It's just another word for afternoon, darling. Like, "See you this arvo!" Imagine saying that! It sounds so… bouncy! See you this arvo! That’s silly! It is a bit silly, isn't it? Reminds me of Uncle David's trip to Australia. He kept trying to use all the phrases he’d learned, even when it didn't quite fit. Did he say “G’day”? He  loved  saying “G’day!” He even tried to greet the postman with it once. The postman looked very confused. Now, come on, let's get some fuel in our bellies.

Honestly, David, this constant doom and gloom about the Conservatives. It’s exhausting. I know you feel strongly, but can’t we just enjoy the scenery for a bit? Cornwall was lovely, wasn't it? Lovely, yes, Eleanor, but backdrop beauty can’t erase the systemic failures, can it? Look at the state of the NHS. It’s crumbling, Eleanor. Crumbling! And they’re celebrating a tiny, minuscule improvement in waiting times. It’s like celebrating getting a flat tyre slightly less quickly fixed. Grandad, with all due respect, waiting times  have  come down a bit, haven't they? My mate Rhys had to wait ages for his knee scan last year. He said it was getting better this time. Rhys. Always Rhys. Bless him. But the underlying problem remains, Cai. Underfunding, mismanagement, the relentless pursuit of privatisation… it's a slow drip, drip, drip of destruction. You young people, you'll be picking up the pieces. Speaking of picking up pieces, I was just editing a manuscript for a local author about the history of tin mining in South Wales. Fascinating stuff, really. It made me think about how reliant Wales was on those industries, and how devastating the closures were. It's a bit like what’s happening with manufacturing now, isn't it? Precisely, Eleanor. Precisely. Industrial decline, ignored by Westminster. A neglect that echoes through the generations. My own grandfather, you know, he was a miner. Worked down the pits from the age of fourteen. Dangerous work, brutal conditions. And for what? So politicians could line their pockets while communities were decimated. I was reading something about that for my history module, actually. The sheer scale of the impact on communities. It’s hard to imagine now, isn’t it? Walking miles to and from the pit, the dust… It’s horrific. And the legacy of those closures – the poverty, the unemployment… it’s still being felt, isn't it? That’s why people are so angry, I think. They feel forgotten. Forgotten, dismissed. They see promises made and broken. They see decisions made in London, distant from their realities, impacting their lives in profound ways. Take the recent changes to agricultural subsidies, for example. Devastating for Welsh farmers. Yeah, I heard about that. Uncle Gareth was saying it's going to force a lot of smaller farms out of business. It’s not fair, is it?

Right, alright everyone. Settle down, settle down! We've got a lot to chat about, haven't we? Especially after that slightly chaotic afternoon. Honestly, trying to build a dragon out of cardboard boxes with two hyperactive five-year-olds… it's a skill in itself, isn't it? It was a  really  good dragon, Mummy! He breathed glitter! Can we build him a castle now? He needed wings. Bigger wings! And a tail that wiggled! He absolutely did, didn’t he? Excellent points, both of you. We’ll definitely need to add wings and a proper tail. Right, let's talk stories, then. I was thinking…remember we were talking about Helen Moss stories? The ones Mrs. Davies used to tell us in assembly? The one with the little girl who talked to squirrels! I liked that one! She made them acorn hats! The grumpy badger. He didn’t like acorn hats. He said they tickled. Exactly! Those were brilliant. Full of such lovely, quirky details. I was wondering if we could try and create our own Helen Moss-style story, you two. Something with a bit of magic, a slightly wonky character, and maybe a talking animal? Ooh! Can the animal be a unicorn? And it can fly! A sparkly unicorn! A penguin could talk. But he’d have to wear a tiny scarf. It’s cold for penguins. A sparkly unicorn  and  a penguin in a tiny scarf? Excellent! That’s a fantastic start. How about this…our sparkly unicorn, let’s call her Luna, is feeling a bit sad. She’s lost her sparkle. And she needs to go on a quest to find it again. And the penguin! What’s his name? Hmm… let’s call him Pip. Pip the Penguin. He’s a very wise penguin, even if he  does  constantly complain about the cold. So, Luna, the sparkly unicorn, is feeling sad, and Pip the Penguin says to her… what does Pip say, eh? Pip says… "Your sparkle is lost because you’re not helping anyone." Wow! That’s brilliant, darling. Really good. See? You’re storytellers already. So, Luna needs to help someone. But who? And what kind of help could a sparkly, but currently rather sad, unicorn offer? She could help a little lost bunny! He needs to find his mummy! A lost bunny! Perfect! And what could Luna do to help the bunny find his mummy?

Honestly, I still feel a bit weird about cultured meat. Like, lab-grown burger? It just… doesn't compute. Feels dystopian, doesn’t it? Dystopian? Nah, I think it's brilliant. Imagine, fewer animals suffering, a drastically reduced environmental impact… It’s potentially amazing. My postgraduate research touched on food sustainability, and it kept coming back to the fact that our current systems are completely unsustainable. Hunting is romanticised, but an abattoir is horrific. At least with cultured meat, you  could  theoretically control the welfare aspect, right? Romanticised is a good word. My dad used to go deer stalking. He’d come back all puffed up and say it was "connecting with nature," but… it was still taking a life. And lets be real, a lot of it ended up being venison sausages. Hardly a spiritual experience. This shmeat, as they call it, at least bypasses that whole bloody business. But is it  ethical  though? Like, what about the cells they need to grow it from? Are they taken ethically? And what about the energy consumption of the labs? It feels like just shifting the problem elsewhere. Plus, veganism is a perfectly viable alternative. Good points. It's definitely not a perfect solution, and those are legitimate concerns. There’s a lot of research still needed to ensure ethical sourcing of the cells and minimise the energy footprint. But the potential benefit, if tackled responsibly, is huge. And it isn’t necessarily replacing veganism; for people who are struggling to completely transition or just occasionally crave meat, it’s a halfway point. I’m still struggling with the ‘craving’ part. I feel like if I’m craving meat, it’s just a habit, a learned response. I've been mostly vegetarian for five years, and it’s genuinely not a thing anymore. Which reminds me, are you two still taking those B12 supplements? You sound like my doctor! Yes, I am. But I wish I didn't have to. It feels… unnatural. Like, why can’t I get everything I need from food? Because our modern diet, even a vegetarian one, often lacks certain nutrients. It's not unnatural, it's just pragmatic. Think of it like needing sunscreen in the summer, or getting a flu jab. It's preventative healthcare. Plus, those chewable ones taste surprisingly like strawberries. Strawberries and oppression. Did you see that documentary about how much land is used to grow strawberries globally, and how it disproportionately affects migrant workers?

Right, nearly ready. Smells alright, doesn’t it? Bit of a gamble with the chorizo, honestly. Never sure if it’ll overpower everything. Smells lovely, love. Just finishing up this email, dreadful thing about the budget cuts. Honestly, they’re trying to squeeze water from a stone. Reminds me of the time they tried to tell me we couldn’t afford new stationery... Stationery? Seriously, Dad? That’s your financial crisis story? I'm starving. Is that chorizo, Mum? I hope it’s not  too  spicy. Just a touch, sweetheart. Enough to give it a kick, but not set your mouth on fire. You've been glued to that phone all afternoon, haven't you? What are you looking at? Just… memes. And checking for New Year’s Eve gigs. There's this amazing DJ coming to London. Might be worth the trek. London on New Year's Eve? Sounds like a guaranteed nightmare. Packed tighter than sardines in a tin. Remember that New Year’s we went to Edinburgh? The crowds were insane! Oh god, don't remind me. I was worried we’d lose little Leo. He was only about three, wasn't he? Running around like a little whirlwind. Speaking of little whirlwinds, has anyone seen the cat? I’m pretty sure Jasper was eyeing my slippers earlier. He's probably hiding under the washing machine again. That’s his favourite spot. The noise doesn't seem to bother him one bit. I tried to tell Brenda from Accounts about it the other day; she said her cat  hated  the noise. Different cats, I suppose. Foreign cats even, she used to go on about how her Spanish cat was far more cultured. Honestly. Brenda and her cats. Always a conversation starter. You know, I was thinking, we really need to purge the garage. It’s a disaster zone. All those Christmas decorations from 2012… Do we  really  need them? Absolutely not. Just be prepared for Dad to fight you on that. He's got a sentimental attachment to every dusty bauble. Hey! I resent that. They’re memories! And some of those baubles were quite expensive, you know. Actually, speaking of things we should be throwing away, I've been meaning to get rid of that old DVD player. No one uses it anymore. It's just taking up space. Good call. We could probably make a few quid on eBay.

Honestly, you two. Butterfly forks. Really? I spent a fortune on proper silverware, and all you want are novelty forks shaped like insects. They’re cool, Mum. More interesting than boring old forks. And I saw one that looked like a dragonfly, not just butterflies. Dragonfly's way better. Butterflies are… predictable. Besides, O said he loves the idea of butterfly forks. O? Honestly, I don't even know where he gets these ideas. He's barely eaten anything tonight except those weird pickled onions. Right, two minutes silence. It’s for Remembrance, you know. It's incredibly important. Not just some arbitrary thing. I know, Mum. It's for people who... you know. Died. My Grandad went. He always used to tell us stories about the war. Really scary ones. He did. A very brave man. Well, let’s be respectful. Six o’clock precisely. Two minutes of complete silence. No phones, no fidgeting. Just remembering. So, about the butterfly forks… Can we at least  look  at some online? Just for fun? Oh, very well. But if we're buying them, they're coming out of your pocket money. And no, I’m not letting you use them for every meal. I’m saving up for a new Lego set anyway. Maybe I’ll just stick to spoons. Spoons are even  more  boring than normal forks! You're a pair. Speaking of saving up, O mentioned he’s trying to learn Russian. Why Russian, of all things? He wants to understand the lyrics to that one song, the really intense one. The one with the… the dark theme. It's about a bear, I think? And a sad violin. It's pretty epic. A sad violin and a bear? That's hardly a compelling reason to learn a notoriously difficult language! Although, I suppose it's admirable his interested in other cultures. Have you considered Spanish, darling? So much easier. And you could order  tapas  on holiday! Tapas are alright, but the Russian one is cooler. He says a lot of modern music borrows from Russian classical composers. He’s certainly pulling my leg. He’s spending all his time on TikTok, I suspect. Though, I must admit, I do like a bit of Tchaikovsky. Reminds me of my grandmother. She’d make us all sit through her record collection every Christmas. My birthday’s coming up in a couple of weeks.

Right then, holiday planning needs to actually  happen  this weekend. I’ve got a pile of GCSE English papers to mark looming, and if I don't sort this out now, we'll be spending August huddled on the sofa watching telly again. Can we go to Adventure Island, Mummy? Please? Like in the books! Adventure Island! Yes! Rollercoasters! Oh, you two are obsessed with that Adventure Island series, aren’t you? They are rather good, though. But Adventure Island is in Southend, love. A lovely day trip, absolutely, but not a whole holiday. Remember, we talked about somewhere with… you know… more space. But the books say it’s brilliant! And they have a pirate ship! And a big wheel! They do, darling, they do. But Cornwall, remember? We looked at those pictures! Beaches and pasties… and rock pools! Think about crabbing, building sandcastles, and paddling in the sea. Much bigger than Southend, and we can find a lovely little cottage. Cornwall? Isn’t it… far? A bit, yes. But that’s part of the adventure, isn't it? A proper family road trip! We can listen to audiobooks, play car games… I’ll even let you pick the music for a bit. Road trip! Road trip! Can I choose the snacks? Well, we need to be sensible about the snacks, don't we? Especially with your tummy, darling. Remember what happened last time we went overboard with the ice cream? I just wanted the pink one. I know, love. It’s just… we need to try and avoid anything with too much dairy and gluten this time. It's a pain, I know, but it’s not worth you feeling poorly the whole holiday. We'll pack plenty of crackers and fruit, and I'll research some good local shops that do gluten-free pasties. It'll be a challenge, but we'll have fun. Can we still have marshmallows? Possibly. Gluten-free marshmallows exist, apparently. We’ll see. Now, Cornwall… I was thinking Padstow. It’s got a lovely harbour, nice beaches nearby, and lots of things to explore. Or perhaps St Ives? Slightly more artsy, with the Tate gallery there. Have you seen anything about that V&A exhibition in St Ives? It's photographing the coastline. Sounds quite interesting. A gallery? That sounds boring. It might be! But it doesn’t have to be the  whole  holiday.

Ugh, Mr. Davies really set us up for failure with that history essay. Seriously, expecting us to analyse the social impact of the Enclosure Acts in 1500 words? Who even cares about that anymore? Tell me about it. I spent ages researching, and it all just felt… pointless. Like, knowing which fields were fenced off in the 14th century isn’t exactly going to help me get a job, is it? Mrs. Patel said it’s about ‘understanding historical context’, but I understood my brain cells slowly dying. Exactly! And he's marking us down for not citing obscure academic papers. Like, I'm in Sixth Form, not doing a PhD! Did you see Liam trying to argue with him after class? He was getting proper red in the face. Yeah, I saw. Liam always gets wound up. He's got a point though, doesn't he? Davies just seems to enjoy being difficult. Remember last year when he made us write a poem about the Magna Carta? Don't remind me! Mine rhymed 'King John' with 'lawn'. It was horrific. At least we can forget about that nonsense now. Have you heard anything else about Chloe’s party next weekend? Apparently, her dad’s letting her hire a bouncy castle. A bouncy castle! On her lawn. It’s going to be mental. Did you manage to get your bike fixed yet? I was thinking it’d be good to cycle over there. Nearly. Dad's been messing with it all evening. He says he's replaced the chain, but it still rattles like crazy. I’m hoping it’ll be sorted by Friday. If not, I’ll have to get the bus, which is a total drag. You should come over to mine before. My mum's making that chocolate cake she does. You know, the one you like. Seriously? You are a lifesaver! I need something to look forward to after that essay. By the way, did you hear about Marcus getting detention? Apparently, he threw a paper aeroplane in Mr. Henderson's class. No way! Marcus? He’s usually so quiet. What subject was it? Maths. Henderson was practically incandescent. Everyone reckons he’s just jealous Marcus is better at maths than him. Typical. These prefects are something else, aren't they? All puffed up and trying to enforce rules that nobody cares about. I saw Bethany prefecting near the bike racks earlier; she looked so smug.

Honestly, this road's a nightmare. Proper pot-holed, isn't it? Makes you bounce about like a bairn in a bouncy castle. You’d think they'd do summat about it. Sunderland's roads are bad enough, but this… this is just criminal. It's not ideal, no. Hertfordshire isn't exactly known for its pristine infrastructure. Though, to be fair, this stretch is a bit worse than most. We'll be off it soon. Are you alright? You sound… particularly disgruntled. Disgruntled? I'm practically vibrating wi' frustration! I was just thinking, you know, a good cycle path along here would be brilliant. Imagine, proper smooth tarmac, not dodging crumbling edges and rogue gravel. Could get a proper cycle in, instead of worrying about breaking me neck. A cycle path, yeah. That's a good idea. City council would have a field day with the planning permissions though, wouldn't they? This area’s surrounded by fields, got historic buildings… It's not like building a cycle path's a quick and easy thing. Remember that kerfuffle about the new cafe near your Mum's? Aye, don't remind me! Took 'em ages, didn't it? Still, we gotta try, haven't we? More folk cycling, less cars on the road… good for everyone. Speaking o' folk, did you catch any o' the cricket yesterday? England weren't having the best time, were they? Not really. I managed to catch the highlights. It wasn’t pretty. Stokes looked a bit off, didn’t he? Still, there's always next time. I was far more engrossed in trying to salvage a spreadsheet before we left. You know, consultant engineer stuff. Exciting, I know. Spreadsheets. Sounds thrilling. You could be out in the sunshine enjoying yourself! Like a proper lad on a bike. Speaking o' bikes, have you ever considered getting a proper touring bike? Like, one o' them ones with the panniers and everything? We could do a proper tour, you know, across the country. A touring bike? Panniers? That does sound rather… ambitious. My trusty road bike gets me around perfectly well. Though, I  have  been thinking about upgrading the tyres. These ones are starting to feel a bit worn. What sort were you thinking? Something more durable, maybe? Definitely! Something that can handle any terrain. I was looking at continental Grand Prix 4 Seasons. They're supposed to be really good, even in wet weather.

Honestly, this menu is a nightmare. So many options! And half of them are things I’ve never heard of. Just order the sweet and sour chicken, Liv. You always get it. Problem solved.
